channel.title: Jaryd's News
channel.description: Daily news digest — stories confirmed by multiple independent outlets, each with a Community Note and, where available, a verified YouTube news clip. Includes Joke of the day and Quote of the day on the homepage. Wire reprints count as one. Sources exclude BBC, CNN, CBC, and Radio-Canada. Viral on social highlights confirmed true videos circulating worldwide, plus select claim checks.

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Thursday, November 26, 2026 (evening edition)
item.description: Evening edition: Alberta’s $8.5-billion surplus; the NDP’s Charter challenge to the riding map; the 1Password breach; Ford and Unifor on tailpipe penalties; two Italians killed in Kuwait; U.K. net migration at 77,000; Altria eyes Imperial Brands; APR buys Dr. Melaxin; a Majorana qubit from Delft; New York’s AI toy ban; SeaWorld’s jump-roping toy soldiers; and Edmonton events.

item.title: Oil money turns Alberta’s forecast $9.4-billion deficit into an $8.5-billion surplus, and the fuel-tax break is extended to March
item.description: Finance Minister Jason Nixon released the second-quarter fiscal update Thursday. The province now expects an $8.5-billion surplus this year, about $18 billion better than the deficit in February’s budget and up from the $2-billion surplus it forecast in August (Edmonton Journal; The Globe and Mail; Government of Alberta).

item.title: Nenshi says the NDP will argue in court that Alberta’s new riding map breaks the Charter right to vote, with papers filed in the coming days
item.description: Nenshi said the challenge rests on two points: the unusual process, in which a government-led committee redrew the lines after rejecting the independent commission’s map, and a result he says doesn’t give voters effective representation (Canada’s National Observer; Edmonton Journal).

item.title: Hackers took names and email addresses from Toronto-based 1Password after breaking into an employee’s GitHub account, but not passwords
item.description: 1Password said it began investigating on Nov. 19 after spotting signs that an employee’s corporate GitHub account had been taken over. The attacker used it to push malicious code to backend servers and download some customer account records (TechCrunch; BleepingComputer).

item.title: Doug Ford and Unifor team up to ask Ottawa to waive tailpipe-emission penalties for carmakers that build in Canada
item.description: In a rare joint statement Thursday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford and Unifor president Lana Payne asked the federal government to exempt Canadian automakers from penalties under its passenger-vehicle greenhouse gas rules (The Globe and Mail; Government of Ontario).

item.title: Two Italian technicians are killed in Kuwait when drones are shot down over a “vital site,” and Iran denies sending them
item.description: Kuwait’s defence ministry said debris from drones it was intercepting struck a key facility, killing two Italians. A Kuwaiti and a Pakistani worker were also hurt (Al Jazeera; ANSA).

item.title: Net migration to the U.K. drops to 77,000, its lowest level since 1997 outside the pandemic
item.description: The Office for National Statistics estimates net migration was 77,000 in the year to June 2026, down from 204,000 a year earlier. About 738,000 people arrived and 661,000 left (ONS; The Guardian).

item.title: Marlboro maker Altria says it may make an all-cash bid for Imperial Brands, and Imperial’s shares jump as much as 17%
item.description: U.S. tobacco company Altria said Thursday it is considering a possible offer for Imperial Brands, the British maker of Winston, Davidoff and Gauloises cigarettes and Rizla papers. It said any offer would likely be all cash (Altria; Alliance News via Morningstar).

item.title: Medicube maker APR takes control of Korean skincare brand Dr. Melaxin, a TikTok Shop best-seller, for about US$265 million
item.description: South Korean beauty company APR said in a regulatory filing Thursday it will take 87.3% of Brand501, the company behind Dr. Melaxin, for about 390 billion won. That’s 320 billion won for existing shares and 70 billion won for new ones (Yonhap Infomax; Seoul Economic Daily).

item.title: Science corner: Delft physicists finally control a qubit made from Majorana particles, after 15 years of trying
item.description: Quantum computers are fragile: their bits, called qubits, lose information at the slightest disturbance. One long-sought fix is to store information in pairs of exotic “Majorana” states that sit apart from each other, so local noise can’t easily scramble them.

item.title: New York outlaws toys with built-in AI chatbots for five years, just as holiday shopping begins
item.description: Gov. Kathy Hochul signed a law banning the manufacture, distribution and sale of children’s toys with built-in AI chatbots, such as talking dolls, stuffed animals and robots, for five years (Governor of New York; NBC News).

item.title: Fans are picking favourites among SeaWorld’s jump-roping toy soldiers, and the joke “lore” videos were made by one of the soldiers
item.description: For two weeks, short videos about the masked toy-soldier jump-rope troupe at SeaWorld Orlando have filled people’s feeds. An AI narrator reads silly stats for each soldier, like Holidave, who can “jump rope while sitting down,” Jackery Jingleson, Big Chestnut and Sugarsnookie, as if they were pro athletes (WIRED).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Thursday, November 26, 2026 (morning edition)
item.description: Morning edition: Alberta’s riding maps clear final debate; Edmonton gets the 2028 Grey Cup; senators amend the lawful-access bill; Carney answers the Pentagon; a tanker fire on Cairo’s Ring Road; a flooded Indonesian gold mine; a Bangkok refinery blast; new U.S. overcapacity tariffs on 14 economies; Christie’s buys Dreweatts; a megawatt gallium oxide power module; FCC approves SpaceX’s Starmind satellites; a mayor’s bike-ramp mishap; and Edmonton events.

item.title: Alberta’s new riding maps clear their last debate, and the NDP says it will take them to court as soon as they become law
item.description: Bill 40, the Electoral Divisions Act, passed third reading in the legislature Wednesday. It still needs royal assent. The maps would grow the legislature from 87 seats to 91 before the 2027 election (The Canadian Press via Global News; MyParliament bill tracker).

item.title: Edmonton will host the Grey Cup again in 2028, its sixth time and first since 2018
item.description: The CFL announced Wednesday that the Edmonton Elks will host the 115th Grey Cup at Commonwealth Stadium (Play Alberta Field) on Sunday, Nov. 5, 2028 (CFL; Edmonton Elks).

item.title: Senators change Ottawa’s lawful-access bill to guard against forced security holes, but keep six months of metadata storage
item.description: Bill C-22 would make tech companies build in ways to preserve data and hand it to police and CSIS with a warrant, and would let the public safety minister order providers to keep user metadata, such as who contacted whom and when, for up to six months (The Globe and Mail; Tech Times).

item.title: Carney answers the Pentagon’s attack on Canada’s military: Trump “has not raised” it with him, and the U.S. warns of “mitigation measures”
item.description: Asked Wednesday before a Liberal caucus meeting, Carney said: “I can assure you that in my discussions with the president of the United States, we’re focused on conflict resolution around the world and he has not raised issues such as has been reported recently” (The Globe and Mail; The Epoch Times).

item.title: A fuel tanker overturns and burns on Cairo’s Ring Road, killing 31 people, and police hold the driver they say clipped it
item.description: The crash happened Wednesday on the Ring Road in Warraq, in Giza on Cairo’s western edge. Egypt’s prosecutors said 31 people were killed and 21 hurt, and the fire spread to about 30 vehicles, including cars, minibuses, taxis and motorcycles. Witnesses said most of the dead were in one minibus (Daily News Egypt; AFP; The Associated Press).

item.title: Sixteen miners are dead and 10 still missing after flooding traps 26 people in an illegal gold mine in Indonesia
item.description: Heavy rain flooded an unlicensed gold mine in Bogor regency, West Java, trapping 26 workers in shafts about 100 metres deep. By Thursday, rescuers had pulled out 16 bodies and were still searching for 10 people (The Associated Press via SBS News; CNBC Indonesia).

item.title: An explosion and fire at Bangkok’s Bangchak oil refinery injures at least seven and sends black smoke over the city
item.description: The blast was reported around 2:50 p.m. Thursday Bangkok time at Bangchak’s refinery on Sukhumvit Soi 62 in Phra Khanong. The company said the fire was out by 3:15 p.m. and the site was “fully under control” by 3:45 p.m. It shut down all production units (Bangkok Post).

item.title: Washington proposes new tariffs of mostly 15–20% on 14 economies it accuses of overbuilding factories, and Canada isn’t on the list
item.description: The U.S. Trade Representative released findings Wednesday from 14 investigations into what it calls “structural excess capacity” in manufacturing, and proposed tariffs for each economy (USTR; Reuters).

item.title: Christie’s buys Dreweatts, a 267-year-old English country auction house, betting on antiques again
item.description: Christie’s said Wednesday it is acquiring Dreweatts, founded in 1759 and based at Donnington Priory near Newbury, Berkshire. The price wasn’t disclosed (Christie’s; The Art Newspaper; Antiques Trade Gazette).

item.title: Science corner: a gallium oxide power switch from Hong Kong handles a megawatt in pulses, about 100 times more than earlier ones
item.description: Power semiconductors are the switches that control electricity in chargers, electric cars and the power grid. Most are silicon, which is close to its limits. Engineers at the University of Hong Kong, working with Virginia Tech and Nanjing University, built a module from six gallium oxide chips that repeatedly switched 1,000 volts and 1,000 amps a thousand times a second, a peak of one megawatt (HKU; Nature Communications).

item.title: U.S. regulators let SpaceX launch up to a million satellites meant to work as AI data centres in orbit
item.description: The Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday approved “Starmind,” SpaceX’s plan for up to one million low-orbit “orbital compute modules” powered by the sun (NPR; NBC News; Ars Technica).

item.title: A mayor in full chain of office opens a £6,200 bike ramp at an English railway station, gets his pedal stuck at the top, and 3.5 million people watch
item.description: Councillor Sam Corcoran, a regular cyclist, was asked to wheel his bike up the new channel on the stairs at Sandbach station in Cheshire and through a ribbon. At the top, his pedal caught on the railing (road.cc).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Wednesday, November 25, 2026 (evening edition)
item.description: Evening edition: a Law Society panel clears Kaycee Madu; Snow Valley delays its opening; Qatar becomes Canada’s protecting power in Afghanistan; Chip Wilson’s Calgary remarks; Colombian forces end a Cartagena supermarket siege; Hungary’s Magyar visits Ukraine; Expedia to acquire Kiwi.com; Dubai Islamic Bank to buy Emirates Islamic; Caltech’s BrainBots; Tidal bans fully AI music; Pinterest’s AI-content control for parents; a poodle rescued from a dump; a baby in the Australian Senate; and Edmonton events.

item.title: A Law Society appeal panel clears former justice minister Kaycee Madu over his call to Edmonton’s police chief after a traffic ticket
item.description: In 2021, then-justice minister Kaycee Madu got a $300 distracted-driving ticket in Edmonton and immediately phoned police chief Dale McFee. A Law Society of Alberta hearing committee later found him guilty of conduct deserving of sanction, reprimanded him and ordered him to pay nearly $39,000 in costs. A seven-member appeal panel set all of that aside in a decision released Tuesday (Calgary Herald, Global News).

item.title: Too warm to make snow: Snow Valley pushes back its opening and hopes to welcome skiers in early December
item.description: Edmonton’s Snow Valley ski hill usually opens in mid-November, but it doesn’t have enough snow yet and hasn’t set a new date. The hill relies on man-made snow, and its snowmaking equipment needs a long stretch of cold weather (Taproot Edmonton, CTV News Edmonton).

item.title: With no embassy in Kabul, Canada names Qatar its “protecting power” to help Canadians in trouble in Afghanistan
item.description: Canada and Qatar signed an investment protection agreement in Ottawa on Wednesday, and also agreed that Qatar will act for Canada on consular cases in Afghanistan. Canada closed its Kabul embassy when the Taliban took power in August 2021, and it lists the Taliban as a terrorist organization (The Canadian Press, Global Affairs Canada).

item.title: Lululemon founder Chip Wilson tells a Calgary women’s leadership forum that men may “import brides from Thailand,” and some of the audience walks out
item.description: Wilson was a featured speaker at the Leadership Forum in Calgary on Monday, run by Axis Connects, a group that works to advance women in leadership. According to people who were there, he said companies might hesitate to hire a 22-year-old woman because she could become pregnant, and that women waiting too long to have children was leading some men to bring in brides from Thailand (The Globe and Mail, The Guardian).

item.title: Colombian special forces storm a Cartagena supermarket after a 17-hour siege and free all the hostages
item.description: Masked gunmen took over an Éxito supermarket in Cartagena around 8 a.m. Tuesday, tying up customers and staff. Police later put the number of hostages at about 70, and AFP reported 76. Ten were let go during the day. Special forces broke in at about 1:30 a.m. Wednesday, set off stun grenades and freed everyone left inside (The Guardian, AFP, AP).

item.title: Hungary’s new prime minister makes his first official visit to Ukraine, and leaves with deals on gas, trains and corn
item.description: Péter Magyar, who defeated Viktor Orbán in April, met President Volodymyr Zelensky in Zakarpattia, the western region home to Ukraine’s Hungarian minority, on Monday. It was their first formal bilateral meeting, and Kyiv Post reports it was the first visit to Ukraine by a Hungarian prime minister since 2015 (Kyiv Independent, Kyiv Post).

item.title: Expedia will acquire Czech flight-booking site Kiwi.com, adding a fourth travel company to its recent shopping list
item.description: Expedia Group announced Wednesday it will buy Kiwi.com, a Brno-based online travel agency known for stitching flights from airlines that don’t partner into one itinerary. Neither company disclosed the price. The deal is expected to close in the first half of 2027 (Expedia Group, Skift, PhocusWire).

item.title: Dubai Islamic Bank agrees to buy rival Emirates Islamic in an all-share deal, creating the world’s second-largest listed Islamic bank
item.description: Dubai Islamic Bank (DIB) will buy all of Emirates Islamic from its parent, Emirates NBD, paying entirely in new DIB shares. The combined bank would hold about AED 585 billion (roughly US$159 billion) in assets, based on Sept. 30 figures (Dubai Islamic Bank, Reuters, The National).

item.title: Science corner: Caltech’s “BrainBots” use a flash of infrared light to push cancer drugs across the blood–brain barrier
item.description: The blood–brain barrier keeps most medicines out of the brain, which makes brain tumours very hard to treat. Wei Gao’s lab at Caltech built nanorobots about 250 nanometres across, shaped like lopsided balloons. Each one carries a drug and a pocket of gas-making fuel sealed behind a heat-sensitive gate (Caltech, Science Robotics).

item.title: Tidal will delete music made entirely by AI, after finding 43% of recent uploads were fully machine-made
item.description: Starting Dec. 9, the streaming service Tidal will remove every track it determines is 100% AI-generated and reject new ones. Songs made with help from AI tools are still allowed (Tidal, The Guardian, TechCrunch).

item.title: Pinterest lets parents turn down how much AI-generated content shows up in their teen’s feed
item.description: Pinterest has added a setting to its parental controls that lets parents set how much AI-generated content appears in a teen’s recommendations. TechCrunch says that makes it one of the first big social platforms to offer such a control (Pinterest, TechCrunch, The Verge).

item.title: A volunteer chases a lost poodle across a dump on a bicycle, posts the video on Facebook, and the owner arrives by taxi just before a storm
item.description: Adrián Contreras volunteers with a group that brings food and water to the dogs living at the dump in Trelew, Argentina. One day their van broke down, so he made his rounds by bicycle. Riding slowly, he spotted a small black poodle that clearly wasn’t one of the regular pack, running scared among the garbage (Diario Jornada, Los Andes).

item.title: An Australian senator gives a speech with her baby in her arms while the senator behind her plays peekaboo
item.description: Independent senator Fatima Payman of Western Australia spoke in the Senate while holding her six-month-old daughter, Aaliyah. Sitting right behind her, Senator Lidia Thorpe made faces and played peekaboo to keep the baby happy (NDTV, Hindustan Times, Al Jazeera).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Wednesday, November 25, 2026 (morning edition)
item.description: Morning edition: Alberta drops its two-flagpole rule for schools; a bill would end automatic inquiries into custody deaths; Macklem brings back CPIX; Squamish declares a flood emergency as king tides hit B.C.; China flies Pakistan’s first astronaut; Solomon Islands picks Australia over China; a U.S. jury convicts Huawei; a backwards peptide grabs rare earths; DeepMind’s Gemini teams find cheaper quantum programs; Nvidia shrinks Paradromics’ speech implant computers; the O Canada flub; Thomas the shelter dog; Seoul’s ginkgo-leaf hearts; and Edmonton events.

item.title: Alberta drops its order for a second flagpole at every school after boards warn it would cost millions
item.description: Education Minister Demetrios Nicolaides announced Tuesday that schools won’t have to install extra outdoor poles to fly both the Canadian and Alberta flags. A school with one pole will fly the Canadian flag outside and display the Alberta flag “prominently” indoors. Schools with two poles fly both outside, and schools with none hang both inside (Edmonton Journal, CityNews).

item.title: Deaths in Alberta jails and police custody would no longer automatically get a public inquiry under a new justice bill
item.description: Bill 44, tabled Monday by Justice Minister Mickey Amery, would end the rule that a judge-led fatality inquiry must be held whenever someone dies in prison or police custody. Inquiries would go ahead only where they “would best serve the public interest,” using criteria set later in regulation (The Globe and Mail, The Canadian Press).

item.title: Macklem admits the Bank of Canada was “too slow” on inflation and brings back an old yardstick, CPIX, to track prices
item.description: Speaking to the Economic Club of Canada in Toronto on Tuesday, Governor Tiff Macklem said the Bank is keeping its 2% inflation target through 2031, but changing how it reads price trends. CPIX, which leaves out eight volatile items like gasoline, mortgage interest and fruits and vegetables, returns as a key core measure alongside CPI-trim. CPI-median moves to a new public inflation dashboard (Bank of Canada, BNN Bloomberg/The Canadian Press, Canadian Mortgage Trends).

item.title: Squamish declares a local emergency and builds sandbag walls as king tides and storms threaten B.C.’s coast
item.description: Environment Canada says a run of king tides, the highest tides of the year, is lining up with storm surge and big waves. That could push water 20 to 50 cm above the highest normal tides, rising each day and peaking Thursday. Coastal flood warnings or statements cover Metro Vancouver, Vancouver Island, Haida Gwaii and the central, Sunshine and north coasts (The Globe and Mail/The Canadian Press, EmergencyInfoBC).

item.title: China flies its first foreign astronaut to space as Pakistan’s Muhammad Zeeshan Ali lifts off for the Tiangong station
item.description: A Long March 2F rocket launched Shenzhou-24 from Jiuquan at 8:18 a.m. Beijing time Wednesday (6:18 p.m. Tuesday in Edmonton). On board were commander Tang Hongbo, flight engineer Wu Yi and payload specialist Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, a former Pakistani military pilot and the first person from Pakistan to reach orbit (AP, Reuters, Space.com).

item.title: Solomon Islands signs a treaty making Australia its main security partner, and Chinese police are expected to leave by mid-2027
item.description: Prime Ministers Anthony Albanese and Matthew Wale signed the Australia–Solomon Islands Treaty in Canberra on Wednesday, days after Honiara said it would end its 2022 security pact with Beijing when it expires in April (The Guardian, AP, Reuters).

item.title: A U.S. jury convicts Huawei of stealing trade secrets and lying to banks about Iran, the case that began with Meng Wanzhou’s 2018 arrest in Vancouver
item.description: A federal jury in Brooklyn on Tuesday found Huawei and three subsidiaries guilty on 10 of 12 counts. They include conspiracy to steal trade secrets, bank and wire fraud, money laundering conspiracy and violating U.S. sanctions on Iran. Huawei was acquitted of the most serious charge, racketeering conspiracy, and of conspiracy to obstruct justice (The Guardian, NBC News, U.S. Justice Department).

item.title: Science corner: a peptide built backwards by mistake, then left in a freezer for years, grabs rare earth metals 10 times harder
item.description: Chemists at Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf were copying the metal-grabbing parts of lanmodulin, a bacterial protein that latches onto rare earth elements. By mistake they assembled their first short peptide in reverse order. They put it in a freezer and forgot about it (Interesting Engineering, HHU).

item.title: Google DeepMind’s Gemini teams find quantum programs up to 12 times cheaper for a fusion problem, and prove each one correct
item.description: Google DeepMind and Google Quantum AI set teams of Gemini 4 AI systems to work improving known quantum algorithms. Every four hours, the teams met at a “virtual conference” to trade and debate ideas. Each improvement had to be proved correct in Lean, a tool that checks math proofs, because the circuits are far too big to test on today’s machines (Google DeepMind, The Next Web).

item.title: A brain implant that speaks for a woman with motor neuron disease needs a cart of computers, and Nvidia aims to shrink it to a box on her wheelchair
item.description: Austin-based Paradromics announced Monday it will use Nvidia’s low-power Jetson modules and Holoscan software to decode brain signals into speech. Its Connexus implant has more than 400 electrodes and lets a Michigan woman named Mary, who struggles to speak because of motor neuron disease, talk through a synthesized voice (Wired, Business Wire).

item.title: A singer belts “we lend our hearts to thee” in O Canada, the Leafs tease “thou lend, thou win,” and then Canadians rally behind her
item.description: Former Broadway performer Sarrah Strimel Bentley sang both anthems before the Toronto Maple Leafs played the New York Islanders on Monday. In O Canada she twice sang “we lend our hearts to thee” instead of “we stand on guard for thee.” Fans posted clips of Auston Matthews looking puzzled, and after the Leafs won 4-2 to end a nine-game losing streak, the team posted “thou lend, thou win” (The Guardian, AP).

item.title: “Thomas the Death Row Dog” waits 160 days at an Oklahoma shelter, then a Facebook video finds him a family three hours before his deadline
item.description: Thomas, a two-year-old pit bull terrier, had been at the Owasso Animal Shelter near Tulsa since May. The shelter set a final deadline of 5 p.m. Monday, Nov. 23 (FOX23, News On 6).

item.title: A Seoul street sweeper turns fallen ginkgo leaves into a row of yellow hearts, some with smiley faces, and 170,000 people hit like
item.description: Near Jonggak Station in Seoul’s Jongno district, a sanitation worker in a fluorescent vest was filmed sweeping bright yellow ginkgo leaves into a line of hearts along the sidewalk instead of bagging them. Some of the hearts have smiling faces made of leaves inside (SBS, The Herald Business).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Tuesday, November 24, 2026 (evening edition)
item.description: Evening edition: Alberta uses its Sovereignty Act against Ottawa’s hate-crime law; RCMP apologize over Fiasal Hussein comments; MPs send the major projects bill back to the House; Regina’s buses roll again; Houthis 60 km from Aden; an air-raid alert on a South Korean island; Netflix buys the Radford studio lot; Cerberus buys Airbus’s U.S. satellite plant; KAIST’s drone-leg battery; GPT-6.2 designs binding proteins; the NHS starts its AI mammogram trial; the Thanksgiving grandma movie; the Georgia Tech couple explain; Miley’s yellow-dress guest; and Edmonton events.

item.title: Smith invokes the Sovereignty Act against Ottawa’s new hate-crime law, saying she doesn’t want “somebody’s pastor” jailed for a sermon
item.description: Premier Danielle Smith’s government said Tuesday it will table a motion under the Alberta Sovereignty Within a United Canada Act targeting the federal Combatting Hate Act, Bill C-9, which took effect in July. The motion was expected in the legislature Tuesday afternoon (Edmonton Journal, CTV News, The Canadian Press).

item.title: Alberta RCMP apologize for suggesting murdered 12-year-old Fiasal Hussein’s “choices” played a part in his death
item.description: In a statement Tuesday, Alberta RCMP commanding officer Trevor Daroux said police “regret that our words caused further hurt” to Fiasal Hussein’s family and friends. He was walking back a line from an Oct. 27 news conference, where a major crimes officer said “whatever challenges or choices may have led to his untimely death, he was still a child” (CityNews Edmonton, CTV News, Edmonton Journal).

item.title: After 100 hours of debate, MPs send the major projects bill back to the House, with one small new check on Ottawa’s power to end strikes
item.description: The special committee studying Bill C-39, the Building Canada Strong Act, voted Monday night to send it back to the House of Commons with a few amendments. Liberal MPs rejected the bigger changes that labour and environmental groups had asked for (The Globe and Mail, Politico).

item.title: Regina’s buses roll again Tuesday after the city and its transit union reach a tentative deal, ending a one-day lockout
item.description: Sunday night’s edition reported Regina would shut its whole bus system Monday over a union overtime ban. Late Monday, the city and Amalgamated Transit Union Local 588 reached a tentative three-year agreement, and the city said full service would resume Tuesday afternoon (Global News, 980 CJME, ATU).

item.title: Yemen’s army says Houthi fighters are about 60 km from Aden and “ready to attack,” and vows the government’s stronghold will hold
item.description: “Yes, Houthi forces are about 60 kilometres from the city. We take that seriously, and we are ready for it,” military spokesman Col. Majid al-Nuzaili told a briefing Tuesday. “Taking Aden is a hypothetical situation. It will not happen” (France 24/AFP, Reuters).

item.title: Residents of a South Korean island get an “EVACUATION, AIR RAID” alert as Russian warplanes fly toward it
item.description: At 7:52 a.m. Tuesday, Korea time, South Korea’s interior ministry told the roughly 8,700 people on Ulleungdo, an island 120 km off the east coast, to take shelter. Several Russian military aircraft had entered the country’s air defence identification zone and flown toward the island. The alert was lifted three minutes later (The Guardian, KBS World, SBS).

item.title: Netflix buys its first Los Angeles studio lot, the Radford Studio Center where Seinfeld was shot, for a reported US$380 million
item.description: Netflix said Tuesday it is buying the 55-acre Radford Studio Center in Studio City. Goldman Sachs took over the lot after its previous owner, Hackman Capital Partners, defaulted on a US$1.1-billion mortgage in January. The Los Angeles Times and The Hollywood Reporter put the price at US$380 million (Los Angeles Times, The Hollywood Reporter, Deadline).

item.title: Cerberus agrees to buy Airbus’s U.S. satellite factory in Florida as Airbus shifts its American arm toward military drones
item.description: Private equity firm Cerberus Capital Management said Tuesday it will buy the Space Systems business of Airbus U.S. Space & Defense, based in Merritt Island, Fla., next to the Kennedy Space Center. The roughly 200,000-square-foot plant was built to mass-produce satellites for the OneWeb broadband network. No price was disclosed, and the deal is expected to close by the end of the year (SpaceNews, Breaking Defense, FlightGlobal).

item.title: Science corner: KAIST builds a bendable battery that fits inside a drone’s hollow legs, so the frame can store power too
item.description: Most drones carry a battery pack as extra weight. A team led by Prof. Il-Kwon Oh at KAIST in South Korea, working with Sweden’s Chalmers University of Technology, wants the drone’s own frame to hold the energy. They grew tiny nickel cobalt selenide nanowires directly onto woven carbon cloth, making a flexible electrode for a lithium-sulfur battery (KAIST, Interesting Engineering, DongA Science).

item.title: OpenAI says a general chatbot model, GPT-6.2, designed proteins that actually stuck to their disease targets in lab tests
item.description: OpenAI reported Tuesday that GPT-6.2 designed small proteins meant to bind five targets linked to cancer and immune disorders, including PD-L1 and VEGF-A. When lab company Onava made and tested them, 35 of 322 designs bound their targets, about 11% (OpenAI, Nature, The Defiant).

item.title: The NHS starts enrolling women in the world’s biggest test of AI for reading mammograms, about 700,000 over three years
item.description: The first women have joined the EDITH trial at Cambridge University Hospitals. It’s the first of 30 U.K. screening sites, and about 700,000 women having routine mammograms are expected to take part over three years. The £10-million study is funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research and led by the universities of Warwick and Cambridge (NHS England, University of Cambridge, The Independent).

item.title: The wrong-number “Thanksgiving grandma” and the teen she invited anyway are getting a Lifetime movie, 10 years after their texts went viral
item.description: In 2016, Arizona grandmother Wanda Dench texted a Thanksgiving dinner invitation to the wrong number. It reached 17-year-old Jamal Hinton. “You not my grandma,” he replied. “Can I still get a plate tho?” She answered: “Of course you can. That’s what grandmas do … feed everyone” (The Guardian, USA Today).

item.title: Students Tallulah Wall and Braden Flournoy tell TODAY their televised stadium “argument” was “completely insignificant,” and the clip told friends they were dating
item.description: This morning’s edition covered the ESPN clip of an unnamed couple arguing, then kissing, at Saturday’s Georgia Tech game. On Tuesday the pair, students Tallulah Wall and Braden Flournoy, appeared on NBC’s TODAY and explained what happened (The Guardian, 11Alive, TODAY).

item.title: One wedding guest wears bright yellow at Miley Cyrus’s all-black wedding, 40 million people notice, and Miley tells her “You look gorgeous!”
item.description: Cyrus married musician Maxx Morando in Palm Springs, Calif., on Nov. 21. Leaked photos showed one guest in a mustard-yellow outfit in a sea of black. One video, set to Ashe’s “Stop the Wedding!”, joked: “Even Miley Cyrus couldn’t get everyone to follow the dress code. Brides, you’re going to be okay” (Entertainment Weekly, The Independent).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Tuesday, November 24, 2026 (morning edition)
item.description: Morning edition: three Calgary officers charged with manslaughter in Jon Wells’ death; Calgary’s 15% tax-hike budget hearing; the Pentagon’s fact sheet on Canada’s military readiness; Masar Badil listed as a terrorist group; emailed bomb threats at hundreds of German schools; Iran says three tankers hit mines in Hormuz; Sanofi buys Insmed; StarHub and M1 merge; Penn’s self-sensing artificial muscle; Meta’s Muse agent reaches the U.K.; ESPN’s “breakup” couple kisses; a Japanese lodge digs out of a snow wall; and Edmonton events.

item.title: Three Calgary police officers are charged with manslaughter in the 2024 death of Jon Wells, a Blood Tribe man pinned face down in a hotel lobby
item.description: Alberta’s police watchdog, ASIRT, said Monday that constables Roy Braun, Filip Poskovic and Vincent Washington were arrested and charged with manslaughter and assault causing bodily harm. They were released on undertakings and the case returns to the Alberta Court of Justice in Calgary on Jan. 6, 2027 (Calgary Herald, APTN News, CityNews).

item.title: Calgary opens a week-long budget hearing on a proposed 15% property tax hike, and one councillor asks staff to show what a 0% budget would cut
item.description: More than 260 Calgarians signed up to speak as city council’s public hearing on the 2027–30 budget began Monday. The plan calls for a 15% property tax increase in 2027, then 10%, 7.7% and 6% in the following years (Calgary Herald, Global News, City of Calgary).

item.title: The Pentagon publishes a “fact sheet” saying only 41.9% of Canada’s air force fleet was ready to fly and that Ottawa has no plan to reach NATO’s 5% target
item.description: The U.S. Defense Department posted the document online Monday after Axios first reported it on Sunday. It says just 41.9% of the Royal Canadian Air Force fleet was serviceable in 2025–26, 53.9% of the navy’s fleet, and that the army’s readiness rate was 48% (Axios, The Globe and Mail, AP).

item.title: Ottawa lists Masar Badil as a terrorist group, days before it planned to host a North American conference in Toronto
item.description: Public Safety Canada added Masar Badil, also called the Palestinian Alternative Revolutionary Path Movement, to the Criminal Code list of terrorist entities on Monday as an alias of Samidoun, which Canada listed in 2024. The government says the two share leaders, fundraising platforms and events (Public Safety Canada, Global News, National Post).

item.title: Hundreds of German schools get the same emailed bomb threat on Monday morning, and police say none of them was real
item.description: More than 400 schools in Baden-Württemberg and more than 250 in Saxony-Anhalt received word-for-word identical threats, with others hit in Thuringia, Lower Saxony and Hamburg, police said. Some schools evacuated as a precaution, but police said there was no concrete danger and advised schools to carry on as normal (DW, Euronews, Tagesschau).

item.title: Iran’s Guard says three oil tankers caught fire after hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz, even with U.S. jets escorting them
item.description: In a statement carried by Iranian state media late Monday, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps navy said three “violating” tankers hit naval mines, one near the southern coast and two in the eastern part of the strait, causing powerful explosions and fires. It said U.S. air cover and escort “failed to prevent” the blasts (CNBC, The Jerusalem Post, Iran International, Reuters).

item.title: Sanofi agrees to buy lung-drug maker Insmed for US$41 billion in cash, the drug industry’s biggest deal in three years
item.description: The French drugmaker will pay US$175 a share, 17.5% more than Insmed’s last close and 46% above its price before Bloomberg first reported talks on Nov. 19. It’s Sanofi’s biggest deal in about two decades and is expected to close in the first half of 2027 (Reuters, CNBC, Sanofi).

item.title: Singapore will go from four phone carriers to three as StarHub agrees to merge with M1 in an all-share deal
item.description: StarHub will issue about 651.7 million new shares to M1’s owners, giving them 27.4% of the combined company. Keppel, M1’s main owner, will end up with about 23% and a board seat. The companies put M1’s enterprise value at about S$1.4 billion and expect to close in the first half of 2027 (The Straits Times, CNA, Keppel).

item.title: Science corner: Penn’s new artificial muscle has a built-in copper coil that heats it and senses how far it has moved, so a robot finger can tap a piano key softly or hard
item.description: Engineers at the University of Pennsylvania wound an ultrathin copper coil inside a fibre made of liquid crystal elastomer, a rubbery material that contracts when heated, reinforced with graphene. They call it CoilLCE. The coil does two jobs: running current through it warms the fibre so it contracts, and its electrical resistance shows how much the fibre has moved (Penn Engineering, Popular Science, Interesting Engineering).

item.title: Meta brings Muse, its AI agent that can shop, book travel and send email for you, to the U.K., and regulators there say they’re watching
item.description: Meta launched Muse in the U.K. on Tuesday for users 18 and older, as an app on iOS and Android, on the web and inside WhatsApp. Users can connect it to email, calendars and shopping apps and give it jobs such as chasing a refund, renewing car insurance or buying Christmas gifts. It’s free, with optional paid plans (Meta, The Guardian).

item.title: ESPN cameras catch a couple in a tense argument at a Georgia Tech game, commentators narrate the “breakup,” then the pair are shown kissing
item.description: It happened Saturday as Wake Forest led Georgia Tech 50-22 late in the game in Atlanta. ESPN kept cutting to a young couple in the stands who appeared to be arguing, while analyst Jesse Palmer, the host of The Bachelor, called it like a dating show: “He wants an answer and he’s not leaving” (Entertainment Weekly, Newsweek, New York Post).

item.title: Staff at a Japanese mountain lodge open the front door to a wall of snow taller than the glass, then dig themselves out by hand at −12°C
item.description: Raichōsō, a hot-spring lodge about 2,370 metres up on the Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route in Japan’s Toyama Prefecture, posted the clip from 6:30 a.m. on Friday, Nov. 20. A worker in a blue snowsuit chips a tunnel through the drift from inside, crawls out, and colleagues join to flatten the wall (FTV News, The Weather Channel).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Monday, November 23, 2026 (evening edition)
item.description: Evening edition: Alberta’s voter-list crackdown and natural gas Crown bill, a Quebec court orders MNAs to swear the oath to the King, Bell’s “agentic” data breach, Puigdemont cleared to return to Spain, Democrats lock in 258 House seats, Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang, ABB buys Ziehl-Abegg, flash-made fast-charging graphite, Virginia and Oregon sue over Grok images, Z.ai’s GLM-5.4, Amazon signs its Decart deal, a golden retriever’s pool rescue, and Vegas at the Oilers Tuesday.

item.title: Alberta moves to keep its voter list away from parties without an MLA or a near-full slate, and to fine leakers up to $1 million, after data on 2.9 million voters spilled out
item.description: Justice Minister Mickey Amery tabled Bill 44 on Monday. To get a copy of the provincewide list of electors, a registered party would have to have elected at least one MLA in the last general election or byelection, or run candidates in at least half of Alberta’s ridings (Edmonton Journal, The Globe and Mail).

item.title: Alberta tables a law that would let it set up a Crown corporation to move natural gas if pipeline companies can’t keep up, and TC Energy warns it could raise costs
item.description: Energy Minister Brian Jean introduced Bill 45, the Natural Gas Infrastructure Act, on Monday. It doesn’t create a Crown corporation. It sets up the legal framework for one to transmit gas, and for a second body to plan the network, if the province decides industry can’t meet demand (Edmonton Journal, The Narwhal, The Globe and Mail).

item.title: A Quebec judge rules MNAs must swear allegiance to the King before they can sit, putting the Dec. 1 return of the legislature in doubt
item.description: Superior Court Justice Ian Demers on Monday suspended Quebec’s 2022 law that made the oath to the King optional. He granted an emergency order sought by lawyer Lawrence David and the Consumer Law Group, and warned that laws passed by members who haven’t taken the oath would be unconstitutional (The Canadian Press via Global News, The Globe and Mail, Le Devoir).

item.title: Bell says an “agentic” attacker got into an internal system last week and may have taken names, addresses and account details of Bell, Virgin Plus and Lucky Mobile customers
item.description: Bell says an unknown party got unauthorized access to an internal system on Nov. 17. Names, mailing addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, account numbers, business names and the date and amount of a customer’s last payment may have been exposed (Global News, BetaKit, The Globe and Mail).

item.title: Spain’s Supreme Court closes the last case against Carles Puigdemont, clearing the Catalan separatist leader to come home after nine years in exile
item.description: The court applied Spain’s amnesty law on Monday to the remaining embezzlement case over Catalonia’s 2017 independence referendum and declared his criminal liability extinguished. The ruling also covers former Catalan ministers Toni Comín and Lluís Puig (Reuters, RTVE, El País).

item.title: Democrats lock in at least 258 U.S. House seats, their biggest majority since 1992, after a recount flips Virginia Foxx’s North Carolina seat
item.description: Democrat Chuck Hubbard beat longtime Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina’s 5th District by a fraction of a percentage point after a recount Foxx requested. She conceded Sunday (NBC News, AP).

item.title: Nvidia’s board brings back Jensen Huang as CEO less than two weeks after he quit, and the stock jumps 31%
item.description: The board voted unanimously on Monday to reinstate Huang as president, CEO and director, effective immediately. It said it “received input from senior levels of the United States government” and is confident his return “poses no national security risk” (CNBC, AP, The Verge).

item.title: Swiss engineering giant ABB will buy German fan maker Ziehl-Abegg for US$2.65 billion to grab a bigger share of the cooling boom driven by data centres
item.description: ABB says it has signed a deal for the family-owned company at an enterprise value of US$2.65 billion, or an equity value of US$2.22 billion. Ziehl-Abegg makes high-efficiency fans and motors used in air conditioning, data centres, clean rooms, farms and elevators (ABB, Reuters, Cooling Post).

item.title: Science corner: a 0.2-second jolt of electricity turns cheap refinery leftovers into battery graphite that handled a four-minute charging rate in lab tests
item.description: James Tour’s lab at Rice University mixes petroleum coke, a low-cost leftover from oil refining, with a pinch of a nickel compound. One powerful electrical pulse heats it to about 2,500°C for two-tenths of a second, and the nickel helps the carbon snap into neat, stacked graphite layers (Rice News, Advanced Materials).

item.title: Virginia and Oregon sue SpaceX, saying its Grok image tool let users flood X with sexualized deepfakes, including of children
item.description: In separate lawsuits filed Monday under state consumer-protection laws, Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones and Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield accuse SpaceX, which merged with Grok maker xAI, and X of ignoring industry-standard safeguards and falsely telling users they were protected (The Verge, AP, Virginia Attorney General).

item.title: China’s Z.ai releases GLM-5.4, a 750-billion-parameter model that runs its own layers twice to reason more deeply without getting bigger
item.description: Z.ai, also known as Zhipu AI, released GLM-5.4 on Monday, its first flagship built as a “loop transformer.” It runs 28 layers of its GLM-5 base model a second time, adding depth without adding parameters (The Next Web, The New Stack, The Decoder).

item.title: Now signed: Decart’s three co-founders and research team will join Amazon, which is also taking over the startup’s chip-tuning software in a deal reported at US$7.5 billion
item.description: Saturday evening’s edition reported Amazon was nearing a deal. On Monday Amazon announced a signed agreement to buy the technology behind the Decart Optimization Stack and bring over co-founders Dean Leitersdorf, Moshe Shalev and Orian Leitersdorf with their team of researchers and engineers (Amazon, TechCrunch, CNBC).

item.title: A young golden retriever named Tereza jumps into a pool and keeps a struggling two-year-old afloat until her mom reaches her, and a security camera catches it all
item.description: It happened Friday in Chapada dos Guimarães, about 65 km from Cuiabá in Brazil’s Mato Grosso state, at the home of the girl’s aunt, who owns Tereza. The video shows little Maitê walking down the pool steps alone, then slipping under. Tereza jumps in, Maitê grabs hold of her and stays partly above water until her mother and older sister rush in (g1, Daily Mail).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Monday, November 23, 2026 (morning edition)
item.description: Morning edition: Smith plans a proof-of-citizenship voting law, Rocky Mountain Icehouse closes, daily cannabis now tops daily drinking for Canadians under 50, Ottawa starts hiring wrongful-conviction commissioners, Ukraine sinks Russia’s Merkury in Libya, Armenia’s peace constitution, Bangladesh vows to arrest Hasina, CrowdStrike buys Zscaler, Tata Steel’s APL Apollo bet, superconducting memory, OpenAI’s shared AI limits, OpenRouter’s prompt-theft purge, Durov’s GTA VI joke, and Vegas at the Oilers Tuesday.

item.title: Smith tells UCP members to “get their papers in order”: a law making voters prove citizenship is likely coming in the spring
item.description: At a virtual town hall for United Conservative Party members on Saturday, Premier Danielle Smith said her government will “probably” act in the spring sitting of the legislature on October’s referendum question about proof of citizenship. Voters in the Oct. 18, 2027, provincial election would need a passport, a birth certificate or one of Alberta’s new driver’s licences that can show a citizenship marker (The Canadian Press, via The Globe and Mail and CityNews).

item.title: Rocky Mountain Icehouse pours its last drink on Jasper Avenue after 12 years, blaming rising costs and downtown’s struggles
item.description: The downtown Edmonton bar and restaurant at 10516 Jasper Ave. closed for good on Sunday, Nov. 22. It opened in 2014 and announced the closure late Friday on Facebook (Daily Hive, CTV News).

item.title: More Canadians under 50 now use cannabis every day than drink alcohol every day, a new CMAJ study finds
item.description: The study, published today in the Canadian Medical Association Journal , used answers from almost 100,000 people in Statistics Canada’s 2023–24 Canadian Community Health Survey. It estimates about 1.8 million Canadians, or 5.7% of adults, use cannabis daily or almost daily, compared with 5.2% for alcohol (CMAJ, EurekAlert).

item.title: Ottawa starts hiring the commissioners who will review possible wrongful convictions, almost two years after the law passed
item.description: Justice Minister Sean Fraser announced Monday that the federal government is recruiting a chief commissioner and four to eight commissioners for the new Miscarriage of Justice Review Commission. Each will serve up to seven years (APTN News, The Canadian Press via CityNews).

item.title: Ukraine says seven sea drones sank Russia’s newest corvette, the Merkury, while it was docked in Libya
item.description: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday that Ukrainian forces carried out Sunday’s attack at the naval base in Benghazi, in eastern Libya. He said seven Ukrainian-made sea drones sank the Merkury and destroyed a Ka-27 helicopter on board, and that a second Russian ship, the cargo vessel MV Angara, was also hit (AP, ABC News, The Guardian).

item.title: Armenia publishes a new draft constitution that drops a key line Azerbaijan objects to, and Pashinyan says he’ll resign if voters reject it
item.description: The draft, posted online Monday for public comment, removes the current constitution’s reference to Armenia’s 1990 Declaration of Independence. That declaration cites a resolution on “reunification” with Nagorno-Karabakh, and Azerbaijan says the line amounts to a territorial claim. Dropping it is one of Baku’s conditions for signing a peace treaty (Meduza, Türkiye Today).

item.title: Bangladesh says it will arrest Sheikh Hasina the moment she comes home, as the ousted leader insists she’ll return from India in December
item.description: State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam told Reuters on Monday that Hasina would be arrested and jailed if she returns. Dhaka wants India to send her back under the two countries’ extradition treaty instead (Reuters).

item.title: CrowdStrike agrees to buy Zscaler for about US$43.9 billion in stock, one of the biggest cybersecurity deals ever
item.description: Zscaler shareholders will get 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for each share they own, worth about US$260.41, a 34% premium over Friday’s close. CrowdStrike shareholders will own about 84% of the combined company (CrowdStrike, CNBC).

item.title: Tata Steel will pay US$1.67 billion for a quarter of India’s biggest steel-pipe maker, and both companies’ shares tumble
item.description: Tata Steel said Monday it will buy a 26.4% stake in APL Apollo Tubes from its founders for 155.1 billion rupees, or 2,100 rupees a share. It will then offer to buy another 26% from other shareholders at 2,301.40 rupees, which would give it control with 52.38% (CNBC, Tata Steel, Moneycontrol).

item.title: Science corner: a superconductor sandwiched between two magnets becomes a memory cell that holds its bit with no power, a step toward super-cold computers that waste far less energy
item.description: Researchers at MIT’s Plasma Science and Fusion Center layered an ultrathin superconducting film between two magnetic layers. When the magnets point in opposite directions, current flows with no resistance. When they point the same way, the film resists. That difference is read as a 0 or a 1 (MIT News, Physical Review Letters ).

item.title: OpenAI’s chief scientist asks every AI lab to agree on a shared “speed limit” for their most powerful models, and Altman backs him
item.description: In an essay called “Perplexity and Intelligence,” published Sunday, OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki proposed that labs measure progress with perplexity, a score of how well a model predicts the next piece of text, where lower is better. Labs would then agree not to pass set limits until tools to understand and monitor AI behaviour reach concrete milestones (OpenAI, TechCrunch).

item.title: OpenRouter drops three AI hosting companies after researchers prove attackers were quietly copying customers’ prompts for months
item.description: The security firm Dragos sent about two million test prompts to AI services from July to November, each carrying a unique fake web link or cloud password. When someone used one, it proved they had read the prompt. Attackers were caught inside three hosting providers, the earliest since mid-July, and none of the three knew (Dragos research reported by The Hacker News and The Next Web).

item.title: Telegram’s founder jokes that the least realistic thing in GTA VI is a crime crew with no Telegram group, and Elon Musk replies 😂
item.description: Telegram founder Pavel Durov posted on X on Sunday: “The least realistic thing about GTA VI is that Jason and Lucia run a whole criminal operation without a single Telegram group.” Jason and Lucia are the game’s two main characters (India Today, Hindustan Times, Moneycontrol).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Sunday, November 22, 2026 (evening edition)
item.description: Evening edition: a judge empties Edmonton’s heatless Stadium Plaza, Regina parks its buses, Becky Druhan makes N.S. Liberal history, a deadly strike on a Dymer apartment block, 24 body bags from Indonesia’s candy-factory fire, a Bombardier strike vote, Wildberries’ CEO exits after EU sanctions, gel-free wearable ultrasound, South Korea’s minister quits over AI cheating rules, Signal blocks AI screen-readers, a sworn-in therapy puppy, a generous Vietnamese teacher, a car that tried to park 868 times, and the Oilers in St. Louis tonight.

item.title: A judge empties Edmonton’s Stadium Plaza apartments, a three-year-old building with no heat after thieves stripped its copper pipes
item.description: Tenants of Stadium Plaza, a 78-unit, six-storey apartment block on 86 Street near Commonwealth Stadium, were moving out on Friday after Court of King’s Bench Justice Michael Lema released them from their leases and ordered them out by noon on Nov. 20. Lema called it a “state-of-chaos apartment building” (Global News, Edmonton Journal).

item.title: Regina shuts down its entire bus system from Monday morning, saying a union overtime ban leaves it unable to run safely
item.description: All regular Regina Transit routes are out of service as of Monday, Nov. 23, the City of Regina says, citing “an operational safety directive.” Paratransit keeps running (City of Regina, 980 CJME, SaskToday).

item.title: Becky Druhan, who left Tim Houston’s cabinet last year, becomes the first woman to lead Nova Scotia’s Liberals
item.description: Former Progressive Conservative education and justice minister Becky Druhan won the Nova Scotia Liberal leadership Saturday at a convention in Halifax. She beat Cape Breton municipal councillor Amanda Mombourquette with 1,915 of 2,869 ballots, or 68% of points under the party’s weighted system (Global News, CTV News Atlantic, 98.9 XFM).

item.title: Part of an apartment block in Dymer, north of Kyiv, collapses in an overnight attack, killing at least five, as a boy is pulled out alive after about 14 hours
item.description: A Russian Shahed drone hit a five-storey apartment building in Dymer, about 45 kilometres north of Kyiv, early on Sunday, collapsing part of it. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy first said 14 people were missing and nine had been evacuated. Through the day, rescuers recovered bodies and officials raised the death toll to at least five, with several more people still feared under the rubble (RFE/RL, Ukrainska Pravda, UNN).

item.title: Rescuers carry 24 body bags out of the burned candy factory near Jakarta, and police say families must give DNA to identify the dead
item.description: Search teams had removed 24 body bags from the burned PT Fonusa Agung Mulia candy factory in Cikande, Serang regency, by 5 p.m. Sunday local time, Serang’s regent said. That was up from seven earlier in the day. Officials still confirm only three deaths, because remains have to be identified before the toll is updated (Jakarta Globe, AP, The Nightly).

item.title: About 2,400 Bombardier workers in Montreal and Dorval reject the company’s “final” offer by 97.5% and vote to allow a strike
item.description: Members of the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers Local 712 at Bombardier rejected the company’s final contract offer by 97.5% on Sunday, then voted 97.8% for a strike mandate at the Palais des congrès in Montreal, the union said (The Canadian Press, Montreal Gazette).

item.title: Tatyana Kim, Russia’s richest woman, steps down as head of the online giant Wildberries days after the EU sanctions her
item.description: Tatyana Kim has left her post as chief executive of Wildberries, Russia’s largest online retailer, Russian media reported on Saturday, citing the company register. Alexei Kulikov replaces her. The EU added Kim to its Russia sanctions list on Nov. 16, freezing any assets she has in the bloc and banning her from travelling there (The Moscow Times, DW, Der Spiegel).

item.title: Science corner: MIT’s dry, rubbery skin layer lets a wearable ultrasound patch image the body for nine days with no gooey gel
item.description: Ultrasound scans usually need a cold, wet gel to carry sound waves from the probe into the body. Engineers at MIT and the Singapore-MIT Alliance for Research and Technology have made a dry, stretchy “bottlebrush” elastomer that does the same job, and they report it this week in the journal Science (MIT News, Science).

item.title: South Korea’s education minister resigns after last-minute rules against AI cheating threw the national university exam into confusion
item.description: Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin stepped down Sunday, and President Lee Jae Myung accepted his resignation within about an hour. Choi said changes made just before the Suneung, the college entrance exam held Thursday, caused “inconvenience” to test takers (Yonhap, The Korea Times, The Guardian).

item.title: Signal starts blocking screenshots on phones to keep Siri, Gemini and other AI assistants from reading your chats
item.description: The encrypted messaging app Signal is now restricting screenshots on iOS 27 and on Android versions where it can detect an AI assistant trying to read the screen. The aim is to stop features like Apple’s Siri and Google’s Gemini from capturing private messages while they do tasks for users (The Verge, BleepingComputer, Reuters).

item.title: A 12-week-old golden retriever is sworn in as a Colorado police therapy dog, snacking through his oath: “so help me dog”
item.description: The Fountain Police Department in Fountain, Colorado, swore in Houston Rocket, a 12-week-old golden retriever puppy, as a therapy dog for the Fountain-Fort Carson School District 8. In the video, an officer holds up his paw for the oath while he digs into a bag of treats. The oath ends: “Paw by paw, heart by heart, I swear to make a difference, so help me dog” (Parade, ABC News).

item.title: A Vietnamese teacher turns down Teachers’ Day gifts and asks for help for an orphaned student instead, and her Facebook post raises 140 million dong
item.description: Ahead of Vietnam’s Teachers’ Day on Nov. 20, math teacher Nguyen Huong Giang of Ly Nam De High School in Thai Nguyen province posted on Facebook asking parents and students not to give her flowers or presents. She wrote, with some humour, that her small family couldn’t finish fruit baskets and already had enough cosmetics and clothes. She asked them to help a boy in her Grade 12 class whose mother had died, giving only what they could and with “no pressure” (Dan Tri, VietNamNet).

item.title: An empty electric car in China tries to park itself 868 times in one night, and the garage camera catches it all
item.description: Security-camera video from an underground garage in China’s Anhui province shows an electric car with nobody inside pulling into a spot, adjusting, reversing and trying again, over and over, at about 3 a.m. A guard went to check after hearing the noise. The owner later said the car’s data showed its automatic parking had switched on 868 times overnight (Times Now, NDTV).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Sunday, November 22, 2026 (morning edition)
item.description: Morning edition: Edmonton’s budget debate opens with 264 speakers, Alberta’s ER and surgery waits worsen, Canada joins NATO’s Innovation Fund, Cavalry FC’s historic CPL double, a deadly candy-factory fire in Indonesia, Belgium’s strike grounds Monday flights, Eisenkot invites Likud to talks, COP31 ends with no deal, MPS calls Intesa’s bid fair, Wacom’s buyout, a microneedle heart-damage patch, Inkling 2 Mini, the Riemann proof certified, Singapore schoolboys’ thank-you lunch, and the Oilers in St. Louis tonight.

item.title: Edmonton council opens up to 10 days of budget debate Monday, with 264 people signed up to speak on a plan for 4.9% higher property taxes
item.description: Edmonton city council starts deliberating its 2027–2030 budget on Monday, Nov. 23, beginning with a public hearing. As of Friday, 264 people had registered to speak. Meetings are booked for Nov. 23 and 24, then Dec. 3, 4, 10, 11, 14, 15, 16 and 18 if council needs them, after which councillors will move and vote on spending changes (Edmonton Journal, City of Edmonton).

item.title: Two reports find Alberta’s waits getting worse, with Edmonton hospitals’ ER stays the province’s longest and surgery waits up to 50 weeks, and Smith says “we have to try new things”
item.description: A Montreal Economic Institute report says the median emergency-room stay in Alberta was four hours last year, 36 minutes longer than five years ago. Edmonton had the longest waits: a median of nine hours at the University of Alberta Hospital, 8 hours 36 minutes at the Misericordia and eight hours at the Royal Alexandra. Calgary’s longest was Foothills, at 7 hours 19 minutes (MEI, CityNews Calgary, Calgary Herald).

item.title: Canada becomes the first North American member of NATO’s Innovation Fund, putting in about $100 million to back defence startups
item.description: Defence Minister David McGuinty announced at the Halifax International Security Forum on Saturday that Canada has joined the NATO Innovation Fund as its 25th member and its first in North America, committing €64.59 million, about C$100 million. The Business Development Bank of Canada will manage the stake (Department of National Defence, BDC, The Globe and Mail).

item.title: Calgary’s Cavalry FC beat Atlético Ottawa 3-2 to win the CPL final, the first club ever to take both the league title and the championship in one season
item.description: Tobias Warschewski scored twice and set up Sergio Camargo as Cavalry beat Atlético Ottawa 3-2 in Saturday’s Canadian Premier League final at ATCO Field in Calgary. Ottawa scored twice, but Cavalry held on to lift the North Star Cup (CPL, TSN, Sportsnet).

item.title: A fire tears through a candy factory west of Jakarta, killing at least three, and rescuers are searching for 36 missing workers
item.description: The blaze broke out Saturday afternoon at the PT Fonusa Agung Mulia confectionery plant in Cikande, Serang district, Banten province, about 50 kilometres from Jakarta. Banten’s governor said about 60 people were inside. On Sunday a search-and-rescue official said three were dead, 36 still missing and four injured; fires were still burning in parts of the building, which partly collapsed (AP, CNA/Reuters, The Guardian).

item.title: Belgium’s national walkout on Monday will ground every flight at Brussels and Charleroi airports, as air traffic controllers join protests against spending cuts
item.description: Belgian air traffic control agency skeyes says it won’t have enough staff to run normal service from 7 a.m. to 9 p.m. local time Monday, Nov. 23, because some controllers are joining a nationwide union walkout. Brussels Airport says all arrivals and departures in that window are cancelled, and Charleroi says no planes will take off or land (Politico Europe, Le Soir, Aviation24.be).

item.title: Gadi Eisenkot invites Netanyahu’s Likud to “marathon” coalition talks starting today, as Likud demands Netanyahu stay prime minister
item.description: Former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, who has the mandate to form Israel’s next government after October’s inconclusive election, told his Yashar party’s negotiators to invite Likud to a “marathon series of talks” beginning Sunday, to “pursue every option for forming a new government” (ABC Australia/AFP, The Times of Israel, Ynet).

item.title: COP31 ends without a deal: the EU and others reject the “Antalya Pact” over its silence on fossil fuels, the first such collapse since Copenhagen in 2009
item.description: At Sunday’s closing session in Antalya, Turkey’s COP31 president, Murat Kurum, told delegates: “We recognize that there is no consensus on this document. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted.” The final draft from co-hosts Turkey and Australia had dropped any direct mention of fossil fuels after objections from Saudi Arabia and other producers (Reuters via Rappler, Al Jazeera/AP).

item.title: Monte dei Paschi’s board calls Intesa Sanpaolo’s €34.5-billion bid “financially fair,” as director Corrado Passera quits in protest before the offer opens Tuesday
item.description: Italy’s Monte dei Paschi di Siena (MPS) said Saturday its board unanimously judged Intesa Sanpaolo’s sweetened cash-and-share offer fair as of Nov. 18, based on its advisers’ opinions, but said it doesn’t fully capture the value MPS expects from its takeover of Mediobanca, and that MPS investors would get too small a share of the gains Intesa expects (Reuters via AOL, Il Sole 24 Ore, Banca MPS).

item.title: Wacom, the maker of the digital pens and drawing tablets used by artists, agrees to a ¥136.6-billion buyout led by MBK Partners at a 50% premium
item.description: Private equity firm MBK Partners plans to take Wacom private in a management buyout at ¥1,030 a share, 49.9% above Thursday’s close, the companies said Friday. Chief executive Nobutaka Ide and Samsung Electronics will reinvest, and activist Asset Value Investors and Kaname Capital, holding about 20% and 5%, have agreed to sell (Nikkei, Japan Exchange Group, M&A News).

item.title: Science corner: a McMaster microneedle patch tracks a heart-damage protein for days without a single blood draw
item.description: Most heart injuries after ordinary surgery are silent, so the only way to catch them is a troponin blood test, hard to do once a patient goes home. Engineers at McMaster University, with the University of Waterloo, built a wearable patch whose painless polymer microneedles reach just under the skin, sip the fluid between cells and pass it to a sensor that reads cardiac troponin continuously over several days (McMaster News, Science Advances).

item.title: Thinking Machines releases Inkling 2 Mini, a free open model that “thinks in loops” and runs on a 32 GB laptop
item.description: Mira Murati’s Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Mini on Nov. 20 under the permissive Apache 2.0 licence. It is a mixture-of-experts model with 26.4 billion parameters that handles text and images and has a one-million-token context window. Its trick is “looping”: 12 of its 24 layers run three times for every token, so it can reason longer internally without writing out more words (The Decoder, Hugging Face, Thinking Machines).

item.title: Lean and Mathlib groups certify the Claude-assisted Riemann hypothesis proof as correct after a day of independent checks
item.description: On Saturday the Lean and Mathlib communities, backed by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative, issued a joint statement saying they have “full confidence” that Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge’s proof is correct. They say the 17-million-line Lean library compiles for dozens of people, proves exactly Mathlib’s vetted statement of the hypothesis, and passed several independent proof checkers, two of which are themselves formally proven unable to accept a false proof (Lean community blog, The Guardian, The Decoder).

item.title: Eight Singapore schoolboys pool $159 to buy fried chicken for the migrant workers building their subway line, and the transit agency says it “warmed our hearts”
item.description: In a TikTok video posted Nov. 17, eight boys in Townsville Primary School uniforms carry five boxes of Wingstop chicken to a Cross Island Line construction site in Ang Mo Kio. They peer through the fence until a worker opens the gate, then shake hands with each worker. “Thank you for building Singapore!” one shouts (AsiaOne, Lianhe Zaobao, 8days).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Saturday, November 21, 2026 (evening edition)
item.description: Evening edition: Edmonton’s 2026 living wage and Banff’s first, Smith promises bike-lane bill amendments, a secret Hegseth memo on Canada defence ties, Navdeep Bains wins the Ontario Liberal leadership, drones hit a Russian cargo ship off Finland, Mexico captures “El Chapo Isidro,” COP31’s second night of overtime, Stellantis keeps talking on Brampton, cacti as living solar panels, killer-robot talks pushed to 2028, Amazon nears a Decart deal, a pizza shop’s meal wall and an unlikely neighbour friendship, and the Oilers in St. Louis on Sunday.

item.title: Edmonton’s living wage is now $22.65 an hour, and Banff, measured for the first time, tops Alberta at $27.45
item.description: The Alberta Living Wage Network’s 2026 rates cover 20 communities, and every one is above Alberta’s $15 minimum wage, unchanged since 2018. Edmonton’s rate rose 1.6% to $22.65, Calgary’s 1.5% to $26.90 and St. Albert’s 6.3% to $27.20, while Spruce Grove’s fell 4.2% to $22.70. Nine communities went up and 10 went down, as rents, costs and government benefits shifted (Alberta Living Wage Network, Rocky Mountain Outlook).

item.title: Two days after tabling it, Smith says her government will amend the bike-lane bill, after Calgary’s mayor says cities were promised they wouldn’t pay for removals
item.description: Speaking on her Saturday radio show, Premier Danielle Smith said her chief of staff met Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas this week and that his concerns were “legitimate.” “We’ve got some amendments to propose to that,” she said. “We want it to be collaborative.” She did not say what would change, and Transportation Minister Devin Dreeshen’s office gave no details (Calgary Herald, CityNews Edmonton).

item.title: A secret Hegseth memo limits Pentagon contact with Canada’s military, while Canadian officials say they’ve seen no change
item.description: The Washington Post reported Friday that U.S. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth signed a classified memo last week restricting parts of the U.S.-Canada defence relationship. At the Halifax International Security Forum on Saturday, Republican Sen. Mike Rounds confirmed it exists, saying it limits meetings between generals and admirals to those that advance U.S. defence goals and requires U.S. defence officials to get permission before attending social events or think-tank conferences (The Washington Post, AP, Reuters).

item.title: Navdeep Bains wins the Ontario Liberal leadership by less than a point, on the third ballot
item.description: The former federal innovation minister took 50.3% on the final ballot, just ahead of MPP and former hospital president Lee Fairclough, after a months-long race in which about 55,000 members were eligible to vote by ranked ballot. Stephanie Bowman and Dylan Marando were also in the race (The Canadian Press, The Globe and Mail, Ontario Liberal Party).

item.title: Drones set a sanctioned Russian cargo ship on fire in the Gulf of Finland, and Finland says Ukraine is likely behind it
item.description: The Sparta II, bound from St. Petersburg for Kaliningrad, was hit Saturday morning west of Suursaari island in international waters, then lost steering and drifted into Finnish territorial waters near Loviisa. Its 16 crew got away in lifeboats with no reported injuries. “It is likely that Ukraine… is behind” the attack, a Finnish armed forces spokesperson said; Ukraine has not claimed it (Reuters, ERR, Kyiv Independent).

item.title: Mexico captures “El Chapo Isidro,” one of the FBI’s 10 most wanted, in a firefight that leaves 11 dead in Sinaloa
item.description: Soldiers and National Guard troops arrested Fausto Isidro Meza Flores in Guasave on Friday night, using intelligence from the United States. Mexico’s defence cabinet said seven suspected gunmen and four soldiers were killed in a battle that ran into the early morning, and seven others were arrested with him (AP, Euronews, Reforma).

item.title: COP31 runs into a second night with no new text, as about 130 countries weigh forcing Saudi Arabia to oppose fossil-fuel language in the open
item.description: The climate summit in Antalya was due to end Friday. By Saturday evening there was still no revised draft, and EU climate commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said it would be “either… a good deal or… no deal.” The EU, the U.K., small island states, the least developed countries and many African nations marched to the presidency office to demand that “transition away from fossil fuels” be put back in (Reuters, The Guardian, RTÉ).

item.title: Stellantis agrees to keep talking with Ottawa about not selling its Brampton plant, as Ford says just keeping it warm costs $135 million a year
item.description: After Friday’s meeting with Industry Minister Mélanie Joly, Ontario Premier Doug Ford and Unifor, the automaker agreed to more talks next week about keeping the idle plant instead of selling it to defence contractor Roshel, a deal it announced Nov. 9 (The Globe and Mail, Global News, Money.ca).

item.title: Science corner: wired-up prickly pear cacti work as living solar panels, and eight of them out-volt a AA battery
item.description: Researchers at UC Santa Cruz found a way to tap the prickly pear’s unusual photosynthesis. These cacti only take in carbon dioxide at night, storing it as malic acid, and sunlight breaks the acid down only on the side of the stem facing the sun. That leaves one side more acidic than the other, and the difference produces a voltage that electrodes inserted into the stem can collect (Plants, People, Planet; Popular Science).

item.title: Countries agree to two more years of talks on “killer robots” in Geneva, but not to negotiate a binding ban
item.description: The 128 states in the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons ended overnight talks early Saturday by agreeing that government experts will work on elements of an international instrument on lethal autonomous weapons through 2028, then propose whether it should become a legally binding treaty (swissinfo.ch/Keystone-SDA, AP, Politico Europe).

item.title: Amazon is close to buying Israeli AI startup Decart for up to US$7.5 billion, months after Anthropic walked away from a deal
item.description: Calcalist and the Financial Times report the deal is in its final stages and could be signed within days, paid in cash, stock and deferred money tied to targets. The founders, brothers Dean and Orian Leitersdorf and Moshe Shalev, would agree to stay five years, with much of the payout coming only then (Calcalist, Reuters/FT, Globes).

item.title: A Michigan pizza shop’s Facebook post about a shy caller asking for leftovers turns into a “meal wall” funded from around the world
item.description: During a dinner rush at Rosco’s Pizza in Union, Mich., manager Shanna Crice got a call from a timid voice asking whether the shop threw food away. She said no, and the caller hung up. Regretting it, she posted on the restaurant’s Facebook page asking the caller to phone back “so we can have a different conversation.” The post passed 100,000 likes, with comments from as far as Australia, Scotland and Nigeria (TODAY, WNDU).

item.title: A teacher annoyed by her “noisy” upstairs neighbour finds an 87-year-old with Parkinson’s, and their friendship videos draw nearly 30 million views
item.description: Heidi Widmer, a middle school teacher who moved from Buffalo to Culver City, Calif., this summer, thought her upstairs neighbour sounded like a midnight bowling league. Then she met Carole, who has Parkinson’s, struggling down the stairs with her recycling. The bowling-ball sound was her walker. “Suddenly, I didn’t care about the noise. I just knew I had to help her,” Widmer told PEOPLE (PEOPLE, ABC7 Los Angeles, Business Insider).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Saturday, November 21, 2026 (morning edition)
item.description: Morning edition: Edmonton City Centre’s $57.3M sale closes, teachers push back on Alberta’s graduation rules, a Canadian AI wingman drone consortium, Ottawa buys carbon-removal credits, Russian missiles land in Poland, Denmark expels Russia’s attaché over a plot to kill a rapper, Intuit sells Mailchimp, Alibaba’s cloud warning, a smart floss that checks blood sugar, California subpoenas Nvidia, OpenAI vs. model copying, a Bangladeshi kids’ guitar school and cowboy-hat deputies, and the Oilers in Carolina at noon.

item.title: Edmonton City Centre sells for $57.3 million, a sixth of its 2019 price, and the buyer wants 1,500 homes in the old Bay store
item.description: Edmonton developer Westrich Pacific has closed its purchase of the downtown mall from Otera Capital (now part of La Caisse), in a sale approved through the Court of King’s Bench after the property went into receivership last year with more than $139 million in unpaid loans. Co-CEO David Sanche confirmed the $57.3-million price; the complex sold for more than $300 million in 2019 (Edmonton Journal).

item.title: Alberta’s teachers’ union says the new high school graduation rules came with no consultation and asks the province to “go back to the drawing board”
item.description: At a Thursday news conference, Alberta Teachers’ Association president Jason Schilling said the updated diploma requirements, announced Nov. 13, were made without talking to teachers, school leaders or post-secondary schools, and called a string of recent education moves “political distractions” (LiveWire Calgary, Alberta Teachers’ Association).

item.title: An Ottawa startup signs 12 Canadian partners, including Pratt & Whitney Canada and Telesat, to build an AI “wingman” drone for the Arctic
item.description: Dominion Dynamics unveiled the consortium behind Scout, an uncrewed aircraft meant to fly alongside fighter jets, on Friday. Pratt & Whitney Canada would supply PW300-family engines, with Thales Canada, Top Aces, PV Labs, SRC Can, North Aircraft Industries and Altitude Aerospace among the others handling avionics, sensors, training and structures (The Canadian Press, The Globe and Mail, BetaKit).

item.title: Ottawa will buy carbon-removal credits from 19 Canadian projects to cancel out emissions it can’t cut, like military jets and ships
item.description: Treasury Board President Shafqat Ali announced a national standing offer on Thursday that lets federal departments buy permanent carbon-dioxide-removal credits from 19 projects, from direct air capture and biochar to mineralization. Ottawa says it’s the first national government to run a competitive purchase like this (Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat, Ottawa Citizen, The Globe and Mail).

item.title: Two Russian missiles and a drone crash in southeast Poland near a European troop exercise, and Tusk calls it a deliberate provocation
item.description: Poland says a Kh-101 cruise missile came down at Nowy Lipowiec, about 50 km from the Ukrainian border, around 6:30 a.m. Friday local time, with a second suspected missile near Rudnik nad Sanem and a jet-powered drone near Mołodycz. It happened during one of Russia’s heaviest overnight attacks on Ukraine. No one was hurt and no damage was reported (AP, Reuters, Al Jazeera).

item.title: Denmark expels Russia’s defence attaché after its spy service says Moscow planned to kill a U.S.-Ukrainian rapper before a Copenhagen-area concert
