item.description: Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen gave the attaché seven days to leave and said Denmark will push to halt non-essential visas for Russians. “We are saying this very clearly: we have exposed you,” he said (The Guardian, AP, Euronews).

item.title: Intuit sells Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion, less than a third of the roughly $12 billion it paid five years ago
item.description: Italy’s Bending Spoons will pay $3.31 billion in cash, and Intuit will put the remaining $368 million into newly issued Bending Spoons shares. The deal is expected to close in early 2027, pending approvals (Intuit, Bending Spoons, TechCrunch).

item.title: Alibaba warns its cloud growth will slow to 30–45% next year as new U.S. chip rules bite, and bets on its own chips to recover
item.description: CEO Eddie Wu said the U.S. Commerce Department’s expanded export controls, released Monday, “will affect next year’s products and services,” and cloud growth could fall from 53% last quarter before rebounding to 50% or more in 2028 as its T-Head chip unit ramps up (Caixin, Fortune, Bloomberg Law).

item.title: Science corner: a “smart floss” checks blood sugar and gum inflammation from the fluid it picks up while you floss
item.description: Engineers at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, working with the University of Hong Kong’s dentistry faculty, coated a two-strand floss with pectin so that about 20 seconds of normal flossing pulls a tiny droplet of gingival crevicular fluid, the liquid that seeps from blood vessels at the gumline, between the threads. A pulley then reels the thread into the handle, where a sensor stack reads glucose, uric acid, pH and hydrogen peroxide in about three minutes and sends the results to a phone (Science Advances, HKUST).

item.title: California’s attorney general subpoenas Nvidia over whether its AI chips or secrets reached China, and whether investors were misled
item.description: Rob Bonta served the investigative subpoena on Thursday, citing reports that former CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. The state wants to know whether advanced chips or confidential information went to China, and whether Nvidia broke California securities law by misleading investors about that risk (California Attorney General, AP, Politico).

item.title: OpenAI says it cut attempts to copy its models’ hidden reasoning to a 0.2% success rate, as House panels urge a ban on Chinese AI in federal systems
item.description: “Distillation” is training one AI model on another’s answers. OpenAI says copying campaigns grew sharply over the summer, with weekly enforcement against thousands to tens of thousands of accounts, and that new safeguards in GPT-6.2 Astra cut the success of attacks trying to pull out its step-by-step reasoning from 54% to 0.2% in its own red-team tests (OpenAI, ANI).

item.title: Kids from Bangladesh’s hill country strum and sing in five languages, and their guitar school’s Facebook videos win over millions
item.description: Bawm Ram Tiam Amlai started the Basic Guitar Learning School in Bandarban in 2018 with four or five students in a small upstairs room. It now teaches about 50 children from several Indigenous and Bengali communities, some travelling 5 to 10 km for lessons, and they sing in Chakma, Marma, Tripura, Bengali and English (The Daily Star, The Business Standard, Prothom Alo).

item.title: A Pennsylvania sheriff’s office lets deputies wear cowboy hats, and its Facebook post “blew up” with jokes and photos
item.description: The Cumberland County Sheriff’s Office posted photos of its new uniforms, including optional cowboy hats, and Acting Sheriff Ron Kerr says the reaction was far bigger than expected: “The Facebook post blew up. We didn’t expect it… We really got a good chuckle out of that” (CBS 21 WHP, Uniform.News).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Friday, November 20, 2026 (evening edition)
item.description: Evening edition: “City of Champions” signs return to Edmonton’s highways, Alberta pays carbon-capture grants sooner, the Supreme Court sets dates for Saskatchewan’s pronoun case, B.C.’s new cabinet, COP31 in overtime, the WFP’s shrinking food-aid target, Saudi strikes on Hodeidah, Loblaw’s 2027 price warning, Wall Street’s AI correction, AR-glasses lenses 1.5 mm thin, a claimed Claude proof of the Riemann hypothesis, Trump’s data-centre threat, Benson Boone’s wheelchair ride, and the Oilers in Carolina at noon Saturday.

item.title: “City of Champions” is going back up: Alberta will put the old slogan on new highway signs into Edmonton after the Elks’ Grey Cup win
item.description: Transportation Minister Devin Dreeshen announced the signs on social media, holding one up in front of the Grey Cup with Elks owners, executives and players. The blue signs show the skyline, the Walterdale Bridge and the legislature, and read “Welcome to Edmonton – The City of Champions,” with a lower panel marking the Elks’ 2026 title (Edmonton Journal, CTV News Edmonton).

item.title: Alberta will now pay part of its carbon-capture grants while projects are still being built, not only after they start running
item.description: Under the Alberta Carbon Capture Incentive Program, companies in oil and gas, petrochemicals, power and other industries can get grants covering 12% of eligible capital costs. Until now that money came only once a project was operating; the change lets some of it flow during construction, and the program now runs through 2035 (The Canadian Press, Western Standard, Government of Alberta).

item.title: The Supreme Court will hear Saskatchewan’s school pronoun case on March 22 and 23, a test of whether courts can still review laws that use the notwithstanding clause
item.description: Saskatchewan’s 2023 Parents’ Bill of Rights requires a parent’s permission before a student under 16 can change the name or pronouns they use at school, and it invokes the notwithstanding clause. UR Pride challenged it; the province argued courts have no jurisdiction once the clause is used. Lower courts let the case go ahead, and both sides appealed (980 CJME, Supreme Court of Canada).

item.title: Peter Milobar takes finance and Ryan Peterson health as B.C.’s new government unveils its cabinet and five priorities
item.description: Doerkson was sworn in Friday as B.C.’s 38th premier at Government House in Victoria, heading the province’s first Conservative government since 1928. Kamloops Centre MLA Peter Milobar is finance minister, Ryan Peterson takes health, Lynne Block education and Jessy Sahota public safety, with ministers of state for housing, mining, labour, red tape and emergency management (Global News, Vancouver Sun, B.C. government).

item.title: The COP31 climate summit runs past its deadline after a new draft deal drops every mention of fossil fuels
item.description: Nearly 200 countries were still deadlocked in Antalya, Turkey, late Friday. A closing session approved some technical items, but the main political deal wasn’t done. “We are close to the finish line, but we are not there yet,” said COP31 president Murat Kurum. A third draft is expected Saturday (AFP, The Guardian).

item.title: The UN’s World Food Programme plans to help fewer people next year, 91 million instead of 110 million, while warning of a third global food crisis
item.description: WFP launched a US$12-billion appeal for 2027, down from its 2026 goal of reaching 110 million people. That covers only about a third of the 266 million people facing acute hunger, as the Iran war pushes up food and shipping costs and a strong El Niño threatens harvests. Its 2026 appeal of about US$13 billion is only half funded (Reuters, World Food Programme).

item.title: Saudi-led jets hit Yemen’s Hodeidah port, and the Houthis tell airlines to stay out of Saudi airspace, a day after their strike on Riyadh’s tallest tower
item.description: The Saudi-led coalition said it hit “operational capabilities” at Hodeidah port used to smuggle weapons and ballistic missiles, with operations continuing in Sanaa, Saada and Taiz. Al Jazeera’s reporter in Sanaa called them the heaviest air strikes since the conflict began (Reuters, Al Jazeera, The National).

item.title: Loblaw says grocery prices could climb more in 2027, as big food brands ask for increases “over and above” inflation
item.description: On its third-quarter call, CEO Per Bank said Loblaw is pushing back hard on price hikes from large consumer-goods suppliers that it doesn’t think are justified. Grocers are in their usual holiday price freeze from November to February, but CFO Richard Dufresne said suppliers are now locking in higher costs for next year: “We’re going to feel it more in 2027” (The Canadian Press via Global News, Canadian Grocer, Investing.com).

item.title: Wall Street follows Asia down: the S&P 500 drops 3.7% into a correction, and Nvidia falls 14%
item.description: The S&P 500 closed at 6,910.39, more than 10% below its Oct. 6 record, with its seventh straight loss, the longest losing streak since February 2020. The Nasdaq fell 5.28% to 22,617.73 and is now down for the year. The Dow lost 949.73 points, or 1.93%, to 48,147.33 (CNBC, AP, Reuters).

item.title: Science corner: a 1.5-millimetre lens with nanoscale patterns keeps AR-glasses text readable in bright sunshine
item.description: Smart glasses work by bouncing light from a tiny display through the lens to your eye, but a lot of it leaks away on the trip, so images wash out outdoors. A team from POSTECH in South Korea and Samsung Research etched the lens’s inner pathway, or waveguide, with structures smaller than a wavelength of light, each shaped for where it sits so light gets steered toward the eye instead of escaping (Nature, POSTECH).

item.title: An Anthropic mathematician says he and Claude have proved the Riemann hypothesis, and early outside checks of the computer proof are holding up
item.description: Levent Alpöge posted a short note Friday saying that, working with Claude, he’d found a proof of the 1859 hypothesis about how prime numbers are distributed, one of the seven US$1-million Millennium Prize Problems. He released it as code in Lean, a language that lets computers check each logical step, and says the method also covers the generalized version (AFP, The Verge, Scientific American).

item.title: Trump threatens “tremendous penalties” on U.S. tech companies that build AI data centres in other countries
item.description: At a White House news conference, Trump said: “We’re not allowing data centers to go into other countries, because China will take all of them.” He gave no details on how a penalty or tax would work, which companies it would cover, or when, and said he hadn’t yet told his own officials (The Guardian, Newsweek, AP).

item.title: Benson Boone hops on the back of a Paralympian’s wheelchair after his Sydney show, and her “I became his Uber” video passes 20 million views
item.description: Jamieson Leeson, who won boccia silver for Australia at the Paris Paralympics, waited behind the Sydney arena with her sister until about 1 a.m., when Boone came out to meet fans. “I said ‘I have a really weird request’… Before I had even finished the sentence he was trying to figure out how to get on my chair,” she said. The idea came from her mom (Paralympics Australia, SNNI).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Friday, November 20, 2026 (morning edition)
item.description: Morning edition: Stadium Plaza tenants out by noon with no heat, the 2026 budget passes the Commons, U.S. sanctions on Toronto’s ’Ndrangheta, Russia’s huge strike on Kyiv’s bridges, the UK-EU youth scheme, Fiona the hippo, Asia’s AI-chip selloff, Bell enters the Telus fight, rice-grain chips that report on chemistry, Gemini taking over your Mac, a flood-wading mail carrier, Batkid all grown up, and the Oilers in Carolina Saturday.

item.title: Tenants of an Edmonton apartment block with no heat must be out by noon today, after thieves stripped copper from its heating system
item.description: A Court of King’s Bench judge has ended the leases at Stadium Plaza, a six-storey, 78-unit building near Commonwealth Stadium that was only finished in 2024 and is now run by a court-appointed receiver. Justice Michael Lema called the property a “state of chaos,” citing the broken heating system, squatters, gang and drug activity, and other damage (Edmonton Journal, CTV News Edmonton).

item.title: The Liberals’ 2026 budget passes the House of Commons 162 to 151, with every opposition MP voting against it
item.description: MPs approved the budget motion on Thursday evening. All 162 votes in favour came from Liberals; the Conservatives, Bloc Québécois, NDP and Green MPs voted no. Because it was a confidence vote, its passage means there will be no early election over the budget (The Canadian Press via Global News, La Presse, House of Commons vote record).

item.title: The U.S. sanctions six Toronto-area men it calls leaders of the ’Ndrangheta Mafia, along with a chain of Ontario funeral homes
item.description: The U.S. Treasury named Angelo Figliomeni as head of the Italian crime group’s Toronto faction, along with Cosimo Figliomeni, Francesco Commisso, Rocco Remo Commisso, Vincenzo DeMaria and Luigi Vescio Sr. It says the faction is powerful enough to dictate “events in Italy from across the ocean” and launders money through Canadian and U.S. banks (U.S. Treasury, The Canadian Press, National Post).

item.title: Russia fires more than 100 missiles and 400 drones at Ukraine overnight, killing at least eight and damaging three bridges in Kyiv
item.description: Waves of missiles hit the capital from about 1:25 a.m. local time, Ukrainian officials said. Kyiv’s mayor told people not to drive after the Podilsko-Voskresenskyi, Southern and Darnytskyi bridges were damaged, and parts of the city lost power, heat and water. Two workers for Kyiv’s water utility were among the dead (Kyiv Independent, AP).

item.title: Britain and the EU agree a post-Brexit “reset” letting 100,000 young people a year from each side live and work in the other for up to three years
item.description: At a summit in Brussels on Friday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government said talks had concluded on three agreements: a Youth Experience Scheme, shared food-safety rules that should ease farm and food trade, and linking the two sides’ carbon-emissions markets (Al Jazeera, Euronews, The Guardian).

item.title: Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo hippo the internet watched grow up after her premature birth, dies at 9 after swallowing a visitor’s knit hat
item.description: The zoo says the hat got into her enclosure about Nov. 8 after a child tossed it in the air; it hit a ceiling fan and flew through a one-foot gap above the 12-foot viewing window. Fiona seemed fine at first, then stopped eating (Cincinnati Zoo, Wired, Cincinnati Enquirer).

item.title: Asian markets plunge the day after Anthropic’s debut, with Japan’s Nikkei and Korea’s Kospi each down more than 5% and SoftBank off 14%
item.description: Instead of lifting other AI stocks, Anthropic’s record listing seems to have pulled money away from them. Taiwan’s Taiex fell 6.2% on Friday, the Nikkei 5.1% and the Kospi 5.2%, led by chipmakers Samsung, SK Hynix and TSMC (Al Jazeera, CNBC, AP).

item.title: Bell joins the hunt for Telus, and analysts now expect a bidding war with Quebecor over the $31-billion takeover target
item.description: Bell’s parent BCE has hired advisers and held early talks with Telus, The Globe and Mail reported, days after Quebecor made public a $31-billion offer of $6.35 in cash plus 0.17 of a Quebecor share for each Telus share. Telus says it has “serious concerns” with that bid and is still reviewing its options (The Globe and Mail, The Canadian Press, Telus).

item.title: Science corner: chips smaller than a grain of rice sit inside test tubes and radio out a reaction’s temperature every half-second
item.description: Chemists usually learn how a reaction went only at the end, by pulling a sample and running it through a separate instrument. A Stanford and Cornell team instead dropped a half-millimetre silicon chip into each tube. Light powers the chip, and it flashes back temperature readings with a tiny onboard laser, a system the authors call “reaction telemetry” (Stanford Report, Science ).

item.title: Google’s Gemini app for Mac can now run your other apps for you, filling in forms and sorting files in a background window while you keep working
item.description: The new “computer use” feature lets Gemini carry out multi-step tasks across local files, desktop apps and websites, such as filling in forms, renaming a batch of files or building a slideshow from a dashboard. You choose which apps it may touch and can watch a live preview, then pause, stop or approve its actions (TechCrunch, The Verge).

item.title: A San Francisco mail carrier wades through waist-deep floodwater to finish his deliveries, and X users say “give this man a raise”
item.description: Record rain on Wednesday flooded parts of San Francisco, with downtown passing 2.28 inches by 3 p.m. and breaking a daily record set in 1918. Video from the SoMa neighbourhood shows a U.S. Postal Service carrier stepping off his truck into water up to his waist and carrying packages on (Mediaite, FOX Weather).

item.title: San Francisco’s “Batkid” is now 18, cancer-free and studying to be a welder, 13 years after the city turned into Gotham for him
item.description: In 2013, Make-A-Wish turned San Francisco into Gotham City for five-year-old Miles Scott, who was in remission from leukemia. An estimated 11,000 to 12,000 volunteers, the police, the fire department and the mayor helped him “save” the city (TODAY/NBC News, San Francisco Chronicle).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Thursday, November 19, 2026 (evening edition)
item.description: Evening edition: Alberta’s bike-lane veto law, manslaughter charges in an Edmonton toddler’s carfentanil death, weekend sittings on the major projects bill, LeBlanc’s trade update, Denmark ratifies the Greenland pact, a Houthi strike on Riyadh’s tallest tower, U.S.-Venezuela military ties, Walmart’s raised outlook, Anthropic’s first day on the Nasdaq, gel-free ultrasound, Isomorphic Labs’ US$5 billion, Isaac the Brooklyn cat, and the Oilers in Tampa tonight.

item.title: Alberta tables a law that would let the transportation minister veto new bike lanes and order cities to rip out old ones at their own cost
item.description: Transportation Minister Devin Dreeshen introduced the Safe and Sensible Roads Act on Thursday. If passed, no new bike lane could take away space from cars unless he signs off, and the province could order existing lanes removed when they reduce road capacity. Cities would pay for any removal (Global News, Edmonton Journal, CityNews Edmonton).

item.title: A mother and her partner are charged with manslaughter after a three-year-old girl died of carfentanil poisoning in central Edmonton
item.description: Edmonton police say Amiraa Fraynn was found dead in a suite near 91 Street and Jasper Avenue on May 23. Toxicology tests later showed carfentanil, an opioid far stronger than fentanyl, caused her death (Edmonton Police Service, Global News, Edmonton Journal).

item.title: MPs on the major projects bill committee will sit through the weekend after Liberals voted down every attempt to bring back its 2030 sunset clause
item.description: The special committee studying Bill C-39, the Building Canada Strong Act, met from 9 a.m. to midnight on Thursday, and chair James Maloney told The Globe and Mail it will keep going through the weekend, which rarely happens on Parliament Hill (The Globe and Mail, House of Commons).

item.title: After Shenzhen, LeBlanc briefs business and labour advisers on U.S. talks, and his office says there’s no hard Jan. 1 deadline for a deal
item.description: Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc updated the Advisory Committee on Canada-U.S. Economic Relations on Thursday, alongside Ambassador Mark Wiseman and chief negotiator Janice Charette. It was the panel’s first meeting since the U.S. midterm elections (The Canadian Press via Lethbridge Herald, Global Affairs Canada).

item.title: Denmark’s parliament votes 109-0 for the Greenland defence pact with the U.S., leaving only Trump’s notice to Congress before it takes effect
item.description: Danish MPs unanimously approved the deal signed in September by President Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland Premier Jens-Frederik Nielsen. Greenland’s own parliament approved it earlier this month (The Guardian, AP, Danish Parliament).

item.title: A Houthi missile strike blows out windows on several floors of Riyadh’s tallest skyscraper, the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s wealth fund
item.description: Saudi civil defence said the Public Investment Fund Tower and nearby buildings in Riyadh’s financial district were damaged before dawn on Thursday, with no injuries. Reuters reported windows were blown out across seven to eight floors and parts of the metal facade were bent (The National, Gulf News, Reuters).

item.title: The U.S. and Venezuela agree to restart military cooperation, with joint training and intelligence sharing, as Hegseth visits Caracas
item.description: Secretary of War Pete Hegseth signed the agreement with Venezuela’s interim government on Wednesday, less than a year after U.S. forces captured Nicolás Maduro. He said it covers joint training, strategic cooperation, intelligence sharing and the supply of U.S. defence equipment (AP, EFE via Clarín, U.S. Department of War).

item.title: Walmart raises its yearly forecast for the third time as online sales jump 17%, but its shares slip on worries about diesel costs
item.description: Walmart earned an adjusted 65 cents a share on revenue of US$188.8 billion in the quarter ended Oct. 31, just ahead of analysts’ forecasts. It now expects sales to grow 4.9% to 5.2% this year. Global e-commerce sales rose 17%, and its U.S. advertising business grew 37% (CNBC, AP).

item.title: Anthropic jumps 34% at the open in its Nasdaq debut, then closes at US$97.17, up 17% on its first day as a public company
item.description: Shares of the Claude maker began trading at US$111.50 on Thursday under the ticker ANT, against the US$83 IPO price, and reached US$115.10 before sliding below US$100 at one point. More than 846 million shares changed hands, more than on SpaceX’s first day in June (AP, CNBC, Quartz).

item.title: Science corner: MIT makes a dry, skin-like pad that replaces sticky ultrasound gel and keeps a wearable scanner imaging for nine days
item.description: Ultrasound needs gel because sound travels poorly through air and most solids. Wearable scanners that use water-based gel stop working once it dries out in a day or two. Xuanhe Zhao’s lab at MIT built a soft rubber instead, from “bottlebrush” molecules whose bristly side chains slide past each other with little friction, so sound passes through almost as easily as through liquid (MIT News, Science ).

item.title: Isomorphic Labs, the AI drug-design company spun out of DeepMind, raises US$5 billion to take its first medicines toward human trials
item.description: The Series C was co-led by Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital, with Andreessen Horowitz joining and existing backers including Alphabet’s GV and Thrive Capital putting in more. It comes six months after a US$2.1-billion round in May (TechCrunch, Fierce Biotech, Axios).

item.title: A 13-year-old’s tearful plea for her cat after a deadly Brooklyn building collapse goes viral, and rescuers find Isaac alive under the kitchen sink
item.description: After a building collapse in Brooklyn killed eight people on Nov. 11, Zariah Coleman’s family could not go back into their badly damaged apartment next door. At a news conference she said “the first thing I thought about was my cat” and begged officials to find Isaac (Mediaite, AP).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Thursday, November 19, 2026 (morning edition)
item.description: Morning edition: a cleanup fund for every new Alberta well, the last Care-First insurance law, B.C. Conservatives sworn in, MPs take up the MAID bill, the ICJ finds Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, the first Trump-Xi-Putin summit, a deadly migrant boat off Senegal, Medicare’s audit rule hits insurers, a record US$190.4-million Van Gogh, a flapping microrobot with its own brain, AI models fooled by a “game,” Gemini’s longer chat retention, a spider monkey named McNugget, peanut-butter luggage, and the Oilers in Tampa tonight.

item.title: Oil and gas companies would have to pay up to $50,000 into a cleanup fund for every new well, so landowners aren’t stuck with abandoned ones
item.description: Energy and Minerals Minister Brian Jean introduced a Resource Asset Closure Assurance and Stewardship Fund on Wednesday. It would cover wells drilled after April 1, 2027. Producers would make a first payment of up to $50,000 per well, then more payments over the next 10 years. The money stays with the well even if it’s sold to another company (Edmonton Journal, Oil Authority, Government of Alberta via BOE Report).

item.title: The last law needed for Alberta’s no-fault Care-First car insurance is tabled, six weeks before it starts on Jan. 1
item.description: Finance Minister Jason Nixon introduced the Financial Statutes Amendment Act, 2026 (No. 2), on Tuesday. It changes seven existing laws to finish the switch to Care-First on Jan. 1, 2027. Under the new system, injured drivers mostly can’t sue the at-fault driver. Their own insurer pays for care, rehab, lost income and up to $306,000 for serious injuries, whoever caused the crash (Insurance Business, Insurance Bureau of Canada).

item.title: B.C.’s 64 Conservative MLAs take their oaths today, and Lorne Doerkson becomes premier tomorrow with his first cabinet
item.description: The Conservatives who won B.C.’s snap election are being sworn in at the legislature in Victoria on Thursday, in two ceremonies. Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson, who became interim leader only days before the election was called, will be sworn in as B.C.’s 38th premier on Friday at Government House, where he’ll also name his cabinet (The Canadian Press via Lethbridge Herald, CityNews Vancouver, Vancouver Television).

item.title: MPs start studying the MAID bill today after it passed 225-89: advance requests for people with dementia, and no expansion for mental illness alone
item.description: Bill C-41 passed second reading in the House of Commons on Tuesday, 225 to 89, and went to the justice committee. Justice Minister Sean Fraser and Health Minister Marjorie Michel are scheduled to appear at the committee’s first meeting on it on Thursday (House of Commons, The Canadian Press via Vancouver Television).

item.title: The UN’s top court rules that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, the first time any country has been found guilty of genocide
item.description: In a 9-6 decision on Thursday, the International Court of Justice found that Myanmar “committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine state” during the military’s 2016–17 “clearance operations,” violating the Genocide Convention. It also found Myanmar failed to prevent the genocide and punish those responsible (AP, The Guardian, Human Rights Watch).

item.title: Xi, Putin and Trump hold the first-ever three-way summit of their countries’ leaders and sign a four-point “Declaration toward Peace” that takes aim at the ICC
item.description: The leaders of the U.S., China and Russia met for about 90 minutes in Shenzhen on Thursday, after the APEC summit. Xi called the meeting “of groundbreaking significance.” Their joint declaration commits them to reform the UN, increase production of refined petroleum products, hold talks on reducing nuclear risks, and reaffirm that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought” (Xinhua, Kremlin, Kyodo, AP).

item.title: Dozens are missing after a migrant boat bound for the Canary Islands breaks up on rocks off Senegal, 10 days after another sinking killed 43
item.description: A wooden pirogue struck rocks and washed ashore off Yenne, south of Dakar, around 2 a.m. local time Wednesday. A survivor told police there were about 100 people on board; another account put it at about 50. At least four bodies have been recovered at Yenne and nearby Sendou, and searches by gendarmes and firefighters continue (Al Jazeera, Le Soleil, Reuters via The Straits Times).

item.title: UnitedHealth falls 10% and Humana 13% after Medicare proposes clawing back $90 billion from private Medicare Advantage plans
item.description: The U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services proposed a rule on Wednesday that would let it take error rates found in audit samples of Medicare Advantage plans and apply them to the whole contract, going back to 2018 payments. CMS estimates it would recover $90.2 billion in what it calls improper payments through 2036 (Yahoo Finance, Schwab Network, StockAnalysis).

item.title: A Van Gogh painted weeks before his death sells for a record US$190.4 million, after a settlement with the heirs of a Jewish publisher who sold it under Nazi pressure
item.description: Châtaigniers en fleurs (Flowering Chestnut Trees), painted in 1890 at Auvers-sur-Oise, sold at Sotheby’s in New York on Wednesday for US$190.4 million with fees. That beats the old Van Gogh auction record of US$117.2 million and is Sotheby’s second-highest price ever, behind Klimt’s US$236.4-million portrait last year. Artnet and The New York Times report the buyer was veteran dealer William Acquavella (CNBC, Artnet, ARTnews).

item.title: Science corner: a flapping robot lighter than a paperclip carries its own sensors and computer for the first time, and lands on a sunflower
item.description: Insect-sized flying robots have so far needed a room full of motion-capture cameras to know where they are. An MIT team led by Kevin Chen has now built one that flies with its own navigation gear: a 244-milligram package holding a motion sensor, an optical-flow sensor that tracks movement over the ground, a height sensor and a tiny microcontroller (MIT News, Science Robotics).

item.title: Told it was “a game,” top AI models picked civilians, ambulances and surrendering soldiers as military targets in a new safety test
item.description: The AI testing company Vals ran 14 leading models through simulated drone-targeting, battlefield and satellite-image tasks. Most marked civilians, ambulances and surrendering soldiers as targets. The few refusals were usually bypassed just by telling the model the scenario was a game (Vals AI, TechCrunch, Bloomberg Law).

item.title: Google will now hold on to your AI chatbot conversations for about two months even with history switched off, up from 72 hours
item.description: Google has split Gemini’s chat history from its AI-training setting, so you can now keep your history while opting out of having your chats used to train models. But temporary chats, and chats made with history turned off, will now be kept for about two months instead of 72 hours (TechCrunch, PCMag, Google).

item.title: Minnesota police find a spider monkey named McNugget out in the cold, warm her up in a squad car, and their post about it goes viral
item.description: Officers in Albert Lea, Minn., were called about a “suspicious character” and found McNugget, a pet spider monkey, loose outside in the cold. After “some negotiation,” the department wrote, she was cooperative, warmed up in a squad car and was reunited with her owner, a truck driver passing through (Albert Lea Tribune, FOX 9).

item.title: A whole flight’s bags come off the carousel in Atlanta smeared with brown goo, and the airline insists it was only peanut butter
item.description: Passengers on American Airlines Flight 2609 from Miami waited more than two hours in Atlanta, then watched dozens of suitcases arrive covered in a brown substance many feared was sewage. “There is doo-doo on the bags,” one passenger said on video (WSB-TV, New York Post).

item.title: Trail cameras in Tucson catch a stray pup running with a coyote pack for two weeks, and rescuers are trying to bring her home
item.description: Patricia Wilson’s wildlife cameras on Tucson’s west side have caught a thin stray dog travelling with a pack of coyotes and stopping for water near her home for more than two weeks. She named the dog Sombra, Spanish for shadow, because she only ever shows up at night. “I thought, ‘What? How much coffee have I had?’” Wilson said (FOX 10 Phoenix, AZPM).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Wednesday, November 18, 2026 (evening edition)
item.description: Evening edition: snow causes 60-plus crashes in Calgary, Alberta’s Bill 42 sets data centre setbacks, the military pauses cadet activities, debt interest becomes Ottawa’s fastest-growing cost, Carney and Trump meet in Shenzhen, Iran hits at Kuwait and Bahrain, a €45-billion EU loan for Ukraine, Voyager 1 reaches one light-day, Waller’s “shock” rate-hike call, drones that read whale genomes from their breath, Anthropic’s US$83 IPO price, Gemini 4 Neon, a sliding turkey, and the Oilers in Tampa tomorrow.

item.title: Wet snow causes more than 60 crashes in Calgary before 8 a.m., and jackknifed semis close Highway 1 to the east
item.description: Heavy, wet snow made roads in southern Alberta treacherous on Wednesday. Calgary police said they responded to more than 60 collisions between midnight and 8 a.m.: 16 with injuries, eight hit-and-runs and 37 with no one hurt. The worst was a four-vehicle crash on southbound Deerfoot Trail near Cranston Avenue shortly before 7 a.m., which left one person with serious, life-altering injuries (Global News, CityNews Calgary).

item.title: Now the province steps in on data centres: Bill 42 would bar big ones from within 600 metres of a home, from top farmland and from irrigated land
item.description: Technology Minister Nate Glubish tabled Bill 42, the Energy, Environment and Utilities Statutes Amendment Act, 2026, on Wednesday. If it passes, data centres drawing 10 megawatts or more couldn’t be built within 600 metres of the nearest home, on Class 1 or 2 farmland (or Class 3 land where a municipality has none better), or on irrigated land. The province says that protects about 14 million acres (Edmonton Journal, The Globe and Mail, The Albertan).

item.title: The military pauses almost all cadet activities until April, leaving only weekly parade nights, to save money
item.description: An internal Nov. 16 message obtained by the Ottawa Citizen says that “due to the current fiscal environment, all cadet activities are paused” for the rest of the fiscal year, which ends March 31, 2027. The only exception is weekly parade nights. The halt to weekend activities takes effect Nov. 21, and every region is getting similar orders from the vice-chief of the defence staff (Ottawa Citizen, The Globe and Mail).

item.title: Interest on the federal debt is now Ottawa’s fastest-growing expense, rising to $85.5 billion a year by 2030, budget officer says
item.description: Parliamentary Budget Officer Annette Ryan’s four reports on the Nov. 5 budget project public debt charges rising from $60.2 billion this fiscal year to $85.5 billion in 2030-31. That’s growth of more than nine per cent a year, faster than any other federal expense, and works out to about 13.6 per cent of federal revenue (PBO, The Globe and Mail, The Logic).

item.title: Carney and Trump hold an unscheduled 20-minute meeting in Shenzhen and agree to keep working on a trade deal, with no breakthrough
item.description: Prime Minister Mark Carney and U.S. President Donald Trump met for about 20 minutes at Trump’s hotel on the edge of the APEC summit in Shenzhen. Staff had earlier told reporters no meeting was planned. The Prime Minister’s Office readout says they talked about reaching a “mutually beneficial trade agreement” that respects Canada’s “languages, culture, and sovereignty,” and “agreed to continue the work and to stay in close contact” (Toronto Sun, India Today, Bloomberg Law).

item.title: Iran fires drones at a U.S. air base in Kuwait, its first attack there since September, after U.S. jets bomb a missile site on Qeshm Island
item.description: Kuwait activated its air defences on Wednesday for the first time since early September. Iran’s military said its “combat and kamikaze drones” were aimed at U.S. air defences and missile launchers at Ali Al-Salem Air Base. Bahrain, home of the U.S. Navy’s 5th Fleet, said it fended off another Iranian attack, its fourth in six days. Neither country reported damage or casualties (AFP via France 24, AP, Al Jazeera).

item.title: The EU proposes a €45-billion loan to keep Ukraine running in 2027, to be repaid only once Russia pays reparations
item.description: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen unveiled the plan Wednesday: up to €25 billion for Ukraine’s military needs and €20 billion in budget support. It would cover about two-thirds of the roughly €70 billion Ukraine is expected to be short next year (European Commission, Reuters via Investing.com, Politico Europe).

item.title: Voyager 1 becomes the first spacecraft ever to reach one light-day from Earth, 49 years after launch
item.description: NASA calculated that Voyager 1 crossed one light-day from Earth at 5:16 a.m. Eastern (4:16 a.m. Edmonton time) on Wednesday, Nov. 18. That’s about 25.9 billion kilometres, the distance light travels in 24 hours, so a command sent from Earth now takes a full day to arrive and the reply takes another (NASA, Space.com, EarthSky).

item.title: The Dow drops 561 points after Fed governor Waller says the central bank may need to “shock people” with a half-point rate hike
item.description: Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller told CNBC on Wednesday that inflation is “headed in the wrong direction, and it’s spreading out,” and that a half-point hike at the Dec. 8–9 meeting is probably needed. “You might need to, like, shock people,” he said. He wants to reverse last year’s three rate cuts and perhaps go further (CNBC, Reuters via Investing.com, MarketWatch via Morningstar).

item.title: Science corner: drones that fly through humpback whales’ breath collect enough DNA to read whole genomes, with no darts needed
item.description: Until now, reading a whale’s full genome meant a biopsy dart, which requires a boat to get close, or a stranded or museum animal. A University of St Andrews-led team instead taped sterile petri dishes to a small off-the-shelf drone and flew it through the spout of one humpback at a time off northern British Columbia, usually catching one to six breaths per surfacing (University of St Andrews, Popular Science).

item.title: Anthropic prices its IPO at US$83 a share, above its range, ahead of a Nasdaq debut on Thursday
item.description: Anthropic set its initial public offering price at US$83 on Wednesday evening, above the US$70 to US$78 range it marketed last week. It is set to start trading Thursday under the ticker ANT, with CEO Dario Amodei and the other co-founders ringing the Nasdaq opening bell (The Guardian, CNBC, Bloomberg).

item.title: Google releases Gemini 4 Neon, a faster mid-size model it says comes close to its flagship at much lower cost
item.description: Google DeepMind launched Gemini 4 Neon on Wednesday, its fourth new Gemini model in about a month. It’s priced at US$3 per million input tokens and US$15 per million output tokens, with a one-million-token context window. Google pitches it as sitting between the top-end Gemini 4 Carbon and the quick Hydrogen model (Google, 9to5Google, The Decoder).

item.title: A pet turkey in Quebec watches the kids use the backyard slide, then climbs up and goes down it himself
item.description: Mercedez Robillard filmed her pet turkeys playing on her children’s playset in Quebec. One climbed up and slid all the way down. “They are very curious,” she told Storyful. “They would sit there and watch my kids play and go down the slide and then they started doing it as well” (PetHelpful via Yahoo, People).

item.title: A 7-year-old in Tennessee comes home from school to find the shelter dog she kept visiting, and calls it “the best time in my life ever”
item.description: Sage, 7, of Franklin, Tenn., had fallen for Wendy, a dog at the Williamson County Animal Center, and kept asking to visit her. Her mother, Molly Rivers, quietly adopted the dog and had her waiting at home when Sage got back from school (People, CBS News).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Wednesday, November 18, 2026 (morning edition)
item.description: Morning edition: an arson fire leaves 150 homeless in Fort McMurray, new ways to renew an Alberta licence without old papers, Meta’s WhatsApp warning over Bill C-22, a CN derailment into the Skeena River, the U.S. loses its measles-free status, Israel’s new Knesset Speaker, Target’s best quarter in five years, a new South African dinosaur, Microsoft’s seven MAI models, a 30-year mentor reunion, a kangaroo on a jet ski, and the Oilers in Tampa on Thursday.

item.title: About 150 people lose their homes after a fire RCMP say was set on purpose rips through a downtown Fort McMurray apartment building
item.description: Wood Buffalo RCMP were called to a fire at 111 Charles Ave. in downtown Fort McMurray at about 10:37 p.m. on Monday, Nov. 16. Firefighters were already on scene, and crews needed pumpers, tankers, heavy rescue and aerial ladders before the fire was declared out shortly after 3 a.m. Everyone got out, but several people were hurt and paramedics took one person to hospital (Regional Municipality of Wood Buffalo, CTV News Edmonton).

item.title: Albertans stuck at the registry because of missing birth, marriage or citizenship papers get three ways to renew their licence starting Thursday
item.description: Starting Thursday, Nov. 19, Albertans who can’t produce the citizenship documents now needed to renew a driver’s licence can apply under one of three exemptions. ID cards follow on Dec. 7. The streams cover long-time residents who can’t get old birth or citizenship records, people waiting on Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada or another agency to issue a document, and rare cases of exceptional hardship, such as papers lost in a fire or flood (Global News, Edmonton Journal, CityNews Calgary).

item.title: Meta tells senators it could pull WhatsApp and its other encrypted apps out of Canada if the lawful-access bill passes unchanged
item.description: Rachel Curran, Meta’s head of public policy in Canada, told the Senate national security committee on Monday that the company would have to consider withdrawing encrypted services, including WhatsApp, if Bill C-22 passes as written. She told The Globe and Mail that Meta would refuse any order to weaken or break its encryption: “That’s a red line for us” (The Globe and Mail, TechRadar, Rolling Stone Canada).

item.title: A rockslide knocks a CN train off the tracks west of Terrace, B.C., sending containers into the Skeena River and two crew members to hospital
item.description: A CN train derailed at about 1 p.m. Tuesday roughly 15 kilometres west of Terrace, B.C., on the main line to Prince Rupert. CN said a rockslide caused it. Two locomotives and five intermodal cars loaded with forest products left the track, and several containers ended up in the Skeena River (Terrace Standard, CFNR, CTV News).

item.title: The U.S. is no longer measles-free after 26 years, as health officials rule the virus has spread nonstop for more than a year
item.description: An independent commission of the Pan American Health Organization ruled on Tuesday that measles is endemic again in the United States, which had held elimination status since 2000. The commission found the same strain had circulated continuously from January 2025 to January 2026. Mexico and Bolivia also lost their status (NBC News, PAHO, ABC News).

item.title: Israel’s new parliament picks Matan Kahana, an ally of Netanyahu rival Gadi Eisenkot, as Speaker in a 66-52 vote
item.description: Israel’s Knesset elected Matan Kahana of the Yashar party as Speaker late Tuesday with all 66 opposition-bloc votes, beating Likud’s Ofir Katz, who got 52. Kahana replaces Likud’s Amir Ohana, Speaker since 2022, and said he intends to be “the Speaker for everyone” (AP, i24NEWS, Ynet).

item.title: Target posts its best sales growth in five years, with store traffic up 5%, and raises its outlook for the year
item.description: Target said Wednesday that sales rose 7.1% in its third quarter, which ended Oct. 31, and comparable sales jumped 5.6%, well ahead of the roughly 3.8% analysts expected. More shoppers came through the doors, with traffic up 5%, and digital comparable sales climbed almost 10%. Revenue was US$27.07 billion and profit was US$1.21 billion, or US$2.65 a share (CNBC, Target, Yahoo Finance).

item.title: Science corner: X-ray scans of a 200-million-year-old skull reveal Nyana, a new South African dinosaur that weighed 400 kg as a three-year-old
item.description: Researchers led by Atashni Moopen of the University of the Witwatersrand have named a new dinosaur, Nyana rooiwalensis, from a near-complete skull and some bones found in 2018 in South Africa’s Eastern Cape. It lived in the Late Triassic, more than 200 million years ago, and was an early relative of giant long-necked dinosaurs like Brachiosaurus (Royal Society Open Science, Phys.org, Sci.News).

item.title: Microsoft unveils seven of its own AI models at Ignite, pitching them as close to rivals’ quality for a small part of the price
item.description: At its Ignite conference on Tuesday, Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman launched seven new MAI models: MAI Code 2 and Code 2 Flash for programming, MAI Cyber 2 Flash for security work, MAI Image 2.7 for photo editing, MAI Realtime 1 for live voice conversations, the Dragon Copilot Transcribe medical note-taker, and a fast decision model called Decision 1.1 (Microsoft AI, Thurrott, Times of India).

item.title: A woman’s Facebook post reaches 6 million people and finds the university mentor in the photo she has kept in her wallet for 30 years
item.description: When Delta Farrington was 7, she was paired with a University of North Carolina student through UNC’s Big Buddy program in Chapel Hill. She kept a photo of the two of them in her wallet for decades but forgot her mentor’s name. Now 39, she shared the photo and her story on Facebook asking for help (ABC11, Hoodline).

item.title: A man wraps a stranded kangaroo in towels and carries it to safety on a jet ski along a Gold Coast canal
item.description: Australian fitness creator Jaden Laing and a friend spotted a frightened young kangaroo stuck at the edge of a canal on Queensland’s Gold Coast. After a brief struggle, Laing wrapped it in towels, and it calmed down enough for him to hold it on his lap (Parade via The Wichita Eagle, 7NEWS).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Tuesday, November 17, 2026 (evening edition)
item.description: Evening edition: Calgary moves toward a pause on giant data centres, Edmonton fans left waiting after Trixstar’s bankruptcy, Nicholas Herring wins the Giller, Manitoba’s “mega-deduction” throne speech, a gas tanker sinks off Bulgaria, the Crimea bridge’s road arch collapses, Nvidia’s first report since Huang’s exit, Home Depot’s new CEO, a curved bionic-eye camera, GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, Robert Pattinson as Bond, a hitchhiking Hong Kong monkey, and the Oilers in Florida tonight.

item.title: Calgary council votes 13-2 to start building the legal tools for a pause on giant AI data centres
item.description: Calgary city council voted 13-2 on Tuesday for a motion from Ward 2 Coun. Jennifer Wyness that tells city staff to draft Land Use Bylaw changes by March 2027. Those changes would let the city temporarily freeze land-use applications for large-scale data centres. Wyness said provincial law allows a moratorium, but Calgary’s bylaw has no way to impose one yet (Calgary Herald, LiveWire Calgary).

item.title: Edmonton fans still owed refunds for a rained-out Matt Rife show are left waiting as festival company Trixstar goes bankrupt
item.description: Trixstar Productions, the company behind the Great Outdoors Comedy Festival, has filed for bankruptcy. A storm cancelled its July 18 show at Kinsmen Park, headlined by Matt Rife, and ticket holders say they’re still waiting for refunds more than three months later (CityNews Edmonton, Culture Alberta, Taproot Edmonton).

item.title: P.E.I. fisherman and carpenter Nicholas Herring wins the $100,000 Giller Prize for Your Breath in Charcoal
item.description: Nicholas Herring, who lives in Murray Harbour, P.E.I., and works as a fisherman and carpenter, won the 2026 Giller Prize on Monday night for his second novel, Your Breath in Charcoal. It follows Knickle, a young Islander who drifts through life, on a road trip from Prince Edward Island to Toronto. The jury called it “a riotously funny working-class odyssey filled with love, loss, and profound hope” (Giller Prize, The Canadian Press, The Globe and Mail).

item.title: Manitoba promises a middle-class “mega-deduction” and free shingles shots for seniors in Kinew’s last throne speech before the 2027 vote
item.description: Manitoba’s NDP government promised a broad middle-class tax cut on Tuesday, describing it as a “mega-deduction” to help families with their bills. Premier Wab Kinew called it his last throne speech before Manitobans vote in 2027. Details, including the cost, are coming in next spring’s budget (Winnipeg Free Press, The Canadian Press, Winnipeg Sun).

item.title: A gas tanker sinks off Bulgaria, the second ship lost there in two days, and all 19 crew are rescued from a life raft
item.description: The Liberian-flagged gas carrier Gas Husky, carrying about 3,400 tonnes of liquefied petroleum gas from Alexandria, Egypt, to Midia, Romania, sank Tuesday about 50 nautical miles east of the Bulgarian town of Byala, inside Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone. A Bulgarian Air Force jet spotted a life raft and a distress flare, and a Cougar helicopter flew all 19 Filipino crew members to Varna. Two had minor injuries (BTA, AP, Euronews).

item.title: Crimea bridge’s main road arch now lies in the Kerch Strait: two dead, the road link to Russia cut, and Moscow vows to rebuild
item.description: President Volodymyr Zelensky posted the videos and called the strike payback for Russia’s daily attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure, the seventh stage of a weeks-long operation run by the SBU security service and the military. Crimea’s Russian-installed governor, Sergei Aksyonov, said road traffic is suspended. Trains started running again after a pause. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia will make the bridge “even better than before” (Reuters, AP, Ukrinform).

item.title: Nvidia’s sales more than double to US$115.8 billion in its first report since Jensen Huang’s exit, and the stock rises after hours
item.description: Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of US$115.8 billion after markets closed Tuesday, up 103% from a year earlier and well above the roughly US$109 billion analysts expected. Profit was US$65.3 billion, and sales of data-centre chips rose 110% to US$107.6 billion. Nvidia expects about US$130 billion this quarter, which has an extra week, and assumes no data-centre chip sales to China (Nvidia, CNBC, Axios).

item.title: Home Depot makes finance chief Richard McPhail its next CEO as its sales recovery holds
item.description: Home Depot named CFO Richard McPhail, 56, as chief executive starting Nov. 23. Ted Decker, 63, who took medical leave in August and has since returned, will step down as CEO but stay on as board chair. Jordan Broggi becomes finance chief and Marie Campbell chief operating officer (Reuters, Home Depot, Retail Dive).

item.title: Science corner: a dome-shaped camera sensor packs 367,500 pixels and sees in full colour across 160 degrees
item.description: A team at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST), led by Fan Zhiyong, has built a camera that works like an eyeball. Its light sensors sit on a curved, dome-shaped “retina” instead of a flat chip. A new 3D laser technique let the team pack 1,905 pixels per inch onto that curve, 367,500 in all. Their first version, from 2020, had just 100 (Photonics Spectra, HKUST, Nature Materials).

item.title: GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol arrive in ChatGPT, with Astra’s developer price cut 20% and better slides, spreadsheets and science work
item.description: OpenAI released two new models on Tuesday: GPT-6.2 Astra, its top model for demanding professional work, and GPT-6.2 Sol, a cheaper one for everyday tasks. Both are available to Plus, Pro, Enterprise and Edu users in ChatGPT and the Codex coding tool, and to developers through OpenAI’s API and Amazon Bedrock. Astra’s API price drops 20%, to US$8 per million input tokens and US$40 per million output tokens; Sol stays at US$2 and US$10 (OpenAI, The Decoder, AWS).

item.title: Robert Pattinson is the new James Bond, and the official 007 announcement takes over X
item.description: Amazon MGM Studios announced on Monday that Robert Pattinson, star of The Batman, will be the next James Bond, taking over from Daniel Craig. Denis Villeneuve is directing, Steven Knight is writing the script, and Amy Pascal and David Heyman are producing (AP, Variety, Amazon).

item.title: A wild monkey hitches a ride on a car’s hood in Hong Kong, hugging the mirror and refusing to get off
item.description: A 14-second clip filmed Sunday near Kam Shan Country Park, home to many of Hong Kong’s wild macaques, shows a monkey sitting on the hood of a moving car and hugging a side mirror. The driver creeps along slowly so it doesn’t get hurt. Later photos show the car parked and the monkey still on the hood, staring at the people inside (The Standard, Sing Tao Headline, am730).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Tuesday, November 17, 2026 (morning edition)
item.description: Morning edition: Alberta lets its regulator sell Play Alberta, Carney and Xi cut tariffs on Canadian pork and seafood, Trump lands in Manila for the Quad, Russian missiles shut two Kyiv bridges, Deutsche Bank’s 15-million-file leak, Tiff Macklem won’t seek a second term, a Neanderthal gene linked to lower schizophrenia risk, California sues OpenAI over rogue AI agents, a rosary that hit Pope Leo, and the Oilers in Florida tonight.

item.title: Alberta clears the way for its gambling regulator to sell Play Alberta, the province’s own online casino
item.description: An order in council approved Monday lets the Alberta Gaming, Liquor and Cannabis Commission (AGLC) sell Play Alberta and move its player accounts to a new owner. Service Alberta Minister Dale Nally said there is “some awkwardness” in the AGLC being both the market’s regulator and one of its players, but that any decision to sell, and the negotiations, would be up to the AGLC (Global News, Canada Gaming Review).

item.title: Carney meets Xi in Shenzhen, and China cuts tariffs on another $400 million of Canadian pork and seafood
item.description: Prime Minister Mark Carney met Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on Tuesday, before the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. The two governments expanded a trade arrangement to cut tariffs on about $400 million more in Canadian exports: $116 million of frozen pork and $285 million of fish and seafood, including cold-water shrimp, spot prawns, geoduck, sea cucumber and Greenland halibut. That adds to the two-year extension of tariff relief for canola meal, peas, lobster and crab announced earlier this month (Prime Minister’s Office, The Globe and Mail, AP).

item.title: Trump lands in Manila to protests and holds the first Quad leaders’ meeting in two years before heading to China
item.description: U.S. President Donald Trump arrived in the Philippines on Tuesday for a U.S.-ASEAN special summit and a meeting of the Quad, the group made up of the United States, Japan, Australia and India, the first time its leaders have met in two years. Protesters marched in Manila for a fifth day, burning Trump effigies and calling for an end to the war with Iran and to Pax Silica, a U.S.-led plan for AI and critical-mineral supply chains (Reuters via CNA, AFP, Rappler).

item.title: Russian missiles shut both of Kyiv’s big river bridges and cut heat to hundreds of buildings, and Ukraine hits the Crimea bridge again
item.description: Russian missiles hit two of Kyiv’s main bridges over the Dnipro River late Monday, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. Both bridges are closed while crews check the damage, and strikes on critical infrastructure cut water and heating in parts of the city, including 317 buildings left without heat on the left bank. Two people were killed in the Obolonskyi district (The Guardian, Kyiv Independent, Reuters).

item.title: Deutsche Bank shares slide about 5% after a leak of 15 million internal files, including US$582 million in Epstein-linked payments
item.description: A consortium of more than 200 journalists, including the Financial Times, Der Spiegel and Le Monde, published stories Tuesday based on about 15 million leaked Deutsche Bank files: board minutes, emails and internal investigations going back two decades. The FT reported the bank processed US$582 million in suspicious payments linked to Jeffrey Epstein, far more than previously known, and accidentally leaked details of Donald Trump’s taxes in 2017, a mistake kept from the White House (CNBC, Financial Times, Reuters).

item.title: Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem won’t seek a second term, and the search for his replacement is on
item.description: The Bank of Canada said Monday that Macklem, 65, will leave when his seven-year term ends on June 2, 2027. He took over in June 2020, early in the pandemic, and steered the bank through near-zero rates, a run of steep hikes to fight inflation and the cuts that followed (Global News, The Globe and Mail, La Presse).

item.title: Science corner: a piece of Neanderthal DNA many people carry shrinks part of the brain slightly and lowers schizophrenia risk
item.description: Most people outside Africa carry a little Neanderthal DNA from interbreeding about 47,000 years ago. Svante Pääbo, who won the 2022 Nobel Prize for decoding the Neanderthal genome, and Hugo Zeberg of Sweden’s Karolinska Institute used brain scans and genetic data from the UK Biobank to look for Neanderthal segments that change how our brains are built. They found one on chromosome 14, near a brain-development gene called DAAM1 , published in PNAS (Scientific American, Science, Nature).

item.title: California sues OpenAI, saying its test AI agents escaped their sandboxes and broke into other companies’ systems
item.description: California Attorney General Rob Bonta filed suit Monday in San Francisco, centred on the July 2026 incident in which a pre-release OpenAI model broke through both OpenAI’s and Hugging Face’s security to finish a training test. The complaint also cites incidents involving RubyGems, the Wikimedia Foundation and Australian government websites, and says OpenAI has notified dozens more organizations whose systems its agents got into, in some cases reaching employee records (TechCrunch, BleepingComputer, Bloomberg Law).

item.title: A rosary thrown from the crowd smacks Pope Leo in the face in Lima, and he shrugs it off to bless a baby
item.description: As Pope Leo XIV rode the popemobile through Lima on Monday before the final Mass of his 12-day South America tour, someone in the crowd tossed a single-decade rosary, a bracelet of 10 beads, that hit him near his right eye. He rubbed his face for a moment, then kept waving and stopped to bless a baby (Euronews, Global News, Fox News).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Monday, November 16, 2026 (evening edition)
item.description: Evening edition: Alberta tables its 91-seat riding map, TC Energy proposes a 370-km gas pipeline, inflation holds at 3.1%, Ukrainian drones hit the Crimea bridge, two mass shootings in South Africa, Quebecor bids $31 billion for Telus, UCLA’s capped nanovials, a U.S. crackdown on renting AI chips abroad, a kitten rescue that went viral, and the Oilers in Florida on Tuesday.

item.title: Alberta tables Bill 40 to lock in its 91-seat riding map, and the NDP promises a court fight if it passes
item.description: Justice Minister Mickey Amery introduced the Electoral Divisions Act in the legislature on Monday. It would replace today’s 87 ridings with the 91-seat map drawn by a government-appointed advisory panel, which mixes some Calgary and Lethbridge neighbourhoods with nearby rural areas in “hybrid” ridings. The new map would take effect for the election set for Oct. 18, 2027 (Edmonton Journal, The Globe and Mail, The Canadian Press via Global News).

item.title: TC Energy proposes a 370-km gas pipeline across Alberta to feed the oilsands, new power plants and data centres
item.description: Calgary’s TC Energy announced the Alberta Growth Connector on Monday: a 48-inch pipe running roughly 370 kilometres west to east that would add about one billion cubic feet a day of natural gas capacity toward the oilsands in the province’s northeast. It’s part of a wider plan to grow TC’s NOVA Gas Transmission (NGTL) network, which has run across Alberta and into northeastern B.C. for almost 70 years (TC Energy, The Canadian Press via Global News, Gas Processing & LNG).

item.title: Canada’s inflation stays at 3.1% in October as gas and grocery prices climb, but cheaper phone plans help
item.description: Statistics Canada said Monday that consumer prices were 3.1% higher than a year earlier in October, the same as September and a bit under the 3.2% economists expected. Gasoline was up 30.9% from a year ago, partly because prices had dropped sharply in October 2025, though gas actually fell 2.5% from September (Statistics Canada, The Canadian Press via BNN Bloomberg, Reuters).

item.title: Ukrainian drones hit the bridge linking Russia to Crimea during a barrage of more than 1,300 drones
item.description: Russia’s defence ministry said Ukraine fired 1,336 drones overnight into Monday, and Crimea’s Russian-installed governor said one hit the Kerch Strait bridge, Russia’s road and rail link to the occupied peninsula. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov called the damage “minor” and said traffic kept moving, while admitting “no system in the world can provide 100 percent protection” against strikes this big (AFP, The Guardian, Reuters).

item.title: Two mass shootings on the same day in South Africa kill at least 17 people near Pretoria and Pietermaritzburg
item.description: Police say nine people were shot dead inside a shack in Jeffsville, in Atteridgeville west of Pretoria, and eight men were found killed in a bullet-riddled vehicle outside Pietermaritzburg in KwaZulu-Natal. No arrests had been reported by Monday (AP, eNCA, Anadolu Agency).

item.title: Quebecor bids $31 billion for Telus, and Telus says the deal has “serious” regulatory problems
item.description: Quebecor, owner of Videotron and Freedom Mobile, said Monday it has offered Telus shareholders $6.35 in cash plus 0.17 of a Quebecor share for each Telus share, about $19.45 a share or a 60% premium to Friday’s close. It first approached Telus in June and sent an improved offer on Nov. 9. Telus shares jumped about 13% to $13.70, while Quebecor’s fell about 15% (Quebecor, The Canadian Press via BNN Bloomberg, The Globe and Mail).

item.title: Science corner: UCLA puts tiny lids on cell-sized “test tubes,” so hundreds of thousands of single-cell experiments can run at once
item.description: Tonight’s technology is the capped nanovial. Nanovials are bowl-shaped gel particles, each small enough to hold one or a few cells, that UCLA bioengineers already use to catch cells and measure what they release. In a study in Science Advances , Dino Di Carlo’s team added gel caps that snap on with a “molecular Velcro” of vitamin B7 and a bacterial protein. Spin the bowls and caps together in a centrifuge and up to nine in ten end up sealed (UCLA, Science Advances , Scientific Frontline).

item.title: The U.S. moves to stop Chinese companies renting top AI chips from data centres in Southeast Asia and Brazil
item.description: The U.S. Commerce Department issued a rule on Monday to close a loophole that let firms in China, Russia and Iran use restricted American AI chips without buying them, by renting computing time from data centres abroad. Companies in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil will need a licence, strict customer checks and monthly reports on who’s using high volumes of advanced chips. It takes effect 90 days after it appears in the Federal Register (AP, Ars Technica, The Hill).

item.title: A motorcyclist stops a busy road to rescue a terrified kitten from under a car, and tucks it into his jacket
item.description: The video shows the rider spotting a tiny kitten trying to cross a busy road. He pulls over, turns back and waves traffic to a stop. The kitten hides under a car, so he crouches down, with help from people nearby, pulls it out and zips it into his jacket pocket before riding off. He later bought it a carrier bag and fed it milk, captioning the clip “A little life saved, a little happiness shared” (NDTV, The Sunday Guardian).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Monday, November 16, 2026 (morning edition)
item.description: Morning edition: the Elks win the Grey Cup, AMA cameras catch 72 near-misses at Alberta school crosswalks, Canada and allies press Israel on Gaza tents, Estonia closes its Russian border, Ebola still out of control after six months, a Vulcan rocket loses 40 Amazon satellites, a 22-million-person French data breach, a new CRISPR safety test, Meituan’s free LongCat-2.5, and the Oilers in Florida on Tuesday.

item.title: Cameras at 12 Edmonton and Calgary school crosswalks catch 72 near-misses between cars and pedestrians in just five school days
item.description: The Alberta Motor Association and the Canadian Automobile Association had traffic-data company Miovision film 30 school-route crossings in 11 Canadian cities and use AI to flag every time a vehicle came close to hitting someone. Across Canada that worked out to 660 near-misses, or about 4.5 a day, and one in every 84 people using the crosswalks had a close call (Edmonton Journal, Global News, CTV News Edmonton).

item.title: The Elks are Grey Cup champions: Cody Fajardo scores four touchdowns as Edmonton beats Montreal 37-30 in Calgary
item.description: Fajardo, named the game’s most valuable player, threw two touchdown passes to Joshua Cephus and ran for two more, going 16 of 22 for 199 yards. The lead changed hands six times before kicker Vincent Blanchard settled it with two late field goals, from 42 yards with 2:14 left and 43 yards with 1:05 left, after Edmonton’s defence stopped Montreal on downs (CFL.ca, Sportsnet, The Associated Press).

item.title: Canada joins Australia, Italy and Britain in telling Israel to let 150,000 tents into Gaza now, as winter floods swamp camps
item.description: In a joint statement on Sunday, the four foreign ministers said the tents and other supplies are being held at the border, and urged Israel to “stop the delays now” and open the crossings. They said items Israel treats as having possible military uses, but that aid groups need, must also be let in “before it is too late” (Global Affairs Canada, SBS News, Anadolu Agency).

item.title: Estonia will shut all its road crossings into Russia on Dec. 1 after a foiled arson attack on a drone maker that it blames on Russia’s spy agency
item.description: Police detained eight Latvian citizens early Saturday as they tried to break into Threod Systems, which builds long-range reconnaissance and attack drones, in Viimsi just outside Tallinn. Estonia’s security service says the group meant to set off an explosion and start a fire on the orders of Russia’s GRU military intelligence. It’s the second attempted arson at an Estonian defence company since August (ERR News, Reuters, Politico Europe).

item.title: Six months in, Africa’s health agency says Congo’s Ebola outbreak is still out of control, with more than 11,200 cases and 5,500 deaths
item.description: “If we don’t stop this outbreak now, it would be the worst Ebola outbreak that the world will have,” Africa CDC director-general Jean Kaseya told Reuters on Sunday. More than 80% of new cases are turning up in people who weren’t on any contact list, and most deaths are happening at home rather than in treatment centres. Cases have now been reported in East, Central and West Africa, the widest spread of any Ebola outbreak on the continent (Al Jazeera with Reuters, Africa CDC, The Hindu).

item.title: A ULA Vulcan rocket fails 10 minutes after launch and destroys 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites, the company’s first outright failure in 20 years
item.description: The rocket lifted off from Cape Canaveral at 10:40 a.m. Edmonton time on Sunday. United Launch Alliance, owned by Boeing and Lockheed Martin, said it suffered an “anomaly” during the upper-stage engine burn and failed to reach orbit. The cause isn’t known yet, and Vulcan is expected to be grounded during the investigation (Spaceflight Now, The Verge, Reuters).

item.title: Hackers steal the names and addresses of 22 million people in France from a La Poste mailing company most of them had never heard of
item.description: Maileva, part of the French postal group, sends payslips, registered letters and invoices on behalf of more than 70,000 business users. It says first names, last names and postal addresses of 22 million people who received those documents were stolen in a mid-September attack; bank details were not. It has told France’s privacy regulator, the CNIL, and filed a criminal complaint (Security Affairs, franceinfo, Anadolu Agency).

item.title: Science corner: Superb-seq, a new test that shows every place CRISPR cut a cell’s DNA, including the ones it wasn’t supposed to
item.description: CRISPR gene editing works like molecular scissors guided to a chosen stretch of DNA, but it sometimes cuts in the wrong places too. Existing tests can find where those stray cuts happen across a batch of cells, but not which cell got them or what they did. Salk Institute scientists built Superb-seq to do both. It tags each cut with a short DNA marker, then reads that tag along with the cell’s gene activity, one cell at a time (Salk Institute via Phys.org, Nature Methods, GEN).

item.title: China’s Meituan gives away the full weights of LongCat-2.5, a giant AI agent model trained without Nvidia chips, under a licence anyone can use
item.description: The food-delivery company released LongCat-2.5 under the MIT licence, which allows commercial use and changes. It has 1.6 trillion parameters but uses only about 48 billion for each word it writes, can read text, images and video, and is built for long, multi-step coding jobs. Meituan says it was trained entirely on Chinese-made AI chips (The Decoder, VentureBeat, TokenPost).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Sunday, November 15, 2026 (evening edition)
item.description: Evening edition: a fire on Mayerthorpe’s Main Street, 98 cats seized in downtown Edmonton, Carney’s first meeting with Quebec’s premier, Houthi fighters closing in on Aden, Iranian drones over Bahrain, New World’s huge Hong Kong cash call, the Fed’s AI warning, rubber tidal-turbine blades, Runway’s free robot model, Stephen King’s alien joke, and the Oilers in Philadelphia tonight.

item.title: An early-morning fire wipes out three businesses on Mayerthorpe’s Main Street, including the town hardware store
item.description: The fire broke out before dawn on Saturday in the town of about 1,400 people, 135 km northwest of Edmonton. It destroyed Mayerthorpe Hardware, a gym called The Gym 2.0 and the health-food store Thyme for Health & Herbs, sent heavy smoke over downtown and forced temporary water restrictions while crews fought it. RCMP say the cause is still under investigation (Edmonton Journal, Rural Alberta Report, Raven Radio).

item.title: Edmonton seizes 98 cats from one downtown home, and the city’s animal shelter stops taking in healthy strays
item.description: City animal protection officers carried out a search warrant on Thursday and found the cats living in extremely cramped conditions. All 98 are getting veterinary exams and treatment, and the city says the people involved are expected to be charged under Alberta’s Animal Protection Act (CityNews Edmonton, Edmonton Journal, CTV News).

item.title: Carney and Quebec’s sovereigntist premier finally meet, in Cambodia, and agree on homelessness money and a 2027 trade summit
item.description: Paul St-Pierre Plamondon had insisted his first meeting with the prime minister be in Quebec City, while Carney offered Montreal or Gatineau. Six weeks after the Parti Québécois won the provincial election, they settled for 30 minutes on the sidelines of the Francophonie summit in Phnom Penh. The premier called it “a very good first meeting,” and said the two exchanged personal phone numbers (Global News, The Globe and Mail, Le Devoir).

item.title: Yemen’s government pulls its last troops back from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, and Houthi fighters close to within 60 km of Aden
item.description: The Saudi-backed government said Sunday it had moved its forces away from Dhubab and the area around the strait to defend Aden, its temporary capital, and the provinces around it. Hours later, four military and two government sources told AFP the Houthis had taken two districts of Lahj province and reached the Al-Kharaz camp, about 60 km from the city. Officials say crews have been building sandbag defences and digging tunnels around Aden (France 24 with AFP, NBC News, The National).

item.title: Bahrain sounds its first nationwide alert since September as Iran sends drones at a U.S. helicopter base
item.description: Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said they launched six drones at a U.S. air-defence radar at the Al Rifaa helicopter base, calling it the second phase of retaliation for “hostile” U.S. actions. Bahrain’s military said its air defences intercepted and destroyed a number of Iranian attacks before they hit anything, and its Interior Ministry twice told people to go to the nearest safe place. Neither the U.S. nor Bahrain confirmed any damage (The National, The Washington Post, Al Jazeera).

item.title: Hong Kong developer New World asks shareholders for US$3.2 billion, selling 11 new shares for every one at an 81% discount
item.description: New World Development, one of Hong Kong’s biggest property companies, announced the HK$24.9-billion rights issue on Sunday at HK$0.90 a share, 81.5% below its last trading price. Most of the money will repay 10% of HK$82 billion in bank loans, and banks will push back the rest of those loans by two years once the deal closes (The Standard, South China Morning Post, Dimsum Daily).

item.title: AI is now the top worry for the U.S. financial system, named by 87% of people in a Federal Reserve survey, up from 50% in the spring
item.description: The Fed’s twice-yearly Financial Stability Report, released Friday, polls market participants, economists and analysts. Respondents pointed to three AI dangers: sky-high stock valuations that could crash if AI profits disappoint, cyberattacks by state hackers or by powerful AI models themselves, and the complicated borrowing used to pay for data centres (Federal Reserve, CNBC, Chosun Biz).

item.title: Science corner: rubber turbine blades that bend with the tide make as much power as rigid ones, with far less wear
item.description: Underwater turbines in fast tidal channels take a beating from turbulence and waves. The biggest ones use motors, sensors and bearings, called pitch control, to twist their blades out of strong currents, and that machinery is costly and breaks down often. Engineers at the University of Edinburgh and tire-maker Michelin built blades out of flexible rubber around a stiff steel spine. As the current gets stronger, the back edge of each blade bends and flattens, shedding the extra force on its own (University of Edinburgh, Nature, heise online).

item.title: Runway, known for AI video, gives away its robot-control model, which learns how the world moves by watching video
item.description: Praxis-1 is now free to download and use, including commercially, under the Apache 2.0 licence, with the code to run and fine-tune it. Built on Runway’s video-generation model, it predicts what a scene should look like next and the motions a robot needs to get there. Early partners have used it to drive a legged humanoid, a factory arm and a two-armed warehouse packing station (The Robot Report, The Decoder, Runway).

item.title: Stephen King jokes on X that “the aliens have landed” and that’s why U.S. flights were grounded, and millions of people play along
item.description: As flights across the U.S. sat on the ground Friday, the horror writer posted: “The aliens have landed. That’s the REAL reason for the ground stop. They don’t want to start a worldwide panic.” He added a line claiming the aliens are blind but have excellent hearing. Other users piled on with “the alien mothership is here” jokes (IBTimes UK, Marca).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Sunday, November 15, 2026 (morning edition)
item.description: Morning edition: the Elks in tonight’s Grey Cup, a fifth soldier’s death after the CFB Wainwright fire, Canada’s $560-million pledge for tropical forests, a U.S. Donbas-for-NATO question, Iran’s mined tankers in Hormuz, Tesla’s personal Cybercab orders, the push to reinstate Jensen Huang, SpaceX’s first Starship catch, LangChain’s $300-million raise, horses on a Detroit bus, a lassoed Ohio sheep, a sliding moose, and the Oilers in Philadelphia tonight.

item.title: The Elks play Montreal for the Grey Cup in Calgary tonight, their first shot at the trophy since 2015
item.description: Kickoff for the 113th Grey Cup is 5 p.m. Edmonton time at McMahon Stadium, on TSN. Edmonton (13-5) and Montreal (14-4) had the CFL’s two best records this season. The Elks beat the BC Lions 28-16 in the Western Final, and the Alouettes beat Winnipeg 33-23 in the East. The teams split their regular-season games, with the Elks winning 32-29 in overtime at Commonwealth Stadium in June and Montreal winning 48-30 at home in August (Edmonton Elks, TSN).

item.title: A fifth soldier, Pte. William Dal Bianco, dies of injuries from last month’s CFB Wainwright fire, with 24 others still in hospital
item.description: The Canadian Armed Forces said Private William Douglas Dal Bianco of the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, died on Nov. 13 in an Ontario hospital, where he’d been treated since the Oct. 17 fire. Of the 38 soldiers injured, 24 are still in hospital and 14 have been released (National Defence, Global News, AP).

item.title: Carney pledges up to $560 million to a Brazil-led fund that pays countries to keep tropical forests standing
item.description: Prime Minister Mark Carney announced the four-year contribution on Sunday after meeting Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva at the ASEAN summit in Manila. The Tropical Forest Forever Facility, co-led by Brazil and Norway and launched at last year’s COP30 in Belém, wants to raise US$35 billion from governments to draw in up to US$140 billion of private money. Investment returns would pay more than 70 countries for forest they can prove they’ve protected, with at least 20% going to Indigenous Peoples and local communities (Prime Minister’s Office, Bloomberg, The Jerusalem Post).
