item.title: U.S. negotiators ask whether Ukraine would leave Donbas in exchange for NATO membership, Zelensky says, the first time the idea has come up
item.description: “The Americans raised the question: ‘What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?’ This was the first time this issue had been raised,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told reporters, in remarks his office released Saturday. Donbas is the eastern region of Donetsk and Luhansk, part of which Russia has never managed to capture (Kyiv Independent, CNBC with Reuters).

item.title: Iran says three oil tankers caught fire after hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz, one of them a supertanker
item.description: Iran’s Revolutionary Guards navy said two tankers that had switched off their radar and tracking systems exploded and caught fire after striking a mine while trying to slip through the south of the strait on an unauthorized route; it said one was a supertanker. Iran’s regular navy said a third tanker hit a mine and stopped in a “prohibited zone” east of the strait. Neither named the ships or said where they were from (Reuters via CNA, AFP via Arab News, Anadolu Agency).

item.title: Tesla starts taking orders for a personal Cybercab at US$29,990, but it only works with a US$299-a-month subscription and inside Robotaxi zones
item.description: Tesla invited “select customers” on Friday to order the two-seat, steering-wheel-free car for personal use, with a US$1,000 non-refundable deposit and an estimated December delivery in Austin, Texas. The US$299 monthly “Autonomy Subscription” is mandatory: without it the car can’t drive, since there are no manual controls. It will only operate inside Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas, which are in Texas and Florida (Electrek, The Verge, TechCrunch).

item.title: More than 100,000 people, including Elon Musk, sign a petition to bring back Jensen Huang, as Nvidia’s board reportedly sounds out Arm’s CEO
item.description: The “Stand with Jensen” petition says Huang was pushed out “without meaningful due process” and asks the board to bring him back while an independent investigation runs. By Saturday afternoon its website listed more than 115,000 signatures, including about 6,000 people who say they’re current Nvidia employees; Musk, Replit’s Amjad Masad, Epic Games’ Tim Sweeney and Y Combinator’s Garry Tan signed on. Organizers said they were removing fakes, such as one signed “Xi Jingping” (TechCrunch, Business Insider).

item.title: Science corner: SpaceX catches a Starship spacecraft with giant tower arms as it returns from orbit, the first time a spaceship has been caught this way
item.description: Rockets usually throw away their upper stage, the part that reaches orbit. On Saturday, after 22 hours and 14 laps of Earth, SpaceX’s Starship spacecraft descended through cloud over Starbase, Texas, flipped upright and settled between two mechanical “chopstick” arms on its launch tower, nicknamed Mechazilla. SpaceX says its heat shield and other systems appear to have worked well (Al Jazeera with AP and Reuters, CNBC, The Verge).

item.title: LangChain, whose free tools are used to build AI agents, raises US$300 million and is now valued at US$3 billion
item.description: Alphabet’s CapitalG fund led the round, joined by IVP, Sapphire Ventures, Singapore’s GIC and DFJ Growth, the Wall Street Journal first reported. The San Francisco startup’s open-source software helps developers hook an AI model up to tools and instructions, link several agents into one workflow, and add steps where a human must approve sensitive actions (SiliconANGLE, Reuters, LangChain).

item.title: Two saddled horses climb onto a Detroit city bus and walk straight off the other end, and the city confirms the viral video is real
item.description: The riders led the horses up the front steps of a Detroit Department of Transportation bus near Seven Mile Road and Strasburg Street on Nov. 7, then out the rear door. The mayor’s office confirmed the video is real, and the city later released the bus’s own camera footage (Detroit Free Press, AP, WXYZ).

item.title: A teenage roper and her horse finally lasso a sheep that outran an entire Ohio town for 45 days
item.description: An American Blackbelly sheep had dodged volunteers, sheriff’s deputies and even drones around Wadsworth, Ohio, for more than six weeks. On Wednesday, Reagan Crumpler rode out on her 18-year-old horse, Catalena. After hours of near-misses, she told her horse, “Come on, Cat. We got this,” and they got in front of the sheep and roped it (New York Post, UPI, News 5 Cleveland).

item.title: A moose steps onto an icy Anchorage driveway and slides all the way to the street on its backside
item.description: Jeremy Saporito’s security camera caught the moose stepping off his lawn early on Tuesday, Nov. 10. Its hooves went out from under it on the sloped, icy driveway, and it slid down on its rear end before reaching the road (UPI, Alaska’s News Source).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Saturday, November 14, 2026 (evening edition)
item.description: Evening edition: Alberta’s coming crackdown on speculative data centres, $200 million for Woodfibre LNG, Russia’s demand to move the world juniors, Carney’s auto-sector line in U.S. talks, buried cash in Hungary, a Turkey-Qatar defence pact, North Korea’s FaceStealer crypto scam, safer water-based batteries, DeepMind’s proof of Signal’s encryption, Kenzie’s duet with Benson Boone, and the Oilers in Toronto tonight.

item.title: Alberta will bring in a law as early as next week to shut out “speculative” data centres and keep big ones away from homes, the tech minister says
item.description: Technology Minister Nate Glubish told The Logic on Friday that the rules will target proposals with no real business plan, no customers or no financing, and projects on “terrible sites.” “That’s not something that Alberta is going to tolerate,” he said. The bill could also set province-wide limits on how close data centres and their power plants can be to homes, and deal with worries about farmland (The Logic).

item.title: Ottawa puts $200 million into B.C.’s Woodfibre LNG so the export plant near Squamish can ship up to 24% more gas to Asia
item.description: Energy and Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson announced the grant Friday. The plant on Howe Sound was designed for 2.1 million tonnes of liquefied natural gas a year; the money should push that to 2.5 to 2.6 million tonnes and lets the owners explore a second phase. It’s about three-quarters built, and the first cargo is expected to sail next year (Natural Resources Canada, The Logic, Vancouver Sun).

item.title: Russia demands the world juniors be moved out of Alberta or cancelled after Canada bars its players, and threatens to seek compensation
item.description: Russian Ice Hockey Federation president Vladislav Tretiak said the IIHF must either let Russia play, move the tournament, not hold it, or punish Hockey Canada, Russian state news agency TASS reported. He also said Russia could seek compensation and asked the IIHF ethics committee to sanction countries organising boycotts (Euronews, AP, Inside the Games).

item.title: Carney draws a line in U.S. trade talks: no deal unless Canada keeps a “viable” auto industry, and he reveals a long call with Trump, Greer and Miller
item.description: “This government will not settle for a deal with the United States that is not consistent with a viable Canadian auto sector,” Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters in Manila on Saturday, calling cars “one of the most challenging issues” in the talks. He said a “quite long, substantive conversation” with Trump this week also included U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller (The Canadian Press via Global News, The Globe and Mail, CP24).

item.title: Hungarian investigators dig up nearly US$20 million in cash, some buried in forests, in a bribery probe of one of Orbán’s former ministers
item.description: Hungary’s new National Asset Recovery and Protection Office said searches on Nov. 12 and 13 in Budapest and three other regions turned up forints, euros and U.S. dollars hidden in farm buildings, warehouses, a home, a safe in a remote spot and holes in the ground in forests. Its video shows officers digging after dark. Finance Minister András Kármán said 12 treasury workers needed eight hours to count it all (Al Jazeera with AP and Reuters, Euronews, DW).

item.title: Turkey and Qatar sign a mutual defence pact, promising a joint response if either is attacked, as the Iran war reshapes Gulf security
item.description: President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani signed the deal in Istanbul on Friday, one of five agreements from their yearly strategic committee. The two countries pledge a “unified position” against any outside armed attack on either one, and will hold joint exercises, train each other’s personnel and build weapons together (France 24 with Reuters and AFP, Anadolu Agency, Qatar News Agency).

item.title: North Korean hackers stole more than US$400 million in crypto by faking video calls with victims’ real friends, the FBI says, as the U.S. seizes their servers
item.description: The FBI calls the scheme “FaceStealer.” Hackers sent meeting invites from hijacked accounts, then played secretly recorded webcam clips of earlier victims so a trusted contact seemed to be on the call. A staged “technical problem” led targets to install malware, and in some cases the thieves waited more than a year before draining wallets. The U.S. Justice Department says it seized the cloud servers behind it and more than 900 recorded webcam videos (DW with Reuters and AP, U.S. Justice Department, BleepingComputer).

item.title: Science corner: a new recipe for the liquid inside water-based batteries lets iodine carry twice the charge, a step toward fire-safe grid storage
item.description: Big battery farms that store solar and wind power mostly use lithium-ion cells, which can catch fire and need mined metals like cobalt. Batteries that use water as their liquid are safer and cheaper but hold less energy. A UCL-led team got iodine, the material that stores the energy, to move four electrons each cycle instead of two (UCL News, Nature).

item.title: Google DeepMind’s AI agents mathematically prove that core parts of Signal’s encryption work as promised, in four weeks instead of years
item.description: DeepMind’s new AlphaProof Code system checked the compiled machine code of libsignal, the library behind the encryption in Signal and also used by WhatsApp and Google Messages. It proved key guarantees, such as that old messages stay safe even if a key is later stolen, using about 6.5 million lines of machine-checked proofs (Google DeepMind, WIRED, The Next Web).

item.title: A 13-year-old fighting cancer for the second time posts an Instagram video hoping to meet Benson Boone, and ends up singing “Beautiful Things” with him in front of 10,000 people
item.description: Kenzie Riddle, from Kingscliff in New South Wales, has Ewing’s sarcoma and is back in intensive chemotherapy after thinking she’d beaten it. A video of her and friends singing Boone’s hit, shared on Instagram by local musician Fergus Hogan, passed 600,000 views (ABC News Australia, Billboard).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Saturday, November 14, 2026 (morning edition)
item.description: Morning edition: Alberta rewrites high school graduation rules, Canada concludes free-trade deals with ASEAN and the Philippines, Trump, Xi and Putin set a first three-way meeting, old copper-line switches blamed for the U.S. ground stop, Applied Materials’ record quarter, chip-based laser cooling for quantum computers, demand for Anthropic’s IPO, superhero window washers in Omaha, and the Oilers in Toronto tonight.

item.title: Alberta cuts the core classes needed to graduate high school from 56 credits to 47, and makes gym mandatory right through Grade 12
item.description: Education Minister Demetrios Nicolaides announced the overhaul Friday at a Calgary charter school. Students will still need 100 credits for a diploma, but optional credits rise from 44 to 53. Grade 10 stays the same for English, social studies, math and science. In grades 11 and 12, the separate English and social studies requirements become 10 combined “humanities” credits, and math and science together need just five (Global News, Calgary Herald, Red Deer Advocate).

item.title: Carney closes two Asian trade deals in Manila: talks are done on a free-trade pact with the 10-country ASEAN bloc and a separate one with the Philippines
item.description: At the ASEAN summit in Manila on Saturday (local time), Prime Minister Mark Carney announced that Canada and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations had “substantially concluded” negotiations on a free-trade agreement. Ottawa says the deal, covering a region of almost 700 million people, could add nearly $2 billion to Canada’s economy and about 14,000 jobs, mainly in farming and manufacturing, with signing aimed for 2027 (Prime Minister’s Office, AP, Philippine Daily Inquirer).

item.title: Trump, Xi and Putin will hold their first-ever three-way meeting next week in China, with nuclear arms cuts and Iran on the agenda but not Ukraine
item.description: The White House said Friday the three leaders will meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, with the meeting set for Nov. 19. Spokeswoman Olivia Wales said Trump wants to talk about reducing nuclear weapons, which he considers “very dangerous.” Trump leaves on his Asia trip Monday (AP, The Japan Times, Anadolu Agency).

item.title: Overloaded 1980s-era switches and copper lines caused Friday’s U.S. ground stop, the longest since 9/11; flights resumed Friday night but delays will last days
item.description: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said switches and routers in the FAA’s older analog network, which still carries voice and radar data over copper lines, became overloaded with data, causing inconsistent radar and radio contact with planes. Newer digital equipment kept working. “It’s an old system that went down and went down everywhere,” he said (Los Angeles Times, AVweb, Al Jazeera).

item.title: Applied Materials posts the biggest quarter in its history, up 53% to US$10.4 billion, yet its shares fall 6% as supply shortages cap its outlook
item.description: The world’s largest maker of chipmaking equipment reported record fourth-quarter revenue of US$10.41 billion after the bell Thursday, with adjusted earnings of US$4.16 a share, both ahead of forecasts. It expects about US$11.1 billion in the current quarter, give or take US$500 million (Applied Materials, Seeking Alpha).

item.title: Science corner: Cornell puts the lasers that chill quantum-computer atoms onto a chip, cooling an ion three times faster than a standard lab setup
item.description: Trapped-ion quantum computers store information in single charged atoms held still by electric fields. Every so often the ions jiggle and have to be cooled with lasers back to almost perfect stillness, and that pause eats up most of a calculation’s time. Cornell engineers built the cooling light into the chip that traps the ion, shaping it into a steady “standing wave” (Cornell Chronicle, PRX Quantum).

item.title: Orders for Anthropic’s US$64-billion IPO hit six times the shares on offer by day three of its roadshow, ahead of a Nov. 18 pricing
item.description: Anthropic began marketing its stock to big investors on Nov. 10, offering 825 million shares at US$70 to US$78 each, which would raise about US$64 billion at the top of the range. It plans to set the final price Wednesday and start trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT on Thursday, Nov. 19 (Anthropic, CNBC, Yahoo Finance).

item.title: Spider-Man, the Hulk and Deadpool rappel down a children’s hospital in Omaha, washing windows and waving to young patients
item.description: A window-washing crew dressed as the Hulk, Wolverine, Spider-Man, Batman, Superman and Deadpool dangled from the roof of Children’s Nebraska hospital this week, cleaning windows while kids inside pressed up to the glass to wave. The hospital’s video of the visit spread widely ahead of World Kindness Day on Friday (AOL via PIX11 and Storyful, USA Today, ABC News).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Friday, November 13, 2026 (evening edition)
item.description: Evening edition: Alberta’s 2% royalty offer for new oilsands projects, Stelco recalls all 175 laid-off Hamilton workers, a nationwide FAA ground stop, the U.S. Supreme Court takes up Trump’s asylum ban, Microsoft’s day-long Outlook outage, a 367,500-pixel bionic eye, OpenAI’s ChatGPT Wallet, a Saskatoon cat rescue’s “Spite for Strays” windfall, and the Oilers in Toronto Saturday.

item.title: Alberta offers new oilsands projects a 2% royalty for their first five years, its biggest incentive yet in the push to double output by 2035
item.description: The province unveiled its Oil Sands Growth Program on Friday. Approved new mines, in-situ projects and expansions would pay a royalty of just 2% of gross revenue for their first five years of production, rising one point a year to 6% in years nine and 10. After that, or if a project misses its production, environmental or regulatory commitments, it drops back to the regular royalty system (Edmonton Journal, The Globe and Mail, Government of Alberta).

item.title: Stelco backs down and will recall all 175 laid-off Hamilton workers by Dec. 1, with back pay, after Ottawa threatened court action
item.description: Stelco said Friday it will restart its Hamilton finishing lines on Dec. 1 and bring back all 175 temporarily laid-off workers, paying them retroactively for the wages they missed. The company said it had lined up enough customer orders to restart, though it will take several weeks to get the lines running again (The Canadian Press via Global News, The Globe and Mail, Reuters via U.S. News).

item.title: The FAA orders every departing flight in the U.S. to stay on the ground after the country’s air traffic control centres lose communications
item.description: The Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop at 3:54 p.m. Eastern (2:54 p.m. Edmonton time) on Friday, holding all departing flights at U.S. airports “due to extraordinary circumstance and reasons for safety.” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said a communications problem was affecting all of the country’s Air Route Traffic Control Centers, the hubs that guide planes between airports. Planes already in the air could keep flying, and international flights headed to the U.S. were handled case by case (AP, The Washington Post, USA Today).

item.title: The U.S. Supreme Court agrees to decide whether Trump can shut off asylum at the Mexican border, with arguments likely next spring
item.description: The justices said Friday they will review a federal appeals court ruling that struck down President Donald Trump’s January 2025 proclamation declaring “an invasion” at the southern border and the Homeland Security guidance that stopped people who cross from applying for asylum. The case is called Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services (AP, SCOTUSblog, Supreme Court order list).

item.title: Microsoft’s Outlook and Teams outage stretches past 24 hours, forcing some firms back to fax and paper, before service finally starts to recover
item.description: Problems began Thursday morning Edmonton time and spread worldwide, knocking out Exchange Online, the cloud system behind Outlook email and calendars, along with Copilot and some security and admin tools. Microsoft says a large number of its servers unexpectedly went down, found no sign of a cyberattack and ruled out AI as the cause. By Friday afternoon a wider rollout of fixes was stabilising things, though the company still had no timeline for full recovery (Reuters, TechCrunch, The Guardian).

item.title: Science corner: a dome-shaped camera ‘retina’ with 367,500 pixels sees in colour across 160 degrees and spots motion while sending almost no data
item.description: Our eyes work so well partly because the retina is curved, so light lands in focus all the way to the edges. Flat camera chips need stacks of extra lenses to fake that. Engineers at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology have built a hemispherical artificial retina instead, using a 3D laser technique to pack 1,905 pixels per inch onto a dome. Their first version, in 2020, had just 100 pixels; this one has 367,500 (HKUST, Nature Materials).

item.title: OpenAI’s new ChatGPT Wallet lets its AI agents buy things for you, using one-time payment tokens and your approval on every purchase
item.description: OpenAI on Friday launched ChatGPT Wallet, which lets its “dots” agents finish a purchase after finding what you asked for. It was built with American Express, Mastercard and Visa: you add a card once, and for each purchase the card network hands the agent a single-use payment token instead of your real card number. You review and approve every purchase with a security check, and you keep your card’s usual rewards and fraud protections (OpenAI, CNBC, Bloomberg Law).

item.title: “Spite for Strays”: a divorcée’s $10,000 donation, made to annoy her ex, turns a Saskatoon cat rescue’s cheeky post into a $30,000 worldwide fundraiser
item.description: A supporter of SOS Prairie Rescue came into some money in her divorce and offered to match donations up to $10,000, knowing that spending it on rescue cats would bother her ex-husband. Rescue president Ashlyn Weninger wrote it up as a joke one Thursday night (“Somewhere, an ex-husband is having a very bad day”), and by the next morning it was circling the world (The Canadian Press via Global News, CTV News Saskatoon, WestCentralOnline).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Friday, November 13, 2026 (morning edition)
item.description: Morning edition: Alberta landowners told to refuse new oil and gas leases, Ottawa drops its appeal on the Impact Assessment Act, a default notice for Stellantis, Indonesia’s vice-president resigns, the Brooklyn collapse toll rises to eight, Cisco’s AI networking surge, light-steered cells from Penn State, Google’s Gemini 4 Hydrogen, Bears fans’ kindness on X, and the Oilers in Toronto Saturday.

item.title: Alberta’s main landowner group tells farmers and ranchers to refuse new oil and gas leases until the province deals with orphan wells and unpaid bills
item.description: The Alberta Surface Rights Federation sent Premier Danielle Smith a letter on Thursday saying it will now “actively recommend that landowners resist further energy development on their lands.” President Bill Heidecker, a central Alberta cattle rancher with dozens of inactive wells on his property, said the group’s private talks with the province had been ignored. “We’re pissed and we’ve had enough,” he told The Orchard (Reuters via EnergyNow, The Orchard, CTV News Calgary).

item.title: Ottawa won’t take its loss on the federal project-review law to the Supreme Court, and will rewrite the act instead; Smith says “Alberta wins again”
item.description: Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin’s office confirmed Thursday that the federal government won’t appeal an Alberta Court of Appeal opinion that found much of the Impact Assessment Act unconstitutional. In a 4–1 opinion released Oct. 9, the court said Parliament’s 2024 fixes didn’t cure the problems the Supreme Court flagged in 2023, and that the law still reaches into areas run by the provinces (The Hub, Canada’s National Observer, The Deep Dive).

item.title: Ottawa serves Stellantis a formal default notice over the Brampton plant sale and gives it 30 days to fix the breach or face a fight to claw back subsidies
item.description: After a four-way meeting in Toronto on Thursday with Stellantis, Unifor and Ontario failed to change the plan to sell the idle Brampton assembly plant to armoured-vehicle maker Roshel, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly served the automaker a notice of default on its 2022 federal funding agreement. Stellantis has 30 days to cure the alleged breaches; if it doesn’t, Ottawa says it can end the deal and seek repayment of subsidies with interest (The Canadian Press via CTV News, The Globe and Mail, AM800 CKLW).

item.title: Indonesia’s vice-president, the son of former president Joko Widodo, resigns after a court ruling questions whether his overseas schooling met the legal requirements
item.description: Gibran Rakabuming Raka, 39, handed his resignation letter to Indonesia’s People’s Consultative Assembly on Thursday. Court rulings had questioned whether his overseas education met the constitution’s requirements for the job, and lawmakers had begun pushing for impeachment. President Prabowo Subianto accepted the resignation “with a heavy heart” at the Merdeka Palace in Jakarta and hugged him at the end of his statement (AP, Reuters, The Straits Times, The Jakarta Post).

item.title: Brooklyn building collapse death toll doubles to eight, including two children, as investigators begin the slow search for a cause
item.description: Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Thursday that eight people died when a three-storey apartment building in Flatbush fell into a neighbouring construction pit: six adults and two children. Six died at the scene and two in hospital. At least 18 people were hurt, including four firefighters, and one person remains in critical condition (CBS New York, NY1, The Washington Post).

item.title: Cisco posts its fastest growth in more than 15 years, with record sales of US$18.5 billion, and now expects US$9 billion in AI networking orders from cloud giants
item.description: Cisco said Thursday that revenue in its fiscal first quarter rose 24% from a year earlier to US$18.5 billion, a record, and adjusted earnings rose 40% to $1.40 a share. Both beat Wall Street forecasts. The company raised its full-year revenue outlook to $74.8 billion to $75.8 billion (Cisco, Reuters via U.S. News, CNBC).

item.title: Science corner: tiny solar cells on a chip use light, not wires, to line up living cells, a step toward lab-printed tissue that grows the right way
item.description: When scientists bioprint tissue, the cells don’t stay where they’re put; they drift and spread. Gentle electric fields can steer them, but that usually means wires and electrodes poking into the sample. A Penn State team led by Ibrahim Ozbolat tried a wireless approach: they dotted silicon solar cells, some only 80 micrometres across, thinner than a human hair, in patterns across a chip (Penn State, Advanced Functional Materials).

item.title: Google’s new everyday AI model, Gemini 4 Hydrogen, replaces its “Flash” line and outscores a bigger sibling on a common benchmark while running faster
item.description: Google released Gemini 4 Hydrogen on Thursday, two days after opening its top-end Gemini 4 Carbon to developers. Hydrogen is the fast, cheaper model meant for everyday chats, coding and AI agents, and it drops the old “Flash” name. It reads up to a million tokens at once, about several long books, and offers four “thinking” levels (Google, 9to5Google, VentureBeat).

item.title: Bears fans searching X for “Burden” injury news find a struggling teen in Australia instead, and flood them with kindness
item.description: When Chicago Bears receiver Luther Burden left Sunday’s game with a concussion, fans searched X for “Burden.” What came up for many was a post from an Australian user named Yuri saying they felt like a burden. After one rude reply, Bears fans piled in with support, from “people love you, and now Chicago Bears fanbase loves you too” to “life is worth living homie, I promise” (CBS Chicago, The Mary Sue, We Got This Covered).

item.title: A four-year-old on a zoo field trip sings “God Bless America” to a rescued bald eagle, and the zoo invites him back
item.description: Ezekiel Saldana of Floresville, Texas, had been practising “God Bless America” in his after-school choir for Veterans Day. On a school trip to the San Antonio Zoo, he spotted a wooden American flag and a bald eagle and started singing on his own while his mom filmed. The video drew millions of views (News 4 San Antonio, Fox News, Hoodline).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Thursday, November 12, 2026 (evening edition)
item.description: Evening edition: Alberta’s $14-million AI boost for MRI scanners, Carney at the European summit in Dublin, the SS United States sunk as a reef, Scott Colom’s Mississippi Senate upset, Putin lets Europe into Ukraine talks, Nebius cuts its forecast, Jensen Huang resigns from Nvidia, self-sensing artificial muscles from Penn, OpenAI’s Daybreak security agents, and the Oilers head to Toronto.

item.title: Alberta puts $14 million into AI software that speeds up MRI scans, after a pilot on 10 machines added almost 12,000 exams
item.description: The province and Acute Care Alberta announced Thursday that they will spend about $14 million to install artificial-intelligence software directly on hospital MRI scanners across Alberta. The software, approved by Health Canada, sharpens images so that scans can be done in less time. A pilot on 10 scanners that began in April 2025 led to almost 12,000 more MRIs (The Canadian Press via Global News and CTV News, CityNews Edmonton).

item.title: In Dublin, Carney is again the only non-European leader at Europe’s big security summit, and he presses Greece and Cyprus on the Canada-EU trade deal
item.description: Prime Minister Mark Carney attended the European Political Community summit in Dublin on Thursday, the second time he’s been the only leader from outside Europe at the table. Leaders discussed economic resilience, security and Ukraine, and Carney joined a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on peace efforts and Europe’s security arrangements (Prime Minister’s Office, Global News, The Globe and Mail).

item.title: America’s record-breaking 1950s ocean liner is sunk on purpose off Florida to become the world’s largest artificial reef
item.description: The SS United States, a 990-foot liner longer than the Titanic, slowly went down on Wednesday about 22 nautical miles southwest of Destin–Fort Walton Beach. Crews flooded it without explosives, and it took hours to disappear; NPR reports it went under about 10 p.m. Eastern time and settled upright roughly 180 feet down. Okaloosa County bought the ship in 2024 after the conservancy that owned it couldn’t turn it into a hotel or museum (AP, NPR, Pensacola News Journal).

item.title: Democrat Scott Colom unseats Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by about 5,600 votes, becoming Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction
item.description: The Associated Press called the race for Colom on Wednesday, eight days after the Nov. 3 midterm vote, once updated counts from Jackson County put him ahead for good. The latest tally has him at about 474,800 votes to Hyde-Smith’s 469,200, or 49.2% to 48.7% (AP, NPR, The Guardian).

item.title: Putin agrees Europeans can join the next round of Ukraine peace talks, after U.S. envoys meet him in the Kremlin and then Zelenskyy in Dublin
item.description: U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff told Russian state TV after Thursday’s Kremlin meeting that “the Europeans will join at the next meeting.” Putin said Russia had never refused to talk with Europe, but warned that sending Western troops into Ukraine after a deal would restart the war. He also proposed a joint Russian-Ukrainian humanitarian mission to Kostiantynivka in eastern Ukraine (Reuters, AP, The Moscow Times).

item.title: AI cloud company Nebius cuts its 2026 sales forecast because data-centre space it rents is running late, and its stock drops about 17%
item.description: Amsterdam-based Nebius, which rents out Nvidia-powered computing to AI companies, said Thursday that some third-party data-centre capacity due this year, including a site in New Jersey, has slipped into the first half of 2027. It trimmed its 2026 revenue forecast to US$3 billion to $3.2 billion, from up to $3.4 billion, even though third-quarter revenue of $981 million beat estimates (Reuters via CNA, CNBC, The Next Web).

item.title: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia’s CEO; finance chief Colette Kress takes over for now and the stock closes down about 4%
item.description: Nvidia said Thursday that its board accepted Huang’s resignation as president, chief executive and director on Wednesday night, effective immediately. Chief financial officer Colette Kress, 59, becomes interim CEO while keeping her finance job, and longtime director Harvey Jones, a former Synopsys CEO, becomes the company’s first board chair. The board will consider inside and outside candidates for a permanent CEO (Nvidia, SEC filing, TechCrunch, Reuters).

item.title: Science corner: Penn engineers make soft artificial muscles that feel their own position, so a robot finger can play piano keys and robot eyes can hold a gaze
item.description: Soft “muscles” made from liquid crystal elastomers shrink when they’re heated, but they’re hard to stop halfway: they keep contracting or relax as they cool. A team led by Shu Yang and Cynthia Sung at the University of Pennsylvania threaded an ultrathin copper coil through a fibre of elastomer mixed with graphene. The coil does two jobs at once. It heats the fibre to make it contract, and its electrical resistance changes as the fibre moves, so it doubles as a built-in sensor (Penn Engineering, Advanced Functional Materials).

item.title: OpenAI launches AI agents that try to hack a company’s own apps and then write the fixes, and says firms will be only as secure as the AI they defend with
item.description: OpenAI unveiled two products in its Daybreak security line on Thursday. Daybreak Red Team, in early access, uses a fleet of AI agents to probe a company’s web apps for weaknesses, check bug reports from scanners and bug bounties, and test whether patches actually work. Daybreak Defense Factory scans codebases for flaws and drafts patches, using OpenAI’s GPT-6 Cyber model, and engineers review and approve each fix before it ships (The Register, OpenAI, The Deep View).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Thursday, November 12, 2026 (morning edition)
item.description: Morning edition: November wildfire advisories across Alberta, Ottawa bars Russian players from the world juniors in Edmonton and Red Deer, Spain’s first general strike in 14 years, a deadly Brooklyn building collapse, Russia’s U.S. ambassador dies, Foxconn’s record AI quarter, Nvidia’s board weighs ousting Jensen Huang, leaf-vein metamaterials from MIT, Gemini Robotics 2.5, a viral −15°C parka-testing room, and the Oilers head to Toronto.

item.title: It’s mid-November and Alberta is under wildfire advisories: Edmonton has had only 58% of its normal fall precipitation
item.description: A dry, unusually warm start to November has pushed fire warnings well past the usual season. Alberta Wildfire issued fire advisories on Nov. 9 for the Rocky Mountain House and Grande Prairie forest areas, citing dry conditions, strong winds and rising fire danger, and is asking people not to burn when winds top 15 km/h. Calgary issued a city fire advisory on Nov. 10, and Lethbridge banned all open fires in its river valley on Nov. 9, with several surrounding counties adding restrictions (Alberta Wildfire, City of Calgary, Global News).

item.title: Ottawa says Russian players won’t be allowed into the world juniors in Edmonton and Red Deer, even if they already hold Canadian visas
item.description: Secretary of State for Sport Adam van Koeverden said Wednesday that Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada will individually assess and stop Russian and Belarusian athletes and officials from entering Canada to compete at the tournament, which starts Dec. 26 in Edmonton and Red Deer. The ban covers players who already have valid visas, including Russians now playing in the Canadian Hockey League (The Canadian Press via Global News, AP, TSN).

item.title: Millions join Spain’s first general strike in 14 years, called by tenants’ groups over sky-high rents and home prices
item.description: The 24-hour stoppage on Wednesday was started by tenants’ associations and then backed by the big unions. Unions reported about 90% participation in the car and port sectors, many schools and universities closed or ran at minimum, and the tenants’ confederation said about 4 million people took part by midday. Pickets and burning-tyre roadblocks shut roads into Barcelona, and public transport there nearly stopped (The Guardian, AP, NBC News, EFE).

item.title: A three-storey apartment building in Brooklyn collapses into a neighbouring construction pit, killing four people and injuring at least 23
item.description: The building at 2625 Bedford Ave. in Flatbush came down just after 4 p.m. local time Wednesday, falling into a hole where crews had been digging that day for a new building on the next lot. FDNY Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said four people were killed and at least 23 hurt, seven of them children, and that officials didn’t yet know how many people might still be in the collapse zone (Gothamist, Engineering News-Record, NBC New York).

item.title: Russia’s ambassador to the United States, Alexander Darchiev, dies suddenly at 66
item.description: Russia’s Foreign Ministry said Wednesday that Darchiev had died in Moscow. Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said he died of a chronic illness she didn’t name. No funeral details were released (AP, Politico, ABC News).

item.title: Foxconn posts a record quarterly profit, up 34%, as AI server racks now bring in more than half its revenue
item.description: Hon Hai Precision, better known as Foxconn, said Thursday that it earned NT$77.5 billion (about US$2.35 billion) from July to September, up 34% from a year earlier and ahead of analysts’ forecasts. Revenue rose 46% to NT$3.02 trillion. Its cloud and networking division, which builds AI servers for Nvidia and big cloud companies, made up 54% of revenue, up from 51% the quarter before (Focus Taiwan, Reuters via Investing.com, Malay Mail).

item.title: Nvidia’s board meets late into the night on whether to oust Jensen Huang after a report of a second affair, and the stock drops about 8% after hours
item.description: The board met Wednesday evening after The Wall Street Journal reported it was preparing to force out the co-founder and CEO, minutes after The New York Times reported he’d had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice-president of health care, who reported to him. No decision had been announced by Thursday morning. Bloomberg reported the board is working with an outside firm on possible replacements (CNBC, The Verge, The Next Web/Reuters).

item.title: Science corner: MIT engineers 3D-print a material patterned like leaf veins, and it soaks up impacts better than neat honeycomb designs
item.description: Most engineered “metamaterials” repeat one tiny building block over and over, like a honeycomb. That works, but if one spot cracks, the identical cells around it tend to give way in the same manner. A team from MIT and Northeastern University tried the opposite: a web of beams of many different sizes, from microns to centimetres, like the veins in a leaf or a dragonfly’s wing. An algorithm draws random lines that get shorter and thinner each round, and two simple settings tune how stiff the result is (MIT News, Nature).

item.title: Google’s new robot brain ties bows and sorts car parts in Mercedes-Benz factories, hitting 96% success, and comes with an open test for tricking robots
item.description: Google DeepMind released Gemini Robotics 2.5, the AI model that turns instructions and camera video into robot movements. Google says it succeeds 30% to 100% more often than the previous version on lab tasks and works 20% to 30% faster. In tests, Apptronik’s Apollo 2 humanoid used it to tie a bow with five-fingered hands, a hard job because ribbon bends and flops (Google DeepMind, Ars Technica, The Verge).

item.title: “Only in Canada”: a Toronto store lets shoppers test parkas at −15°C, and the video tops 18 million views
item.description: Toronto- and L.A.-based creator Josie Ewing filmed herself stepping through two glass doors into the Cold Room at a Canada Goose store, a small fitting room chilled to −15°C and decorated with fake snowy rocks, so shoppers can see how a parka really feels before buying it. “Only in Canada would they have a −15 degree winter simulation room,” her caption reads, set to an instrumental O Canada (Know Your Meme, Index.hr).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Wednesday, November 11, 2026 (evening edition)
item.description: Evening edition: Alberta’s Remembrance Day ceremonies honour the four soldiers killed at Wainwright, a pilot dies after a Remembrance Day flypast in Quebec, U.S. charges in the foiled RAF Fairford plot, Abu Dhabi talks end with a prisoner-swap deal, Bank of Canada signals more hikes may come, CoreWeave soars, DeepMind’s AlphaGenome 2, Claude’s new office tools, a room full of thank-you cards for Jackie the eagle’s carers, and Flyers at Oilers tonight.

item.title: About 300 members of the soldiers’ own battalion march to the cenotaph as Alberta’s Remembrance Day ceremonies honour the four killed in the Wainwright training fire
item.description: The 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry paraded to the cenotaph in St. Albert on Wednesday, where Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton; Pte. Shaun Farrell, 23; Pte. Aidan Goulding, 23; and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, were remembered by name. The Globe and Mail reported that at least 2,000 people lined the downtown street for the service (Global News, The Globe and Mail).

item.title: A pilot in his 60s is killed when his small plane crashes near Saint-Georges, Que., minutes after flying in the town’s Remembrance Day ceremony
item.description: Quebec provincial police say the crash happened around 11 a.m. local time Wednesday in a wooded area near the Saint-Georges airport, in the Beauce region about 100 kilometres south of Quebec City. The pilot, a local man in his 60s, was alone on board and was pronounced dead at the scene. The city says he had just taken part in its Remembrance Day commemoration and was coming in to land when the plane went down and caught fire (Global News, Toronto Sun, The Globe and Mail).

item.title: U.S. prosecutors say a jailed operative for Tehran’s Revolutionary Guards used coded calls home to help plan September’s foiled attack on RAF Fairford, the British base hosting American bombers
item.description: An eight-count indictment unsealed in New York on Tuesday charges three men linked to Iran’s Revolutionary Guards and the Iraqi militia Kata’ib Hezbollah: Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, Mohsen Mohajeri and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani. Prosecutors say al-Saadi, held in a U.S. jail since May on earlier terrorism charges, passed messages through relatives in Iraq, and that al-Hassani then paid people in Britain to scout the base, buy vans and fuel barrels, research chemical accelerants and buy metal that could serve as shrapnel (U.S. Justice Department, The Guardian, Politico).

item.title: Two days of talks end with a deal for a large prisoner swap but no breakthrough on territory, and Kushner and Witkoff head to Moscow to brief Putin
item.description: The U.S.-brokered talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi, their first face-to-face round since February, closed Wednesday. Russia’s chief negotiator, Vladimir Medinsky, said both sides agreed on a large-scale exchange of prisoners and reached “mutual understanding” on some issues. U.S. envoy Jared Kushner called it “the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners” and said numbers would be settled Thursday. Russia’s TASS news agency says the swap should happen in two to three weeks (Al Jazeera, AP, Euronews).

item.title: Bank of Canada notes show its leaders think more rate hikes may be needed as high energy costs start feeding into other prices
item.description: The central bank’s summary of the talks behind its Oct. 28 decision, released Tuesday, shows the six-member governing council weighed holding its key rate at 2.25% or raising it to 2.5%. It chose the hike, its first since 2023, because oil was about US$35 a barrel above what it assumed in July and businesses were signalling they would pass more of their fuel, chemical, plastic and computer-chip costs on to customers (Bank of Canada, The Globe and Mail, Financial Post).

item.title: Shares soar almost 25%, their best day in more than three months, after CoreWeave says it expects an adjusted profit by early 2028
item.description: Investors piled back into the AI cloud company on Wednesday, the day after its results. CoreWeave closed up 24.7%, its biggest one-day gain in more than three months and its highest close in two weeks, after telling investors it would turn profitable on an adjusted basis in the first half of 2028 (Reuters via Investing.com, Yahoo Finance, CNBC).

item.title: Science corner: DeepMind’s AlphaGenome 2 predicts which cell types a DNA spelling change affects, matching in minutes a lab finding that took 18 months
item.description: Almost all of our DNA doesn’t code for proteins. Instead it works like a set of switches that turn genes up or down, and different switches matter in different cells. AlphaGenome 2, released Wednesday, takes a stretch of DNA up to a million letters long plus a chosen cell type, such as a gut immune cell or a heart muscle cell, and predicts how a single-letter change will affect gene activity in that cell. It was trained on measurements from more than 100 million individual cells across 68 tissues, and it can be pointed at a new cell state, like vaccine-activated immune cells, using a sample of just a few dozen cells (Google DeepMind, Nature, The Verge).

item.title: An AI office suite to rival Microsoft’s: Claude Sheets, Whiteboards and Meetings arrive, and Microsoft stock slips for a second day
item.description: At an event in San Francisco on Tuesday, Anthropic launched new Claude tools for office workers who don’t write code. Claude Sheets lets the AI build and edit spreadsheets alongside people, Claude Whiteboards gives teams a shared brainstorming board, and Claude Meetings can join a call, take notes and turn the discussion into tasks. Sheets and Whiteboards are in beta for all paid plans, Meetings is in beta for Team and Enterprise customers, and Claude Data, a dashboard tool, is now generally available (The Verge, TechCrunch, Anthropic).

item.title: Fans of Jackie, Big Bear’s famous livestream eagle, sent so many cards to the centre that cared for her that it papered a whole room with them
item.description: Jackie and her mate, Shadow, had been watched by millions on a nest camera above Big Bear Lake, California, since 2018. In July she was found weak and unable to fly after a fight with two younger eagles, and she was treated at the Ojai Raptor Center until she died in August (Los Angeles Times, NBC Los Angeles).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Wednesday, November 11, 2026 (morning edition)
item.description: Morning edition: an NDP bill to end doctors’ dual practice in Alberta, Carney slams Stellantis’s Brampton plant sale, a deadly fog pile-up in Bulgaria, the House shelves Hegseth impeachment, Costco’s US$30 special dividend, CoreWeave’s earnings beat, a robot that builds in orbit, Google’s new confidential AI chips, Punch the monkey all grown up, and Flyers at Oilers tonight.

item.title: An NDP private member’s bill would ban Alberta doctors from billing medicare and charging patients privately at the same time
item.description: Sarah Hoffman, the NDP’s critic for hospital and surgical health services, introduced Bill 214, the Alberta Health Care Insurance (Protecting Public Health Care) Act, in the legislature on Nov. 5. It would amend the Alberta Health Care Insurance Act to undo the government’s move to let physicians work in the public system and a private, patient-pay system at once. Doctors could still opt out of medicare entirely, but they couldn’t pick case by case who pays (Red Deer Advocate, Insurance Business, Legislative Assembly of Alberta).

item.title: Carney calls Stellantis’s sale of its idle Brampton car plant to armoured-vehicle maker Roshel a “betrayal” and vows to claw back public money
item.description: Stellantis confirmed on Monday that it sold its Brampton, Ont., assembly plant to Roshel, a Brampton-based maker of armoured vehicles, for an undisclosed price. The plant stopped making cars in late 2023 to retool for a new vehicle, but that work was paused in 2025 after U.S. tariffs on Canadian-made cars, and the planned Jeep Compass moved to Illinois. About 2,200 workers are still on layoff (The Globe and Mail, CP24, The Trillium).

item.title: Thick fog sets off pile-ups involving about 86 vehicles on Bulgaria’s main Sofia–Burgas motorway, killing 11 people
item.description: The crashes began around 7:10 a.m. local time on Tuesday on both sides of the Trakia motorway near Yambol, in southeastern Bulgaria. Officials say a bus and a truck collided in dense fog, with visibility down to about 30 metres, and dozens of cars and trucks piled in behind them. Rescuers had to cut people out of crushed vehicles, including tanker trucks (Euronews, DW, BTA).

item.title: The U.S. House votes 211–204 to shelve Thomas Massie’s bid to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
item.description: The House voted Tuesday to send the impeachment resolution to the Judiciary Committee, which effectively kills it. Massie, a Kentucky Republican who lost his primary this year and leaves Congress in January, was the only Republican to side with Democrats. His eight articles accused Hegseth of waging the war with Iran without approval from Congress, ignoring rules meant to limit civilian deaths, ordering deadly strikes on suspected drug boats, the seizure of Venezuela’s Nicolás Maduro, and retaliating against Sen. Mark Kelly (NBC News, CBS News, U.S. House Clerk).

item.title: Costco declares a record US$30-a-share special dividend, about US$13.3 billion in cash, and renews a US$4-billion buyback
item.description: Costco’s board said Tuesday it will pay the one-time dividend on Dec. 4 to shareholders on record at the close on Nov. 24. The company also approved a new program to buy back up to US$4 billion of its stock through November 2030, replacing a 2023 program under which it had already spent US$3.1 billion (Costco, GlobeNewswire, Yahoo Finance).

item.title: CoreWeave beats revenue forecasts with US$3.66 billion in the quarter and raises its outlook, easing some worries about an AI data-centre slowdown
item.description: The AI cloud company’s third-quarter revenue rose 168% from a year earlier to US$3.66 billion, ahead of the roughly US$3.55 billion analysts expected, and its loss per share was smaller than forecast. It raised its full-year revenue guidance to US$13 billion to US$13.3 billion and said its order backlog reached US$133 billion (CNBC, Investing.com, Dow Jones via Morningstar).

item.title: Science corner: a Caltech robot puts together part of an antenna frame in orbit, the first structure built in space by a machine
item.description: ASTRA, short for Autonomous In-Space Tensioned Reflector Assembly, is a box about one cubic metre in size holding a robotic arm, dispensers full of carbon-composite struts and aluminum joints, and an onboard computer. It launched in March on a SpaceX rideshare mission. In orbit it unfolded two sections of truss built on the ground, then picked parts out of its dispensers and snapped together a third section on its own (Caltech, Interesting Engineering, New Atlas).

item.title: Two more custom AI chips in one year: TPU 8tx keeps data encrypted while it’s being processed, and TPU 8i Max doubles up for huge prompts
item.description: Google added two systems to its eighth generation of Tensor Processing Units, its in-house AI chips, on Monday. TPU 8tx uses the same silicon as the training-focused TPU 8t, paired with AMD EPYC processors, and adds hardware-level confidential computing, so sensitive data and model weights stay protected even while the chip is working on them. Google says it’s aimed at governments and regulated businesses, and that some customers will be allowed to install it in their own data centres (Google, Data Center Knowledge, The Verge).

item.title: Punch, the orphaned zoo monkey who once clung to a stuffed orangutan, is now filmed gently watching over a newborn
item.description: Punch is a Japanese macaque at Ichikawa City Zoo, near Tokyo. He became famous online in February, when photos showed the tiny monkey, rejected by his mother, carrying a big orange plush orangutan everywhere. Staff had given him the toy for comfort and to help him build the strength to cling, as baby macaques do to their mothers (India Today, NDTV, Moneycontrol).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Tuesday, November 10, 2026 (evening edition)
item.description: Evening edition: Veterans’ House opens 40 homes for veterans in Edmonton, another big storm soaks B.C., Canada reimposes Iran sanctions, Storm Charles shuts Portugal’s schools and Web Summit, Pope Leo’s 2.5-million-person Mass, hot U.S. inflation, the Claude maker’s IPO price range, a megawatt gallium oxide chip, Gemini 4 Carbon, two feel-good viral clips, and Flyers at Oilers tomorrow.

item.title: A 40-unit home for veterans who have nowhere else to go opens in Edmonton’s Athlone neighbourhood, two days before Remembrance Day
item.description: Veterans’ House Canada cut the ribbon on Monday at its new Edmonton home, just north of the CN tracks in Athlone. The building has 40 permanent, affordable studio units for Canadian Armed Forces veterans who are homeless or at risk of it, plus on-site help with jobs, addiction and mental health. It also has a fitness room, a library, a garden, a meditation park and a park for service dogs and pets. Nine former service members have already moved in, and residents share a community meal every Wednesday (Edmonton Journal, CTV News Edmonton, Veterans’ House Canada).

item.title: Another “very robust” Pacific storm hits B.C., with up to 250 mm of rain forecast for Vancouver Island after weekend storms that left two people dead
item.description: Environment Canada has orange rainfall warnings out for west and central Vancouver Island, calling for 150 to 200 mm of rain, and possibly more than 250 mm in places, from Tuesday morning through Thursday morning. Howe Sound and the Sea to Sky corridor could get 120 to 160 mm. The B.C. River Forecast Centre has a flood watch for much of the south coast, Vancouver Island and the north Fraser Valley, and warns that rivers will rise quickly, with mild temperatures melting some high-elevation snow (Environment Canada, B.C. River Forecast Centre, Today in BC).

item.title: Canada reimposes sanctions on 11 Iranian banks, insurers and a tanker firm, a decade after lifting them under the nuclear deal
item.description: Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand announced on Tuesday that Canada is putting sanctions back on 11 Iranian entities it says contribute to Tehran’s nuclear and ballistic-missile programs or help finance violence abroad. Canadians are now barred from financial dealings with them. The list includes banks, insurance providers and a tanker company (Global Affairs Canada, The Canadian Press via The Globe and Mail).

item.title: Portugal closes schools nationwide and Web Summit cancels its second day as Storm Charles brings a risk of 160 km/h gusts to Lisbon
item.description: Portugal’s government ordered schools and non-essential public services across the mainland closed on Wednesday and banned access to the coastline, riverbanks and flood-prone areas as Storm Charles moves in. Lisbon is shutting its tunnels, parks, gardens and cultural venues from midnight. The weather service IPMA forecast gusts of up to 120 km/h, and forecasters warned that a rare “sting jet” could push gusts above 160 km/h, especially around Greater Lisbon (Euronews, The Next Web, Diário de Notícias).

item.title: Pope Leo draws an estimated 2.5 million people to Buenos Aires, his biggest Mass yet, after visiting a disability home hit by Milei’s cuts
item.description: The Vatican says about 2.5 million people attended Pope Leo XIV’s first Mass in Argentina on Monday at the Monument of the Spaniards in Buenos Aires. That is the largest crowd of his papacy, at the same site where John Paul II said the last papal Mass in Argentina nearly 40 years ago. The government declared a national holiday so people could attend, and President Javier Milei sat in the VIP section (The Associated Press via NBC News, El País, Buenos Aires Times).

item.title: U.S. prices rose 0.4% in October, a bit hotter than forecast, and traders now see a December Fed rate hike as a sure thing
item.description: The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics said consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, down from 0.6% in September but slightly above what economists expected, the second hotter-than-forecast month in a row. Core prices, which leave out food and energy, rose 0.3%. The bureau didn’t publish a year-over-year figure because of data-collection problems from October 2025. Futures markets now price a 100% chance that the Federal Reserve raises its key rate by at least a quarter point in early December, and some traders are betting on a half point. Fed Governor Christopher Waller said tightening is needed “sooner, rather than later” (Investopedia, The Associated Press, Yahoo Finance).

item.title: The Claude maker sets its IPO at $70 to $78 a share, which would value it at up to about US$1.4 trillion when it lists as “ANT”
item.description: In an updated filing on Tuesday, Anthropic said it will offer 825 million Class A shares at US$70 to US$78 each, raising US$57.75 billion to US$64.35 billion. At the top of the range it would be worth about US$1.404 trillion on a fully diluted basis. That is up from US$965 billion in a May funding round, but below the US$2 trillion it was reportedly aiming for a few months ago. Separately, AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC agreed to buy US$26 billion of non-voting shares at the IPO price, with Google and Nvidia putting in US$10 billion each (TechCrunch, Investopedia, Reuters via Investing.com).

item.title: Science corner: a six-chip gallium oxide switch handles a megawatt in bursts, more than 100 times what this class of chip had managed before
item.description: Engineers at the University of Hong Kong, working with Virginia Tech and Nanjing University, built a power module from six gallium oxide chips that switched 1,000 volts and 1,000 amps a thousand times a second. That is a peak of 1 megawatt, the first time a multi-chip module made from an “ultrawide-bandgap” semiconductor has reached that level. The work is published in Nature Communications (University of Hong Kong, Interesting Engineering, Nature Communications).

item.title: Google opens Gemini 4 Carbon, which it calls its strongest model yet, to paying developers and Ultra subscribers, and previews agent “swarms”
item.description: Google began rolling out Gemini 4 Carbon to the public on Tuesday, two weeks after giving it to a small group of cybersecurity defenders. It is available through the paid Gemini API in AI Studio and to business customers, and to Google AI Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app, AI Mode in Search and the Antigravity coding platform. Google says Carbon is built for long, multi-step coding, debugging and open-ended scientific research, while last month’s Argon model stays the better pick for most everyday work (Google, The Verge, 9to5Google).

item.title: South Carolina’s game-warden K-9s get picture day, and almost none of them will sit still for it
item.description: The South Carolina Department of Natural Resources tried to take official photos of its K-9 team. The dogs licked their handlers’ faces, wandered off their marks, chased squeaky toys, got the zoomies and barked at the camera. “Say cheese! Picture day with our K9 team went about as well as expected,” the agency posted. The behind-the-scenes video took off, and NBC’s Today show featured it on Nov. 6 (WCBD News 2, The State, WYFF 4).

item.title: An IndiGo pilot asks passengers to switch on their phone torches for Diwali, and the whole cabin lights up mid-flight
item.description: IndiGo pilot Pradeep Krishnan wished his passengers a happy Diwali over the PA system, reminded them it is the festival of lights, and asked everyone to take out their phones and turn on their flashlights. They did, and the darkened cabin filled with tiny beams of light thousands of feet up. Krishnan posted the video on Instagram with the caption “May every sweet you eat today magically turn into protein!” (India Today, NDTV, News18).

item.description: Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said on Monday that the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps was behind the Oct. 11–12 attacks, which took over digital thermostats on thousands of freezers and chiller …

item.description: Taking a tumour out of a kidney while saving the healthy part is fiddly work, because the organ shifts and squishes as the surgeon cuts, and the tumour you saw on the CT scan isn’t quite where it …

item.description: Meta Superintelligence Labs launched Muse Ember on Monday, its smallest and cheapest model so far. Meta says it is built for “the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, …

item.description: Iraqi photographer Othman Khamis Hilal filmed the moment on a rain-soaked, muddy road in Anbar province: a young boy wading carefully through deep puddles with his small sister held tight in his …

item.description: During a halftime corgi race at the Carolina Panthers–Denver Broncos game in Charlotte on Sunday, one dog in a Carolina-blue sweater ignored the race. …

item.description: Evening edition: triage doctors start in six Alberta ERs; a $2 stamp in 2027; Ottawa’s $22.1-billion supplementary estimates; the Kraków market-square shooting; Stephen Miller becomes Trump’s chief of staff; Airbnb’s blowout quarter; a cuff-free smartwatch hypertension check; an AI-found proof of the Aaronson–Ambainis conjecture; and Edmonton events.

item.description: Premier Danielle Smith said on her Saturday call-in radio show that physician triage teams were in place as of Saturday in six emergency departments. …

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Thursday, November 5, 2026 (evening edition)
item.description: Evening edition: Alberta’s new “Strong and Free” licence plate, eye surgeons vs. optometrists, Bill 39’s involuntary-treatment changes, a Nanos immigration poll, the $62.3-billion federal budget, Kutryk’s finished spacewalk, Paraguay’s president quits over a bank collapse, the Nasdaq’s 5.5% plunge, a Bank of England hike, a smell-sending wearable, Meta buying Conductor, SNL UK’s “Nigerian Wicked,” and Oilers vs Ducks tonight.

item.title: Alberta unveils its first new licence plate in more than 40 years: Moraine Lake, and a “Strong and Free” motto
item.description: Albertans can pick up a newly designed standard licence plate at registry agents starting Monday, Nov. 9. The plate shows Moraine Lake in Banff National Park and swaps the old “Wild Rose Country” line for “Strong and Free.” It is the province’s first new official plate design in more than four decades (Alberta.ca, Edmonton Journal, CTV News Edmonton, CityNews Edmonton).

item.title: Eye surgeons ask Alberta to reverse a new rule letting trained optometrists do laser treatments and minor surgery; the minister says no
item.description: Since Nov. 1, Alberta optometrists who complete extra training and get approval from their regulatory college may perform selected office-based laser treatments for glaucoma and minor procedures such as removing benign eyelid lesions and treating styes. Alberta is the first province to allow it (The Canadian Press, Edmonton Journal, Alberta College of Optometrists).

item.title: Bill 39 rewrites how Alberta’s involuntary addiction-treatment law will work before it opens next spring, and ends funding for some lab tests
item.description: The province tabled Bill 39, the Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2026 (No. 2), on Wednesday. It changes the Compassionate Intervention Act before it takes effect: applications would be triaged by risk and by how many beds are open, registered psychiatric nurses could apply for an order, applications could be withdrawn, and the rules on giving medication without consent are spelled out (Alberta.ca, Edmonton Journal, Red Deer Advocate/The Canadian Press).

item.title: Most Canadians still want fewer newcomers in 2027: 52% back lower immigration levels, a Nanos poll finds
item.description: A Nanos Research survey for CTV News, taken Oct. 31 to Nov. 2, asked about Ottawa’s plan to admit 380,000 permanent residents and about 385,000 temporary workers and students. About 52% of respondents said Canada should accept fewer, a level Nanos says has barely moved since March (Nanos Research, CTV News).

item.title: Ottawa projects a $62.3-billion deficit in “Masters of our Destiny,” pairing a 50% grocery-benefit boost with $36 billion in business write-offs
item.description: Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne tabled Budget 2026, titled “Masters of our Destiny,” in the House on Thursday. It forecasts a $62.3-billion deficit this fiscal year, about $62.5 billion next year and $52.9 billion in 2030–31. Ottawa says stronger growth, high oil prices and cuts to the public service, which is on track to shrink by 10%, trimmed earlier projections, but roughly $146 billion in new measures soaked up most of the gain (iPolitics, Parliament Today, Department of Finance).

item.title: Done in 6 hours 59 minutes: Kutryk and Menon bolt on the ISS’s eighth and final new solar array
item.description: Joshua Kutryk of the Canadian Space Agency and NASA’s Anil Menon wrapped up a 6-hour-59-minute spacewalk on Thursday after installing and deploying the last of eight roll-out solar arrays on the station’s 3B power channel. NASA says that completes a campaign begun in 2021 and lifts the station’s power-generating capacity from about 160 to about 215 kilowatts (NASA, Canadian Space Agency, The Globe and Mail).

item.title: Paraguay’s president quits, then is impeached 78–0, after a bank tied to him collapses and freezes the savings of 3 million people
item.description: President Santiago Peña announced his resignation in a video on X on Thursday, apologizing “if at any point I failed.” Minutes later the lower house voted 78–0 to impeach him, sending the case to the Senate, with members of his own Colorado Party joining the opposition. Vice-President Pedro Alliana was expected to be sworn in to serve out the term to August 2028 (NPR/AP, The Guardian, Infobae).

item.title: Nasdaq plunges 5.5%, its worst day since April 2025, as a Qualcomm warning sets off a chip-stock wipeout
item.description: U.S. stocks erased their post-midterm rally on Thursday. The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.52% to 24,315, more than 10% below last month’s record, which puts it in a correction. The S&P 500 dropped 4.36% to 7,353.73 and the Dow shed 1,833 points, or 3.44% (CNBC, AP, Yahoo Finance).

item.title: Bank of England raises rates to 4%, its first hike in more than three years, and warns another may follow
item.description: The Bank of England’s Monetary Policy Committee voted 8–1 on Thursday to lift Bank Rate a quarter point, from 3.75% to 4%, citing energy-driven inflation from the Middle East war. Catherine Mann voted for a bigger jump to 4.25% (Bank of England, The Guardian, Reuters).

item.title: Science corner: Scentronic, an AI “e-nose” and a scent-puffing wristband that can send a smell over the internet
item.description: Ohio State materials scientist Jinghua Li and colleagues have built a two-part smell system. An electronic nose samples the air and a machine-learning model names the odour; the result is sent online to a small wearable, worn as a wristband, necklace or ring, that atomizes tiny amounts of stored scent liquid to recreate it at the other end. The study is in Science Advances (Ohio State News, Science Advances, CNA).

item.title: Meta buys Conductor, a two-year-old startup that runs teams of AI coding agents side by side, and its cloud service shuts Nov. 20
item.description: Meta has acquired Conductor, a startup whose app lets software developers launch several AI coding agents at once, each working on a separate piece of a project in its own isolated workspace. Axios first reported the deal on Wednesday; Meta confirmed it but did not disclose a price (TechCrunch, Axios, The Verge).

item.title: SNL UK’s “Nigerian Wicked,” a Nollywood-style spoof with Cynthia Erivo as Glinda, passes 7 million YouTube views
item.description: In a three-minute pre-taped sketch from her Oct. 24 hosting turn on Sky’s Saturday Night Live UK, Cynthia Erivo swaps her movie role as Elphaba to play Glinda, opposite cast member Ayoade Bamgboye as the green witch, in a deliberately low-budget Nollywood take on Wicked. Instead of Oz, they head to “LagOz,” where Hammed Animashaun’s Wizard turns out to be much less rich than advertised (LateNighter, NME, Chortle).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Thursday, November 5, 2026 (morning edition)
item.description: Morning edition: UCP votes to legislate Alberta’s contested riding map, Edmonton’s 4.9% draft tax hike, Kutryk’s second ISS spacewalk, federal budget day, Europe flight bomb-threat diversions, Hormuz/Qatar tanker hits, Organigram’s Aurora deal, oil under US$100, AutoDNA’s self-driving lab, OpenAI Images 2.6, three feel-good viral clips, and Oilers vs Ducks tonight.

item.title: UCP MLAs vote to turn Alberta’s contested 91-seat riding map into a bill, as Nenshi vows a court fight
item.description: Premier Danielle Smith’s United Conservatives used their majority on Wednesday to pass a motion, 45 to 36, endorsing a proposed 91-seat provincial electoral map and urging the government to introduce a bill that would lock the new boundaries into law. Justice Minister Mickey Amery says he wants the legislation through by the end of the year, ahead of the scheduled Oct. 18, 2027, election (Edmonton Journal, The Globe and Mail, CTV News Edmonton, Global News).

item.title: Mayor Knack backs Edmonton’s draft budget with a 4.9% property-tax hike for 2027, saying about $20 a month more buys real services
item.description: Edmonton city council gave an early nod this week to a proposed 2027–2030 operating budget that would raise residential property taxes 4.9% next year, then 4.7%, 4.5% and 3.9% in the three years after. Mayor Andrew Knack said the increases are lower than the hikes of 2023–2026 and that roughly $20 a month more for a typical homeowner should fund better snow clearing, more police funding and five new fire halls (Global News, CTV News Edmonton, Taproot Edmonton).

item.title: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk heads outside the ISS today for his second spacewalk, to finish the station’s solar-array upgrade
item.description: Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk and NASA astronaut Anil Menon are scheduled to leave the International Space Station today for a roughly seven-hour spacewalk to install the eighth and final rollout solar array in an upgrade campaign that began in 2021. NASA says the arrays can raise the station’s power capacity by up to about 30%. Coverage begins on NASA’s live channels mid-morning Edmonton time (Canadian Space Agency, NASA, Space.com).

item.title: Budget day in Ottawa: Champagne tables Carney’s second budget this afternoon as economists warn against spending the oil windfall
item.description: Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne will table the federal Liberals’ 2026 budget in the House this afternoon around 4 p.m. Eastern (2 p.m. Edmonton). He has previewed a plan centred on affordability, cultural sovereignty and making the economy less dependent on U.S. shocks, after nearly 20 months of American tariffs and the Iran war’s effect on fuel prices (The Canadian Press, The Globe and Mail, Reuters).

item.title: More than a dozen European flights divert or land early after a fresh wave of bomb threats, the second scare this week
item.description: Airlines and airports across Europe scrambled on Thursday morning after bomb threats hit multiple commercial flights. Authorities said more than a dozen aircraft from cities including Copenhagen, Dublin, Helsinki, Madrid, Milan and Warsaw were targeted; several made emergency diversions while others landed at their destinations for searches. Inspections so far have found no explosives or suspicious devices (AP, The Guardian live blog).

item.title: A tanker is hit by projectiles off Qatar while Iran’s Guard says two oil tankers and a tug caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz
item.description: The British military’s UKMTO warned that a tanker was struck by two unidentified projectiles about 50 nautical miles north of Madinat ash Shamal, Qatar, late Wednesday. Crew status, damage and any spill were unconfirmed as of early Thursday (AP, UKMTO).

item.title: Organigram agrees to buy Edmonton-based Aurora Cannabis for about $561-million, topping Curaleaf’s hostile bid
item.description: Aurora Cannabis, the Edmonton-rooted medical grower, has agreed to a friendly takeover by Organigram Global worth about $561-million. Organigram is offering $7.80 a share in cash, shares or a mix — roughly a 21% premium to Curaleaf Holdings’ latest hostile cash offer of US$5 a share. Aurora’s board unanimously supports the deal; a shareholder vote is expected in December, with closing targeted for January 2027 if courts and regulators agree (The Globe and Mail, Edmonton Journal, company release).

item.title: Brent slides back under US$100 as traders bet the U.S. midterm rout cools Iran-war escalation risk
item.description: Brent crude settled more than 8% lower on Wednesday — its weakest close since late August — and was changing hands near US$96 early Thursday after briefly dipping under US$100. West Texas Intermediate was around US$88–89. Traders linked the sell-off to hopes that Democrats’ sweep of Congress will push President Donald Trump toward diplomacy rather than fresh strikes on Iran, even as analysts warn a renewed escalation could shove Brent back into the US$110–125 range (CNBC, Anadolu Agency, Gulf News).

item.title: Science corner: a Shanghai “self-driving” biology lab where AI agents and robots run DNA experiments from a single prompt
item.description: Researchers at Shanghai Jiao Tong University describe AutoDNA, a molecular-biology lab built so that a team of AI agents can design an experiment, drive more than 20 kinds of instruments and finish thousands of steps with almost no human pipetting. After the prompt, people mainly refill reagents and fix hardware. The work is published in Nature (Nature news, Nature research article, Shanghai Jiao Tong University).

item.title: OpenAI ships Images 2.6 with native GIFs, SVG export and a six-second “Flare” model for faster AI pictures
item.description: OpenAI released Images 2.6 on Wednesday across ChatGPT, Codex and its API. The company says generation is about 50% faster than the previous version, and developers get two API models: GPT-Image-2.6 Flare for quick drafts (as little as about six seconds at low quality) and Sunburst for higher-detail edits. New tricks include animated GIF output, SVG exports for sharp logos and icons, markup-guided edits and a “complexity” knob that controls how hard the model plans a scene (OpenAI, MarkTechPost).

item.title: A contortionist “stuck” in a tennis racket baffles the internet — and the man who filmed it says the performer walked it off
item.description: An 11-second clip shows a man with his torso and one leg jammed through a stringless tennis racket while bystanders argue about whether to help. A late-October repost drove more than 23 million views on X, with jokes that the fire department would talk about it for generations (USA Today).

item.title: A Sand Springs 12-year-old refills a stranger’s empty Halloween bowl with his own candy — then still says “trick or treat”
item.description: Chance Dunaway, dressed as the Cat in the Hat, found an empty candy bowl on a porch near 51st Street and 129th West Avenue in Sand Springs, Okla., around 9 p.m. on Halloween. He poured in two scoops from his own haul so other kids could have a good night too, then walked back up and cheerfully called “trick or treat.” A doorbell camera caught it; the video passed 110,000 views (News On 6, Hoodline).

item.title: Elmo drops a simple Election Day reminder — “Elmo loves you” — and exhausted voters reply in droves
item.description: On U.S. midterm Election Day, Sesame Street’s Elmo posted a short video: “Hi! Elmo doesn’t know who needs to hear this today, but remember, Elmo loves you.” Within two hours the Instagram clip drew more than 400 comments, from thank-yous to jokes that the message was for everyone “except Rocco,” Zoe’s pet rock (USA Today).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Wednesday, November 4, 2026 (evening edition)
item.description: Evening edition: Russia confirms Abu Dhabi talks with Ukraine next week, Serbia detains police over abuse of protesters, a British Ebola case evacuated from Congo, China extends tariff relief on canola meal, peas and lobster to 2028, a suspected grizzly attack near Bella Coola, an Edmonton police probe into a $20-million cellphone scam, De Havilland’s water-bomber expansion, CVS’s breakup plan, a Webb telescope ‘digital twin’, Google’s AI defaults for student accounts and a viral ‘Thunderstruck’ on mallets.

item.title: Edmonton police say a phone-delivery scam run from Pakistani call centres has cost Edmontonians an estimated $20 million
item.description: The Edmonton Police Service says callers posing as Rogers, Telus and Virgin Mobile offered free or deeply discounted phones and plans. Victims ordered real devices through their own carriers. Then a second call claimed the wrong phone had been shipped and asked them to send it to another address, where people tied to the ring collected the phones and resold them. Police link the scheme to several call centres in Lahore, Pakistan, and say it has run since at least October 2024 (EPS, Edmonton Journal, CityNews Edmonton).

item.title: Ottawa backs De Havilland with up to $2.5 billion in loans to double water-bomber output, adding about 1,200 jobs
item.description: Calgary-based De Havilland Aircraft of Canada says Export Development Canada and the federal government will provide up to $2.5 billion in financing. The money will pay for a second production line for its DHC-515 amphibious firefighting plane. Final assembly happens in Calgary for now and will move to De Havilland Field, the plant and airfield being built in Wheatland County, west of Strathmore. The company says the deal could put planes in customers’ hands as early as 2030; it had been sold out until about 2034 (Calgary Herald, De Havilland Canada, The Globe and Mail).

item.title: China keeps tariffs off Canadian canola meal, peas and lobster until the end of 2028, and Canada extends a steel break in return
item.description: After the first ministerial-level meeting of the Canada–China Joint Economic and Trade Commission in Beijing, Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu says China will keep suspending its 100% tariffs on canola meal and peas and its 25% tariffs on lobster and crab through the end of 2028. The relief had been set to expire on Dec. 31, 2026.
