In return, Canada is extending tariff remission on some Chinese steel and aluminum products that aren’t made in Canada (Global Affairs Canada, The Globe and Mail, BNN Bloomberg).

item.title: A mother and daughter are killed in a suspected grizzly attack near Bella Coola, B.C., and officers say more than one bear may be involved
item.description: Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed were reported missing on Sunday after going for a walk on Saturday on the Snooka West Trail near their home outside Bella Coola, on B.C.’s central coast. Searchers found Balcarras on Monday and Reed on Tuesday (The Guardian, The Globe and Mail, CBS News).

item.title: Russia confirms it will send negotiators to U.S.-brokered talks with Ukraine in Abu Dhabi next week, the first such round since February
item.description: The Kremlin says a Russian delegation led by Vladimir Medinsky will be in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10 and 11 for three-way talks with Ukraine and the United States. U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are expected to take part. Officials say the agenda covers post-war security arrangements, de-escalation and humanitarian issues. It would be the first trilateral round since meetings in Abu Dhabi and Geneva in January and February (Reuters, Anadolu Agency, CNBC).

item.title: Serbia detains elite police officers accused of torturing protesters in a government garage during last year’s anti-corruption demonstrations
item.description: Serbia’s interior ministry says it detained serving members of an elite police unit and one former officer on Wednesday. They’re suspected of using force and threats against several people held in the garage of the government compound in central Belgrade on Aug. 14 and 15, 2025, to get information from them and to intimidate and punish them. The ministry released only the suspects’ initials. Serbian media, including the public broadcaster RTS, report that the commander of the SAJ special anti-terrorist unit is among them (The Guardian, B92, RTS).

item.title: Ebola reaches a British patient for the first time in this outbreak as a health worker is flown from Congo to the U.K.
item.description: What changed: Since this outbreak was last covered here on Oct. 31, a British aid worker has become the first U.K. case and been flown home, and the death toll has passed 5,300.

item.title: CVS will break itself in two, splitting Aetna and Caremark from its 9,000 drugstores a decade after the Aetna megamerger
item.description: CVS Health says it will separate into two publicly traded companies by the first half of 2028. CVS Health, led by CEO David Joyner, will keep the Aetna insurer, the Caremark pharmacy benefit manager, specialty pharmacy, Oak Street Health and Signify Health. CVS Pharmacy, led by group president Prem Shah, will take the roughly 9,000 stores, mail-order pharmacy, MinuteClinic and the Health100 platform. Shareholders will own stock in both (CVS Health, Axios, Healthcare Dive).

item.title: Science corner: a software “twin” of the Webb telescope pulls a faint planet out of the starlight in two-year-old data
item.description: Northwestern University astronomers built FLIP, short for Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets. It models how the James Webb Space Telescope’s optics wobble and blur light, then tunes millions of settings so it can subtract a star’s glare and reveal faint planets beside it. Published in Nature on Nov. 4, the method was 2 to 15 times more sensitive than the standard technique on test targets (Nature, Northwestern University, Scientific American).

item.title: Google will switch Gemini and even Google Search off by default for K-12 student accounts, but schools can’t turn on Search without its AI
item.description: Google says Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Google Search will all be off by default for K-12 student accounts until school administrators turn them on. Vice-president Chris Phillips announced the change Tuesday. After pushback, Google said schools can turn on Search by itself, but it keeps AI Overviews and AI Mode, which is gaining a step-by-step “guided learning” option. That means there’s no AI-free Google Search for students (NBC News, AP, Education Week).

item.title: A Pittsburgh-area marching-band senior nails AC/DC’s “Thunderstruck” riff on mallets, and the clip passes 5 million views
item.description: The video shows Layla Clark, a senior at Thomas Jefferson High School in Jefferson Hills, Pa., playing the fast opening riff of AC/DC’s “Thunderstruck” on mallet percussion with her marching band’s front ensemble. The footage is from last season’s show. An Oct. 30 X post had about 5.3 million views by Nov. 3, and it spread further when composer John Mackey shared it on Threads and film producer Franklin Leonard reposted it on X (USA Today, TribLIVE, PennLive).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Wednesday, November 4, 2026 (morning edition)
item.description: Morning edition: Democrats win both houses of the U.S. Congress, Spain’s transport minister resigns over the Urda crash, Israel certifies its election, Carney says the U.S. is asking less in trade talks, Calgary’s Stage 4 water limits, an Alberta teen terrorism peace bond case, AMD’s record quarter, euro-area inflation at 4%, a light-sorting photonic chip, Tencent’s Hy4, two feel-good family videos, and new Edmonton events.

item.title: Calgary goes back under Stage 4 water limits today for about four weeks while crews hook up its new feeder main
item.description: City-wide Stage 4 water restrictions took effect in Calgary on Wednesday, Nov. 4, as crews begin connecting the replacement Bearspaw South Feeder Main to the rest of the water system. The City says the limits should last about four weeks, and the new pipe is targeted to be in service by the end of the year (City of Calgary, Calgary Herald, CityNews).

item.title: RCMP arrest a 17-year-old Albertan after months of online contact with ISIS-linked accounts and seek a terrorism peace bond
item.description: The RCMP’s Integrated National Security Enforcement Team says it began investigating in February 2026 after finding online correspondence between a user and accounts affiliated with the Islamic State group. Officers arrested a 17-year-old Alberta youth on Oct. 26. The teen was released on conditions, and the case first came before Fort McMurray Provincial Court on Tuesday, Nov. 3 (RCMP, Edmonton Journal, Global News).

item.title: Carney says Washington is now “asking less and offering more” in trade talks, and some of Canada’s red lines are off the table
item.description: Speaking at the Commonwealth leaders’ meeting in Antigua on Tuesday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said trade negotiations with the United States have become “more intense” since they collapsed in August. “They’re asking less and they’re offering more, but we’re not quite there,” he said (The Globe and Mail, Bloomberg, Global News).

item.title: Democrats win both the House and Senate in the U.S. midterms, flipping Senate seats as far afield as Kansas and Texas
item.description: Democrats will control both chambers of the U.S. Congress from January after Tuesday’s midterm elections, according to projections by AP and NBC News. They flipped at least seven Senate seats, in Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas, where James Talarico became the first Democrat to win a Senate race since 1988. The Guardian’s tally early Wednesday had Democrats at 54 Senate seats (including two independents) with two races uncalled, and at 228 House seats with about 70 races still to call; NBC projects Democrats will end with at least 258 House seats (AP, NBC News, The Guardian, Euronews).

item.title: Spain’s transport minister resigns over the Urda train crash, which has now killed 69, and quits the Nov. 29 election race
item.description: Óscar Puente announced at the end of a long parliamentary hearing on Tuesday that he is stepping down as transport minister and withdrawing his name from the Socialist lists for Spain’s early general election on Nov. 29. He had ruled out resigning several times since the Oct. 28 collision near Urda, about 130 km south of Madrid, in which a Renfe train ran into the back of a stopped Iryo train after a control centre let it proceed while an automatic safety system was down (The Guardian/AFP, Euronews, Politico Europe, Al Jazeera).

item.title: Israel’s election committee certifies last week’s results after finding no fraud, rejecting Netanyahu’s “stolen election” claims
item.description: Israel’s Central Elections Committee certified the results of the Oct. 27 vote on Wednesday after reviewing 9,069 polling stations and examining every complaint. It found no irregularities that compromised the election or changed its outcome. The committee’s chair, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, cast the deciding vote after Likud and Shas representatives abstained, and said those casting doubt on the results pose “a real danger” to Israel’s democracy (Al Jazeera/AP, AFP, Ynetnews).

item.title: AMD posts a record US$13.4-billion quarter as data-centre chip sales nearly double, and its shares jump about 8% after hours
item.description: AMD said Tuesday that third-quarter revenue rose 45% from a year earlier to a record US$13.4 billion, above the top of its own forecast. Data-centre sales, led by its Instinct MI450 AI chips and EPYC server processors, rose 97% to US$8.5 billion, almost two-thirds of the total. Adjusted earnings were US$2.09 a share, while gaming revenue fell 40% (AMD, CNBC, Investing.com).

item.title: Euro-area inflation hits 4%, a three-year high, as energy prices jump almost 21% and a December ECB hike looks likely
item.description: Annual inflation in the 21-country euro area rose to 4.0% in October from 3.8% in September, according to Eurostat’s flash estimate on Wednesday, the highest since September 2023. Energy prices were up 20.8% from a year earlier, while services inflation was 3.3% and food, alcohol and tobacco 1.6% (Eurostat, CNBC, Euronews).

item.title: Science corner: a fingernail-sized light chip that pulls a jumble of laser light apart into clean, separate beams
item.description: Engineers at Stanford and the Institute of Science and Technology Austria (ISTA) have built a silicon photonic chip, about the size of a fingernail, that takes in “partially coherent” light (a blend of light waves that only partly march in step) and sorts it into separate, completely independent beams. Physicists described how this could work in the 1980s, but the team says this is the first device to actually do it. The work is published in Nature Photonics (Stanford via Phys.org, ISTA, Nature Photonics).

item.title: Tencent releases Hy4, an open AI model it trained without hacking know-how to make it harder to turn into a cyberweapon
item.description: China’s Tencent released Hy4 on Wednesday, the newest model in its Hunyuan family, with image understanding, long-document handling, computer use and “agent” abilities for multi-step tasks. Tencent says it ranks among the top tier of open-source models and is available through its products and APIs now, with downloadable weights and safety documentation promised in the coming days (Reuters, Nikkei Asia, South China Morning Post).

item.title: A deaf Indianapolis dad “talks” to his 2-day-old daughter in sign language at 3 a.m., and she can’t take her eyes off his hands
item.description: In the video, Robert Haney, who lost his hearing to meningitis at age 3, signs to newborn Matilda, or Tilly, in American Sign Language in the middle of the night: “You are a beautiful girl. Your daddy is deaf. You’re hearing ... I can’t wait to teach you sign language. Mommy’s tired. I’m tired. But you’re worth it.” Tilly stares at his hands the whole time (TODAY.com, Fox 5 New York, Crescer).

item.title: An Atlantic City dad serves his grown daughter breakfast with a song and dance, once dressed as an Oompa Loompa, and fans now call him “Tío”
item.description: Miguel Batista, a Dominican dad in Atlantic City, N.J., has gone viral for videos in which he brings meals to his daughter Michelle, who is in her 30s, while singing, dancing and describing every dish. In an Oct. 27 clip he arrives as an Oompa Loompa with eggs, avocado, tostones and chicharrones. Michelle points out that her mom, Ramona, actually cooks the food and usually plays an instrument or sings along off camera (TODAY.com, Crescer).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 (evening)
item.description: Evening edition: Alberta’s Bill 38 on campus neutrality and tuition, Enoch Cree Nation’s 166 new homes, a Salvation Army survey on skipped meals, U.S. strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island, UN warnings on ice loss, Marathon’s refinery sale, a bacteria-powered computer, Anthropic’s IPO filing, and JD Vance as Dumbledore.

item.title: Alberta tables Bill 38: universities must stay officially neutral on political issues, and the 2% tuition cap ends after next year
item.description: Advanced Education Minister Myles McDougall introduced Bill 38, the Advanced Education Statutes Amendment Act, in the legislature on Tuesday afternoon. It would require Alberta’s public universities and colleges to adopt “institutional neutrality” policies, so the schools themselves can’t take official positions on political, social or ideological matters unrelated to their academic mission. Students, faculty and staff would keep the right to voice their own views, and the bill also sets minimum standards for student codes of conduct (Edmonton Journal, The Globe and Mail, The Gateway).

item.title: Enoch Cree Nation breaks ground on 166 homes to bring members back, backed by a $30-million federal infrastructure loan
item.description: maskêkosihk Enoch Cree Nation, just west of Edmonton, has started building 166 affordable single-family homes for members, aimed at a housing waiting list of about 350 families. The Canada Infrastructure Bank has closed a $30-million, 27-year loan for the roads, water and sewer lines, utilities and solar installations the homes need, the bank’s largest investment in an Indigenous housing project so far (Canada Infrastructure Bank, Edmonton Journal, Enoch Cree Nation via Newswire).

item.title: Nearly one in three Canadians skipped or shrank meals this year because food cost too much, Salvation Army survey finds
item.description: The Salvation Army’s 2026 Canadian Poverty and Socioeconomic Analysis, released Tuesday, found 31% of Canadians skipped meals or cut portions because they couldn’t afford groceries, up from 27% last year. Use of food banks and other community food supports rose to 15% from 11% (The Salvation Army, Global News, CityNews, Le Devoir).

item.title: U.S. hits Iran’s Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, calling it a limited defensive strike, as Iran sets terms to reopen the strait
item.description: The United States carried out strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island, in the Strait of Hormuz, on Monday. U.S. officials, speaking anonymously, said the strikes were limited, aimed at Iranian forces firing surface-to-air missiles at U.S. aircraft, and were not a return to major combat. Iranian state media had reported several explosions on the island. U.S. Central Command didn’t comment (Reuters, The Associated Press, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, Al Jazeera).

item.title: Two UN-backed reports warn that passing 1.5°C of warming would do lasting damage to glaciers, ice sheets and permafrost
item.description: Two reports released Monday by the UN Environment Programme and the International Cryosphere Climate Initiative say that overshooting 1.5°C of global warming, even temporarily, will bring “large-scale and in many cases irreversible” losses to the world’s ice: glaciers, polar ice sheets, permafrost, sea ice and polar oceans (AFP via France 24, The Guardian, ICCI).

item.title: Marathon Petroleum sells its Minnesota and North Dakota refineries to Icahn’s CVR Energy for US$4.2 billion as war-time margins soar
item.description: Marathon Petroleum, the largest U.S. refiner, agreed Tuesday to sell its St. Paul Park refinery in Minnesota and its Mandan refinery in North Dakota, plus a fuel-marketing business, to Carl Icahn-controlled CVR Energy for US$4.2 billion. Marathon gets US$3.45 billion and its pipeline arm MPLX gets US$750 million for related assets. The two plants can process 177,000 barrels a day; the deal is expected to close by year-end (Marathon Petroleum, CVR Energy, Reuters via Investing.com, Oil & Gas Journal).

item.title: Science corner: a McGill computer made of living bacteria that solves puzzles by multiplying through a maze
item.description: Ordinary computers check possible answers to a hard puzzle one after another, which can take impossibly long. A team led by McGill University bioengineer Dan Nicolau tried another approach: they etched a tiny network of channels in which each path stands for one possible answer to a classic maths problem, called subset sum, then let swimming bacteria loose inside (McGill University via TechXplore, Nanowerk, Microsystems & Nanoengineering).

item.title: Anthropic’s updated IPO filing shows almost US$17 billion in revenue in one quarter, and US$895 billion promised for computing power
item.description: Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI models, filed an amended IPO prospectus on Monday adding its third-quarter results. Revenue for the three months to Sept. 30 was about US$17 billion, roughly 12 times a year earlier, bringing nine-month revenue to US$33.24 billion (CNBC, Business Insider, Moneycontrol).

item.title: JD Vance dressed as Dumbledore for Halloween with his baby son as Dobby, and the internet had opinions about the wig
item.description: U.S. Vice President JD Vance posted a Halloween video in a long silver wig, pointed hat and shiny silver robe, holding his baby son in a knitted Dobby the house-elf outfit. “Vice President Dumbledore here with little Dobby the Elf wishing you a Happy Halloween. Have fun. Be safe. Eat a lot of candy,” he said. A family photo showed the rest of the Vances in Harry Potter costumes too (The Indian Express, The Independent, IBTimes UK).

item.title: Edmonton Oilers at New Jersey Devils
item.description: Tonight, 6:30 p.m. Edmonton time, Prudential Center, Newark.

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 (morning)
item.description: Morning edition: Porter’s first international flights from Alberta, Champagne’s small-business budget promise, the Komyshuvakha aid-centre bombing, Belgium’s government crisis, Europe’s supermarket-fridge cyberattack, Ryanair’s fuel squeeze, a robot that perfects solar films, OpenAI’s grid pledge, robots climbing Mount Tai, and Edmonton events.

item.title: Porter flies its first international routes from Alberta starting today, with Edmonton to Puerto Vallarta
Champagne promises Thursday’s federal budget will simplify taxes for small and medium-sized businesses
Russian bombs destroy a Ukrainian aid centre and its shelter in Zaporizhzhia, killing at least 31
Belgian PM De Wever offers to resign after budget talks collapse, and the King puts the decision on hold
Cyberattack switches supermarket fridges to defrost overnight in at least nine European countries
Ryanair’s half-year profit falls 15% as fuel costs double, and it weighs pay freezes and smaller cabin crews
Science corner: a robot that watches solar-cell films form in milliseconds, then learns how to make better ones
OpenAI pledges to cut up to a gigawatt of data-centre power use whenever the grid is under strain, starting in Georgia
Robots raced up China’s Mount Tai carrying eggs and watermelons, and a few of them tumbled down the stairs
Edmonton Oilers at New Jersey Devils
Jaryd’s News — Monday, Nov. 2, 2026 (evening)
item.description: Evening edition: Alberta’s wildfire season ends, the proposed riding map revealed, B.C. nations challenge Pacific Link, SCOTUS and California ballots, alert-app hacks, Oracle’s raise, silk fish vaccines, Meituan’s LongCat, and Edmonton events.

item.title: Alberta’s wildfire season ends with less than 3% of the usual forest burned, after a record-wet June
Revealed: Alberta’s proposed 91-riding map splits Lethbridge four ways, and two panel members say it breaks the panel’s own mandate
St’át’imc chiefs take Ottawa to Federal Court over fast-tracking the Pacific Link oil pipeline
Carney lands in Antigua for his first Commonwealth summit, pitching 56 countries on trade beyond the U.S.
Supreme Court turns down the Trump administration’s bid to wall off 20,000 California mail ballots on the eve of the midterms
Hackers hijack both Ukraine’s and Russia’s emergency-alert apps, pushing fake nuclear and chemical warnings overnight
Oracle files to raise US$20 billion in new shares and bonds for AI data centres, and its stock falls almost 9%
Science corner: tiny silk needles that vaccinate baby fish underwater, then melt away
Meituan, China’s food-delivery giant, launches a 1.6-trillion-parameter AI model built to code for hours on its own
A young jeweller gave Funke Akindele homemade earrings, and the star swapped them in on the spot, then cheered her business from the stage
Jaryd’s News — Monday, November 2, 2026 (morning edition)
item.description: Morning edition: Alberta’s first workday on permanent Alberta Time, the justice minister refuses to delay the 2027 election, six federal byelections on Dec. 7, 300,000 displaced in Yemen, the Oleshky truce ends, Marvell buys Lumentum, Affle buys Perion, a light-up electronic skin, SenseTime’s looped open model, a Chinese orphan’s wedding full of strangers, and new Edmonton events.

item.title: Alberta’s first workday on permanent “Alberta Time”: darker school mornings, a one-hour gap to Toronto, and some phones still showing the wrong hour
item.description: Clocks did not fall back on Sunday. Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, northwestern Ontario and the Northwest Territories stayed on daylight time, so Alberta now sits at UTC−6 all year, a setting the province calls Alberta Time (ABT). Today is the first school and work day under the new clock (The Canadian Press via National Observer, Calgary Herald, Government of Alberta).

item.title: Justice minister refuses to delay Alberta’s 2027 election, as the disputed riding-map report heads to the legislature
item.description: On Oct. 31 we reported that McClure asked MLAs either to drop the new riding map or to push back the vote. On Sunday the government turned down both options, and the boundaries report itself is due in the legislature this week.

item.title: Six federal byelections set for Dec. 7, from Saskatchewan’s Yorkton–Melville to three Quebec seats
item.description: Prime Minister Mark Carney announced Sunday that voters will fill six empty House of Commons seats on Dec. 7: Brantford—Brant South and Scarborough North in Ontario; Laurier—Sainte-Marie, Rosemont—La Petite-Patrie and Saint-Hyacinthe—Bagot—Acton in Quebec; and Yorkton—Melville in Saskatchewan (Prime Minister’s Office, Global News, CTV News, paNOW).

item.title: More than 300,000 Yemenis forced from their homes in two months as fighting flares in the west, UN migration agency says
item.description: The International Organization for Migration said Sunday that more than 300,000 people have fled fighting in western Yemen, almost all of them in September and October. Families face soaring prices, too little shelter and checkpoints that slow aid (IOM, Arab News, Khaleej Times, Free Malaysia Today).

item.title: Kherson braces for shelling again as the six-day Oleshky truce expires, after Ukraine moves 167 civilians to safety
item.description: The local ceasefire around Russian-held Oleshky in southern Ukraine expired late Sunday, and Anadolu reports neither side recorded a violation during it. Ukraine’s General Staff said its troops used the window to evacuate 167 civilians, including 22 children and 21 people with limited mobility, from threatened settlements in the Kherson region (Reuters via Investing.com, Ukrinform, Al Jazeera, Anadolu).

item.title: Marvell agrees to buy laser maker Lumentum in a US$115-billion all-stock bet on AI data-centre links
item.description: Chipmaker Marvell Technology will pay 4.5 of its own shares for each Lumentum share, about US$1,132 apiece, a 23.9 per cent premium to the Oct. 28 prices before deal talk leaked. Marvell shareholders would own about 67 per cent of the combined company and Lumentum’s about 33 per cent (Marvell, Reuters via Investing.com, CNBC).

item.title: India’s Affle will take Israeli ad-tech firm Perion private for US$420 million in cash
item.description: Affle agreed to pay US$11.70 a share for Perion Network, about 35 per cent above Friday’s close of US$8.70. Perion shares jumped about 31 per cent in premarket trading Monday (MarketWatch, ExchangeWire, InsideArbitrage).

item.title: Science corner: a paper-thin electronic skin that draws a picture of every touch in light
item.description: Most touch sensors turn pressure into numbers that software has to draw on a screen. A team at the National University of Singapore built one that draws the picture itself. Called eLuminator, it is about 70 micrometres thick, thinner than a sheet of office paper, and shines light in the exact shape and strength of each press (NUS via EurekAlert, Nature Communications, SmartWearGuide).

item.title: SenseTime gives away a 9-billion-parameter model that runs its own layers twice to think deeper
item.description: China’s SenseTime has released SenseNova-Loop-9B-Preview as an open model under the Apache 2.0 licence, with weights on Hugging Face and code on GitHub. It reads text and images and writes text, and is aimed at document reading, coding and tasks that call outside tools (TechNode, Hugging Face, GitHub, MindStudio).

item.title: An orphan in China with almost no family invited strangers to his wedding, and thousands drove to his mountain village to celebrate
item.description: Xu Chenghong, 24, from Zhaotong in Yunnan province, lost his father at three and was raised by his grandmother, who also died while he was a child. He saved more than 160,000 yuan to marry his girlfriend, Luo Chui, but worried there wouldn’t be enough guests to fill even a few banquet tables, so he invited the public on Douyin (AsiaOne, Malay Mail, Global Times).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Sunday, November 1, 2026 (evening edition)
item.description: Evening edition: Russia’s reinstatement and the world juniors in Edmonton and Red Deer, Canada–U.S. trade talks set to restart, Poilievre’s budget demands, Bulgaria’s first woman president, riots in Frankfurt, Mayon volcano evacuees, Aramco’s HUMAIN deal, the FBI blames North Korea for the Binance heist, Egyptian Blue brain imaging, DeepSeek’s open coding agent, a bus-stop bench that went viral, and new Edmonton events.

item.title: A sports court lets Russia back into world hockey, and its federation says its next stop is the world juniors in Edmonton and Red Deer
item.description: The Court of Arbitration for Sport ruled on Friday that the International Ice Hockey Federation must reinstate Russia, overturning the ban imposed after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine. The IIHF says the ruling touches five 2027 tournaments, starting with the world junior men’s championship that opens Dec. 26 in Edmonton and Red Deer. Russia’s federation named the Alberta tournament as its next major event (The Canadian Press via Sportsnet, CTV News, Daily Faceoff).

item.title: Canada–U.S. trade talks are set to restart after a Carney–Trump call, and Trump says Keystone XL is part of the deal
item.description: Prime Minister Mark Carney said on X on Sunday that he had a “good conversation” with President Donald Trump, building on recent talks about the outline of a trade deal, and that both teams would work “in the coming weeks” to deliver it. A source told The Globe and Mail the call happened Saturday and that formal negotiations, stalled since Canada walked away in August, should resume within days (The Globe and Mail, Reuters, Politico).

item.title: Poilievre’s budget wish list: no federal diesel tax until Canada Day, and cancel the Toronto–Quebec City fast train
item.description: In a letter to Carney ahead of Thursday’s budget, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre asked Ottawa to drop all federal taxes on diesel until Canada Day, suspend the GST on fuel until summer and permanently scrap what he calls the fuel standard tax (Global News, The Canadian Press via Toronto Star, The Canada Brief).

item.title: Bulgaria elects its first woman president, Iliana Yotova, who wants dialogue with Russia
item.description: Acting President Iliana Yotova won Sunday’s runoff with about 58 per cent of the vote, according to early results and pollsters, against roughly 38 to 39 per cent for former interim prime minister Andrey Gyurov, who conceded. Turnout was low, around 29 per cent by exit-poll estimates (DW, AP, Euronews).

item.title: Germany’s “Gen Z” protests turn violent in Frankfurt: 17 shops damaged and more than 100 police hurt
item.description: Tens of thousands of mostly young people rallied in dozens of German cities on Saturday under the banner “Gen Z regelt” (Gen Z takes charge), protesting school cuts, the cost of living and military conscription. Most marches were peaceful, but after police broke up the Frankfurt march in the evening, rioters smashed windows, looted five stores including a gun shop, set fires and threw petrol bombs, stones and bottles (Reuters, Tagesschau, ZDF).

item.title: Hundreds of Philippine families spend All Saints’ Day in shelters after Mayon volcano erupts
item.description: Mayon, the Philippines’ most active volcano, had a “moderately explosive eruption” on Friday, sending up an ash plume. The volcanology agency Phivolcs raised the alert to Level 3, meaning a new phase of magma eruption, and police sealed off the six-kilometre danger zone (Inquirer, ABS-CBN, GMA News).

item.title: Oil giant Aramco closes a US$2.6-billion deal for 49% of Saudi Arabia’s national AI company
item.description: Saudi Aramco has completed its purchase of a 49 per cent stake in HUMAIN, the AI company launched by the Public Investment Fund in May 2025; the PIF keeps 51 per cent. Aramco is putting in about 9.9 billion riyals (US$2.6 billion) in cash this year plus its own AI, computing and digital assets (Arab News, Argaam, Arabian Business, Aramco).

item.title: The FBI now blames North Korea for the record US$6.3-billion Binance heist
item.description: The FBI said Thursday’s theft from Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, was the work of TraderTraitor, the North Korean group also behind last year’s US$1.5-billion Bybit hack. It says the hackers are converting the stolen coins mainly into ether and will likely try to launder them through DeFi and instant-swap services, and it asked exchanges to block linked addresses (AP via PBS, Al Jazeera, Euronews).

item.title: Science corner: a 4,500-year-old Egyptian paint, rebuilt as glowing flakes that light up the living brain
item.description: Egyptian Blue, one of the first human-made pigments, coated ancient statues and tomb walls. It has a hidden talent: under near-infrared light it glows in a band that cameras can see through skin and bone. Swiss researchers have now turned it into ultra-thin flakes that glow far brighter (Empa via Nanowerk, News-Medical, Tech Times).

item.title: DeepSeek open-sources an always-on coding agent that waits in a GitHub repo and answers with pull requests
item.description: China’s DeepSeek has released dsh-superagent, a free, MIT-licensed research prototype from its Harness team. It watches one GitHub repository and, optionally, a Feishu chat; when an approved person asks for something, it opens a separate work session for that job and replies, often with a pull request (GitHub, MarkTechPost, AI Affairs).

item.title: A student kept sitting in the dirt at a bus stop, so the couple who lived there built her a bench, then a little library
item.description: Florida teachers Maren and David Douglass noticed on their security camera that a student assigned to a bus stop at the end of their driveway sat on the ground next to a busy road every morning. They were in hospital at the time for David’s cancer treatment, so they ordered a bench online and set it up as soon as they got home (People via Yahoo, Good News Network, The Times of India).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Sunday, November 1, 2026 (morning edition)
item.description: Morning edition: Pflag Canada says Alberta’s new school flag rules will keep Pride flags out, Enoch Cree Nation breaks ground on 166 homes, Ottawa’s five-month deficit nearly halves, Iran offers to reopen Hormuz in two days on its terms, a record 50 million early U.S. midterm votes, about 150,000 at Taiwan Pride, OPEC+ holds December output, an implant that burns off blood sugar, Anthropic’s reported talks for a Sturgeon County data centre, Apple Intelligence reaching China, and a fed-up s’more Lab.

item.title: Pflag Canada says Alberta’s new school flag rules will effectively ban Pride flags from January
item.description: Under Alberta’s new Flag Display Regulation, school boards must fly only the Canadian and Alberta flags outside their buildings during the school year starting Jan. 4, 2027. Any flag that would “constitute a political, social or ideological statement” by the board is not allowed, and boards that want to show a flag not on the approved list, such as a Pride flag, have to apply to the education ministry in writing (Edmonton Journal, The Globe and Mail, Government of Alberta).

item.title: Enoch Cree Nation breaks ground on 166 family homes just west of Edmonton, the first step toward 500
item.description: Enoch Cree Nation held a groundbreaking on Friday for a neighbourhood of about 166 homes, to be leased at affordable rates only to its members. The nation says about 350 families are on its housing wait list, and this is the first of five phases meant to deliver more than 500 homes (Edmonton Journal, Canada Infrastructure Bank, CFWE Northern Alberta).

item.title: Ottawa’s deficit for the first five months of the year is less than half last year’s, at $5.36 billion
item.description: The Finance Department’s monthly Fiscal Monitor shows a $5.36-billion deficit for April to August 2026, down from $11.07 billion in the same months of 2025. Revenue rose about 7 per cent to $215.54 billion, helped by personal income tax and GST, while customs duties and energy taxes brought in less (Finance Canada, The Canadian Press via CityNews, Reuters via Investing.com).

item.title: Iran says it could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days, if Washington meets its terms
item.description: Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Al Jazeera that talks with Qatari mediators had produced a plan to reopen the strait in two days, down from the five days Qatar had suggested. Iran’s conditions include lifting sanctions, fewer U.S. forces in the region, restored oil waivers and the release of its frozen funds (Dawn, Middle East Eye, Times of India, AP).

item.title: More than 50 million Americans have already voted ahead of Tuesday’s midterms, a record
item.description: More than 50.5 million early ballots had been cast by Saturday morning, according to a University of Florida analysis, already about 5 million more than all early votes in the 2022 midterms. Texas alone passed 7 million (The Guardian, Reuters via CNA, Aju Press).

item.title: About 150,000 people march through Taipei for Taiwan Pride, calling for an end to stigma seven years after marriage equality
item.description: Organizers estimated 150,000 or more people from Taiwan and abroad joined the 24th Taiwan Pride parade on Saturday, looping out from Taipei City Hall Plaza under the theme “Our Voices, Our Journey,” with more than 180 groups taking part (Focus Taiwan, AP, Taiwan News).

item.title: OPEC+ holds oil output flat for December, with Brent near US$118 and Hormuz still closed
item.description: Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria and Oman met online on Sunday and agreed to keep December production targets at September’s level, about 31 million barrels a day combined. Their statement announced no new increases and set the next meeting for Nov. 29 (OPEC, The National, Reuters via CNBC).

item.title: Science corner: a USB-stick-sized implant that burns off extra blood sugar with a dash of electricity
item.description: Swiss researchers at ETH Zurich have built an implant called ECHO that tackles high blood sugar without any drug. Inside is a graphite pad covered in tiny gold flakes dusted with platinum. When a small current runs through it, it turns glucose into gluconate, which the body either burns or sends out in urine (Science, ETH Zurich, Scientific American).

item.title: Anthropic is negotiating to lease an 800-megawatt AI data-centre campus in Sturgeon County, sources say
item.description: The Globe and Mail, citing two unnamed sources, reports that Anthropic, which makes the Claude chatbot, is in talks to be the tenant of Calgary-based Beacon Data Centers’ planned Heartland campus, about seven kilometres east of Gibbons, northeast of Edmonton. Neither company would comment, and no lease has been announced (The Globe and Mail, Reuters, Culture Alberta).

item.title: Apple Intelligence finally reaches China, with Alibaba’s Qwen built into Siri, in a beta starting Wednesday
item.description: Apple says its AI features will reach China in iOS 27.3. A developer beta arrives on Wednesday, Nov. 4, and the public release follows in December. Alibaba’s Qwen models power parts of Siri, Writing Tools and Visual Intelligence, much as ChatGPT does elsewhere (The Verge, The Next Web, China Daily, Xinhua).

item.title: A chocolate Lab named Tank becomes the chocolate in a s’more costume, and his glare wins 14 million views
item.description: Austin, Texas, dog owner Ally Floth sandwiched Tank between two cardboard graham crackers and puffs of pillow-stuffing “marshmallow,” turning the chocolate Labrador into the chocolate in a s’more. Her caption calls Halloween “his least favorite holiday,” and the video has topped 14 million views (TAG24, PetHelpful via Yahoo).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Saturday, October 31, 2026 (evening edition)
item.description: Evening edition: Elections Alberta warns the 2027 vote may need a delay or the old map, Canada’s big banks block personal AI agents, Poland’s top-court standoff, a US$2.1-billion Patriot sale to Ukraine partly paid by Canada, DoorDash buys Instacart, the Bank of Japan hits its inflation goal, a 3D chemical microscope for living cells, a shared AI-training opt-out, OpenAI’s smaller funding round, and Borneo firefighters celebrating rain.

item.title: Alberta’s chief electoral officer tells MLAs to shelve the new riding map or push back the October 2027 election
item.description: In a letter on Friday to Speaker Ric McIver and all 87 MLAs, Chief Electoral Officer Gordon McClure said Elections Alberta cannot properly roll out new electoral boundaries in time for the fixed Oct. 18, 2027, vote. He asked MLAs either to run that election on the current map, or to adopt the new map and extend the election date “where legally authorized and necessary” (Edmonton Journal, The Globe and Mail, The Canadian Press via CTV News Edmonton).

item.title: Canada’s biggest banks shut personal AI agents out of online banking, starting with RBC
item.description: Royal Bank of Canada says it is blocking third-party personal AI agents, such as Meta’s Muse, from logging in to online banking and its other secure digital services after a security review. Existing connections through those tools stop working; customers can still bank through RBC’s own app, website and phone lines (RBC, Bloomberg via Insurance Journal, The Globe and Mail).

item.title: Poland’s top court splits in two as a judge suspends its chief, and protesters face police for a second night
item.description: Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska on Friday ordered Constitutional Tribunal president Bogdan Święczkowski and his deputy suspended for a month, and said she was taking charge as the longest-serving judge. Święczkowski, who was appointed under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government, rejected the order and called it a “coup d’état” (Politico Europe, Euronews, NBC News).

item.title: Washington clears a US$2.1-billion sale of 500 Patriot interceptors to Ukraine, paid for partly by Canada
item.description: The U.S. State Department approved a possible sale to Ukraine of 500 PAC-3 MSE Patriot interceptors, plus parts and support, worth an estimated US$2.1 billion. Ukraine will pay with money from Canada, Germany and Norway routed through a U.S. program called Jumpstart, plus European Union loan funds. Lockheed Martin is the main contractor (AP, NBC News, The Guardian).

item.title: DoorDash agrees to buy Instacart for about US$17 billion, and Canada’s Competition Bureau will take a look
item.description: DoorDash will pay US$65 a share for Instacart, a 26 per cent premium to its Oct. 22 closing price and about US$17 billion in all, with at least 75 per cent in cash. The deal needs shareholder and regulatory approval and is expected to close in late 2027 or the first half of 2028 (Instacart and DoorDash, Reuters via Investing.com, Global News).

item.title: After 13 years of trying, the Bank of Japan says it has finally hit its 2% inflation goal
item.description: The Bank of Japan held its key interest rate at 1.25 per cent on Friday in an 8–1 vote, with one board member pushing for 1.5 per cent, and said underlying inflation had generally reached its 2 per cent target for the first time since it set the goal in 2013 (CNBC, Nikkei Asia, Euronews).

item.title: Science corner: a Tokyo microscope films the chemistry inside living cells in 3D, about 400 times faster than before
item.description: University of Tokyo physicists built a dye-free microscope that pulses mid-infrared light into a living cell. Each kind of molecule soaks up that light at its own frequency and warms very slightly, and visible light shone in from 11 angles picks up those tiny changes to rebuild a 3D chemical map of the cell (University of Tokyo, Nature Communications, Phys.org).

item.title: OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Anthropic agree to honour one shared ‘don’t train on my site’ signal
item.description: The four companies say they will respect a single token in a website’s robots.txt file that tells their crawlers not to use the site’s content for AI training, instead of making publishers block each company’s crawler one by one. The signal comes from a proposal at the Internet Engineering Task Force written by Anthropic’s Kevin Kelley (The Verge, Engadget, The Next Web, OpenAI).

item.title: OpenAI trims its fundraising goal by US$10 billion as the AI stock slide makes investors cautious
item.description: OpenAI is now seeking up to about US$20 billion in its latest funding round, down from about US$30 billion, after the Financial Times first reported the cut. The FT said the target valuation also fell, to US$1.25 trillion from US$1.4 trillion, as some investors trimmed their commitments before a Friday deadline (CNBC, Bloomberg, TechCrunch).

item.title: Firefighters in Borneo dance, jump and kiss the ground as rain finally falls after months of wildfire smoke
item.description: Video from Palangkaraya, the capital of Indonesia’s Central Kalimantan province on Borneo, shows exhausted volunteer firefighters leaping, dancing and bowing to the ground as heavy rain poured down this week. Months of forest and peat fires had choked the city in smoke, with its air-quality index reported to have peaked around 4,000 (The Indian Express, CNA, Channels Television).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Saturday, October 31, 2026 (morning edition)
item.description: Morning edition: Alberta’s single, frozen education property tax rate, the cost of removing Edmonton’s bike lanes, Ottawa fast-tracks Roberts Bank Terminal 2, a Supreme Court ruling on momentary inattention, Congo’s Ebola toll passes 5,000, the G20 in Atlanta, France’s Halloween protests, Western Sahara’s UN mission lapses, Exxon and Chevron highs, gold’s one-year low, a robot moth that grows a sensor, Google’s satellite haiku, OpenAI’s new teen limits, and Halloween events in Edmonton.

item.title: Alberta will charge one education property tax rate everywhere and freeze it for three years, trimming about $99 million
item.description: Starting with Budget 2027, Alberta will replace its town-by-town education property tax calculation with a single provincial rate: $2.65 per $1,000 of assessed value for homes and farmland, and about $3.98 for non-residential property. The rate is locked for three years, then reset and frozen again (Government of Alberta, CochraneNow, LiveWire Calgary).

item.title: Tearing out Edmonton’s bike lanes would cost $150 million to $170 million, city staff estimate, as a provincial bill looms
item.description: An internal city email to council puts the cost of removing bike lanes and active-transportation routes that took away a traffic lane at roughly $150 million to $170 million. The single biggest piece is 132 Avenue, which was fully rebuilt and would cost $100 million to $120 million to undo (CTV News Edmonton, Taproot Edmonton, Canadian Cycling Magazine).

item.title: Ottawa fast-tracks a $5.9-billion container terminal at the Port of Vancouver, aiming to open it four years sooner
item.description: The federal government has listed Roberts Bank Terminal 2 in Delta, B.C., as a project of national interest, giving it up-front certainty on the remaining federal permits. The three-berth terminal on a new artificial island would add 2.4 million containers a year, about 50 per cent more container capacity at Canada’s largest port (Transport Canada, Vancouver Sun, Canada News Media).

item.title: Supreme Court orders a new trial in the crash that killed a Vancouver toddler, ruling a moment of inattention can be dangerous driving
item.description: In a 5-4 decision, the Supreme Court of Canada ordered a new trial for Seyed Moshfeghi Zadeh, whose SUV ran a red light in downtown Vancouver in July 2021, was hit, and flipped onto a sidewalk, killing 18-month-old Ocean Oshi Noelle and badly injuring her father. He had been acquitted of dangerous driving (Supreme Court of Canada, Canadian Lawyer, Global News).

item.title: Congo’s Ebola outbreak passes 5,000 deaths, the second-largest on record, with no approved vaccine for this strain
item.description: Government figures released Friday show more than 5,000 people have died and more than 10,000 have been infected since the outbreak was declared in May. It has reached eight of Congo’s 26 provinces, and Uganda, Kenya and, last week, Nigeria have reported cases (AP, Reuters via Arab News, Al Jazeera).

item.title: G20 foreign ministers wrap up in Atlanta with no joint statement, after Europe refused a group photo with Russia’s Lavrov
item.description: Secretary of State Marco Rubio cancelled the traditional “family photo” at the meeting’s start after delegations including EU countries, Britain and Australia, said they would not pose beside Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov. (The Guardian, Euronews, DW).

item.title: France deploys 70,000 police for a third weekend of youth-led cost-of-living protests, on Halloween
item.description: Young people, students and unions march across France today for a third straight Saturday against living costs and school conditions. Authorities have banned marches in city centres; in Paris, the Council of State moved the route to the eastern edge, from Porte de Bagnolet to Porte de Charenton (Euronews, AP, France 24).

item.title: The UN’s Western Sahara mission loses its mandate at midnight after the U.S. and Russia block each other’s plans
item.description: The Security Council rejected two rival drafts on Friday. Russia vetoed a U.S. text that had 11 votes in favour, one against and three abstentions. Russia’s own extension then drew only three votes in favour, with the U.S. against and 11 abstaining (UN Meetings Coverage, AP, DW).

item.title: Exxon and Chevron shares hit all-time highs as tight diesel supply swells refining profits
item.description: ExxonMobil earned US$15.4 billion in the third quarter and Chevron US$9.9 billion, both beating analysts’ forecasts. Exxon’s Gulf Coast refineries ran at full capacity and Chevron’s U.S. plants at 98 per cent to meet tight global diesel demand (CNBC, Reuters via Investing.com, AP).

item.title: Gold sinks below US$3,900 to a one-year low and silver drops under US$50, pulled down by the tech sell-off
item.description: Spot gold fell more than 3 per cent on Friday to about US$3,880 an ounce, its lowest since October 2025, and silver lost about 6 per cent to break below US$50 for the first time in 11 months. Platinum and palladium also slid into “oversold” territory (Reuters via Longbridge, Kitco News, FXStreet).

item.title: Science corner: a robot moth with artificial blood grows a brand-new light sensor where UV light hits its wing
item.description: Engineers at the University of Tartu in Estonia and the Italian Institute of Technology 3D-printed a clear plastic robot shaped like a blue underwing moth and pumped about 3 millilitres of “artificial hemolymph” through veins in its wings. The fluid carries pyrrole, a chemical building block, and a light-activated starter (Advanced Science, Tech Xplore, Reflect.ee).

item.title: Google’s first data-centre satellite runs an AI model in orbit, and its first message home is a haiku
item.description: A Project Suncatcher prototype launched this month on a SpaceX Falcon 9 carries four Google TPU chips and up to 1 kilowatt of solar power. After about three weeks of checks, engineers prompted the onboard Gemma 4 model, and it beamed back: “Blue marble below / Data streams in silent grace / Starlight feeds my core” (Google, TechCrunch, The Verge).

item.title: OpenAI will cut off chats that fixate on violence and hold back weapons details from teen users
item.description: OpenAI says ChatGPT will be able to end conversations automatically when a user seems fixated on violence or harming others, and may pause accounts temporarily after repeated cases. For users under 18, it will restrict practical information on weapons and security systems even when a question looks harmless (OpenAI, Reuters via CNA, CNBC TV18).

item.title: A pizza delivery worker loses his cool at a $10 prank, and strangers raise more than half a million dollars for him
item.description: Video shows a young streamer approaching Walt, a Red Baron pizza delivery worker stocking freezers in a Michigan Meijer, and faking an Apple Pay sound to pretend he had taken $10. “My life is hard enough as it is,” Walt told him, saying he had four kids at home who went to bed without him and a mortgage he could barely pay (NBC Chicago, WDIV ClickOnDetroit, CBS Detroit).

item.title: Insulted by Trump, Norway’s tourism board answers with photos of its most stunning toilets
item.description: After President Trump called Norway a “shit house country,” Visit Norway reworked an old page on its scenic roadside restrooms, such as the Stegastein lookout and Ureddplassen, and declared that Norway makes toilets “great again!” (AP, Skift, NRK).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Friday, October 30, 2026 (evening edition)
item.description: Evening edition: Alberta approves one of Edmonton’s eight speed-camera requests, Premier Smith’s leaked texts, Parks Canada ends Banff’s rescue-dog program, the Canada-EU Alliance for the Future, Patrick Stewart dies at 86, Novaya Gazeta closes, Pope Leo votes by mail, Oleshky evacuation, Intel’s 29 per cent plunge, Canada’s stalled economy, a metallic carbon nanoribbon, the U.K. probe of Meta’s publisher terms, Reddit’s login shift, and Edmonton events.

item.title: Edmonton asked to switch eight speed-on-green cameras back on; Alberta says yes to one
item.description: The provincial government has approved just one of the eight intersections where Edmonton wanted to restore speed-on-green photo enforcement, a north-end crossing where crashes have increased. Four requests were rejected and three are still under review (Taproot Edmonton, CTV News Edmonton, Global News).

item.title: Leaked texts put Premier Smith on the spot: she told a separatist lawyer to wait for new petition rules
item.description: Separatist lawyer Jeffrey Rath posted screenshots of a June 30, 2025, exchange in which a contact labelled “Danielle” wrote, “told you not to submit before the new rules came in,” and later, “I told you and Mitch to wait til the new rules came in.” That was four days before her government lowered the signature threshold for citizen petitions (Edmonton Journal, Alberta Radio, The Deep Dive).

item.title: Parks Canada scraps its 55-year-old search-and-rescue dog program in Banff, and thousands sign a petition to save it
item.description: Parks Canada has eliminated its only dog-handler position, in Banff National Park, ending a program that has found avalanche victims, lost hikers and poachers since the early 1970s. The decision came days after the handler finished training a new dog to replace Leroy, who retired in August, and amid about $145 million in agency-wide cuts and roughly 500 job losses (Rocky Mountain Outlook, CTV News Calgary, Calgary Herald).

item.title: Summit ends with an “Alliance for the Future”: Carney sets June 2027 to make Canada the EU’s first associate member
item.description: As the two-day Montreal summit wrapped up, Carney, Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa announced more than 20 measures, including a competition-enforcement pact, work on linking instant-payment systems, full Canadian entry into the Horizon and Erasmus programs, and up to $2.5 billion in financing for Alberta’s De Havilland to build more water bombers in Wheatland County (Prime Minister’s Office, Euronews, The Guardian).

item.title: Patrick Stewart, Star Trek’s Captain Picard and X-Men’s Professor X, dies at 86
item.description: Sir Patrick Stewart died on Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles after what his family called a brief journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia, his publicist announced Thursday. He was 86 (AP, NPR, The Guardian).

item.title: “They killed us”: Novaya Gazeta, the Russian paper of Anna Politkovskaya and a Nobel-winning editor, will close Nov. 9
item.description: Novaya Gazeta, Russia’s best-known independent newspaper, said it will formally stop operating on Nov. 9, a day after authorities began evicting its last staff from their Moscow offices. “They killed us,” its editors wrote on Telegram, in a post that by law had to carry a “foreign agent” warning (RFE/RL, AP, NBC News).

item.title: Pope Leo mails in his ballot, the first pope known to vote in a U.S. general election
item.description: The Vatican confirmed that Pope Leo XIV, born Robert Prevost in Chicago, voted by mail in Illinois ahead of Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections. It is the first known ballot cast by a pope in a U.S. general election (Vatican News, AP, USA Today).

item.title: Buses roll out of Oleshky: hundreds of residents leave the besieged town, by way of Russia and Belarus
item.description: A convoy of 25 buses and ambulances entered Russian-held Oleshky on Friday, delivering food and medicine and carrying out people who wanted to leave. Those heading to Ukrainian-held land, just 5 km away across the Dnipro, must travel to Anapa in southern Russia, fly to Belarus, then take buses into Ukraine’s Chernihiv region (The Guardian, AP, Kyiv Independent).

item.title: Intel stock crashes 29 per cent, its worst day since the 1970s, on a weak forecast and a deadly plant explosion
item.description: Intel shares fell about 29 per cent on Friday after the chipmaker forecast fourth-quarter revenue of US$15 billion to US$16 billion and adjusted earnings of 25 cents a share, well below the roughly US$17.1 billion and 43 cents analysts expected (CNBC, Yahoo Finance, NDTV Profit).

item.title: Canada’s economy stalls for a second straight month, and an early read says it shrank in September
item.description: Statistics Canada says real GDP was essentially unchanged in August, the second flat month in a row. Retail rebounded 1.2 per cent and rail jumped 3.6 per cent on a record wheat crop, but wholesale trade fell 1.4 per cent and oil and gas extraction slipped for a third month as some oil-sands mines underwent maintenance (Statistics Canada, BNN Bloomberg, Financial Post).

item.title: Science corner: chemists build a carbon ribbon less than a nanometre wide that conducts like a metal
item.description: Researchers at the University of Science and Technology of China made the first precise nanoribbons built only from five- and seven-sided rings of carbon atoms, about 0.9 nanometres across. Theorists predicted in 1996 that such a carbon pattern could behave like a metal; nobody had been able to make it until now (Nature, Phys.org, USTC News).

item.title: Britain opens a competition probe into Facebook’s owner over terms that could let it feed publishers’ content to its AI
item.description: The U.K. Competition and Markets Authority has opened a formal investigation into whether Meta abused a dominant position with new commercial terms for publishers and advertisers. The terms could let it crawl businesses’ websites and use that content, including for AI products, without a meaningful way to opt out (CMA, Reuters via StreetInsider, Euronews).

item.title: Reddit will start requiring logins to shield its posts from AI scrapers, as AI search cuts its Google traffic
item.description: Reddit says it is moving to a mainly “logged-in experience,” with tests in some markets outside the U.S. this quarter and no date yet for everyone. It says the change protects its content from AI scraping, so it can license it to AI companies instead (TechCrunch, The Verge, Ars Technica).

item.title: Obama tosses his mic to an aide without looking, and a slow-motion replay racks up five million views
item.description: After stumping for Michigan Democrats Abdul El-Sayed and Jocelyn Benson in Detroit on Oct. 24, Barack Obama casually flipped his microphone to a waiting aide as he walked off. The El-Sayed campaign posted a slow-motion clip on Oct. 27 and it passed five million views on X, with users joking that he was “aura farming” (The Independent, WION, The Economic Times).

item.title: A Texas school board asks its retired janitor to unroll a red carpet, and she reads her own name on a new school
item.description: Marilyn Hampton cleaned buildings for Texas’s Aubrey school district for 39 years, while also buying supplies for kids, helping them study and running the football ticket booth. Invited to an Oct. 21 board meeting on a pretext, the 76-year-old was asked to unroll a small red carpet that read “Marilyn Hampton Elementary School” (The Guardian, WFAA, NBC’s TODAY).

item.title: A strawberry farmer’s real phone number ended up in a Chinese English exam, and one curious student finally came for dinner
item.description: For more than a decade, Beijing strawberry grower Wang Xinghai has fielded calls and messages from students across China, because an old ad of his, phone number included, was turned into an English reading-comprehension question. He tells each of them the same thing: study hard, and come visit after you graduate (Phoenix New Media, Xiaoxiang Morning Herald, Good News Network).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Friday, October 30, 2026 (morning edition)
item.description: Morning edition: Alberta skips the fall-back clock change, Ottawa’s first national-security plan in 20 years, Bay Street law-firm breaches, Salvadoran troops in Haiti, a ship sunk off Bulgaria, Israel’s final count, the record Binance theft, U.S. growth at 3.4 per cent, MIT’s magnetic muscle sensors, Meta’s Style Sketch, and Edmonton events.

item.title: No “fall back” for Alberta this Sunday: clocks stay put for good as the province moves to year-round Alberta Time
item.description: For the first time, most Albertans will not set their clocks back an hour on Sunday, Nov. 1. The province is staying on what it calls Alberta Time, which is UTC−6, all year, so the clock you use now is the one you keep through the winter (Government of Alberta, timeanddate.com, The Canadian Press).

item.title: Ottawa’s first national-security plan in 20 years says Canada must prepare for threats up to and including war, and names frontier AI as a top danger
item.description: Prime Minister Mark Carney released The Plan for a Stronger Canada on Thursday, the country’s first national-security strategy in more than two decades. The 13-page document covers defence, foreign policy, economic security, public safety and intelligence, and says Canada must be ready for everything from cyberattacks and economic coercion to a major war (Prime Minister’s Office, The Globe and Mail, National Post).

item.title: Hackers steal client files from two of Canada’s biggest law firms, McCarthy Tétrault and Davies
item.description: McCarthy Tétrault says it found a coordinated social-engineering attack on Oct. 22 in which an outsider got into some files, including client information, and it began notifying those affected on Oct. 25. A source told The Globe and Mail about 31,000 files were taken, a number the firm has not confirmed (McCarthy Tétrault, The Globe and Mail, The Logic).

item.title: About 2,000 Salvadoran soldiers land in Haiti to hunt for four missing colleagues and take on the gangs
item.description: El Salvador has rushed roughly 2,000 troops to Haiti, days after four Salvadoran technicians serving with the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force went missing in a gang ambush. A security official says the deployment will be capped at about 2,500 for now (Reuters, AP, El Mundo).

item.title: Drones sink a Greek-owned container ship off Bulgaria; all 18 crew are rescued
item.description: The Liberian-flagged Contship Jet, chartered by Israeli line Zim and sailing from Haifa to Constanța, Romania, sank in the Black Sea after three sea drones struck it off Bulgaria’s coast on Wednesday. All 18 crew, 14 from the Philippines and four from Ukraine, were rescued and taken to Varna (AP, Maritime Executive, Naftemporiki).

item.title: Final Israeli count: Netanyahu’s bloc ends at 53 seats, eight short of a majority, and Likud calls the vote “stolen”
item.description: With all votes counted, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc won 53 of the Knesset’s 120 seats, short of the 61 needed to govern. Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition bloc took 48 and Arab-led parties 19. Likud is still the biggest single party, with 27 seats (Ynet, JNS, AP).

item.title: About US$6.3 billion drained from Binance in the biggest crypto theft ever; investigators point to Pyongyang’s TraderTraitor hackers
item.description: Starting around 2:05 p.m. Edmonton time on Thursday, an attacker moved about US$6.3 billion out of Binance wallets on 10 blockchains, most of it within 20 minutes. That is roughly four times the previous record, the US$1.5 billion Bybit hack in 2025 (TRM Labs via BleepingComputer, Chainalysis, AP).

item.title: U.S. economy grows at a 3.4 per cent pace, its fastest in a year, days before the midterms
item.description: U.S. gross domestic product rose at a 3.4 per cent annual rate from July to September, up from 2.2 per cent in the spring and above the roughly 3.2 per cent economists expected, the Commerce Department’s first estimate shows (U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, USA Today, Axios).

item.title: Science corner: tiny magnets implanted in muscle could let amputees steer a bionic leg more naturally
item.description: MIT engineers implant a few three-millimetre magnetic beads into the remaining muscles of a person’s leg. Sensors worn on the skin track how the beads move, so a computer knows how long each muscle is and how fast it is changing, wirelessly and in real time. The team calls the method magnetomicrometry (MIT News, Nature Sensors).

item.title: Meta quietly tests Style Sketch, an AI app that builds a closet from your Instagram photos and picks outfits from what you already own
item.description: Meta has released Style Sketch, a stand-alone app that scans your Instagram photos, or pictures you upload, to build a digital wardrobe. It then suggests outfits from clothes you already have, shows them on a model matched to your body shape and skin tone, and can plan a trip’s outfits around the weather and your schedule (TechCrunch, Gadgets 360, Storyboard18).

item.title: ChatGPT gets the blame: a Flávio Bolsonaro ally says the chatbot slipped “president-elect” into his deleted letter
item.description: Flávio Bolsonaro, who lost Brazil’s presidential runoff to Lula by more than four million votes, briefly posted a letter calling himself the country’s “president-elect,” then deleted it about an hour later and swapped in “leader of Brazil” (Reuters, NDTV, O Globo).

item.title: A five-year-old’s stuffed “Cakey Cat” falls down a storm drain, and a city worker has it back at her door within the hour
item.description: In Riverside, Ohio, a little girl dropped her favourite stuffed cat into a storm drain at her school bus stop. Her mom called the city, and public-services worker Kevin Miller came out with a grabber tool, fished it out and returned it about an hour later (People, UPI, Dayton 24/7 Now).

item.title: Dawid, a 26-year-old grey seal in Poland, rolls happily through autumn leaves and racks up more than 10 million views
item.description: A clip from Zoo Borysew near Łódź shows Dawid the grey seal rolling and wiggling through a pile of colourful fallen leaves. It passed 10 million views on Instagram and TikTok and was picked up by news outlets around the world (TVP Info, The Weather Channel, Zoo Borysew).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Thursday, October 29, 2026 (evening edition)
item.description: Evening edition: Alberta’s report-card and daycare-notice bill, official referendum results, Ottawa’s stake in Cohere, Kutryk’s completed spacewalk, the Dnipro station strike, the Oleshky aid convoy, the ECB pause and Lagarde’s early exit, Amazon’s miss, Alphabet’s record drop, an ultrathin chip material, Mistral Large 4 and a viral salon door.

item.title: Alberta moves to set province-wide report-card standards and make daycares warn parents fast about abuse or neglect
item.description: Education and Childcare Minister Demetrios Nicolaides tabled the Securing Parental Involvement bill on Thursday. It would let the minister set province-wide report-card standards, starting in the 2027–28 school year, while school boards still choose the format. Boards would have to tell parents what happens on non-instructional and professional-development days, and public boards would need the minister’s approval before naming or renaming a school (Government of Alberta, CTV News Edmonton, The Canadian Press via CityNews).

item.title: Referendum results are now official: 70.4 per cent turnout, the highest in a provincial vote in at least 50 years, and 74.95 per cent chose to stay in Canada
item.description: Elections Alberta released the certified results on Thursday. On the separation question, 1,556,316 people (74.95 per cent) voted to remain in Canada and 520,233 (25.05 per cent) voted to start the process toward a binding separation vote. The questions on provincial control over immigration passed, and the four constitutional questions were rejected (Elections Alberta, CTV News Edmonton, The Canadian Press via CityNews).

item.title: Ottawa will invest up to $1.6 billion for a stake in Toronto AI company Cohere, which promises to keep its headquarters and 1,000 new jobs in Canada
item.description: The federal government announced the equity investment on Thursday as part of a new funding round for Cohere, led by Germany’s Schwarz Group, that aims to raise about $7 billion and would value the company at roughly $36 billion. Nvidia and Bell are also investing (Prime Minister’s Office, The Canadian Press, Reuters).

item.title: Kutryk’s first spacewalk is a success: he and Anil Menon spend 7 hours 11 minutes outside and unroll a new solar array
item.description: Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk and NASA’s Anil Menon finished their spacewalk at 3:08 p.m. Eastern (1:08 p.m. in Edmonton) after 7 hours and 11 minutes. They installed and deployed the seventh of eight roll-out solar arrays on the International Space Station (NASA, Space.com, CBS News).

item.title: Russian drone hits a crowded train station in Dnipro, killing 14 people
item.description: A Russian jet-powered drone struck a platform at the station in Dnipro, central Ukraine, at about 11 a.m. local time on Thursday as a commuter train and a passenger train bound for Zaporizhzhia were stopped there. Ukrainian officials say 14 people were killed and 14 injured, including an 11-year-old. Passengers had been told to leave about 10 minutes before the hit (AFP, Kyiv Independent, Interfax-Ukraine).

item.title: Oleshky aid convoy cleared to roll: Russia and Ukraine say mine clearing is done and residents can start leaving
item.description: In nearly identical statements on Thursday, the human-rights commissioners of Russia and Ukraine, Yana Lantratova and Dmytro Lubinets, said routes into the Russian-held town had been demined and “the humanitarian convoy is ready for departure.” It will head to the district hospital, and residents who want to leave will be given a set window to go (Reuters, Kyiv Independent, AP).

item.title: European Central Bank leaves its rate at 2.5 per cent as Christine Lagarde announces she will step down early, in February
item.description: The ECB left its deposit rate unchanged on Thursday after raising it in June and September. Euro-area inflation is running at 3.8 per cent, nearly double the 2 per cent target, pushed up by energy prices that are 18.8 per cent higher than a year ago (European Central Bank, CNBC, Euronews).

item.title: Amazon shares slide after hours as profit and holiday-quarter forecast fall short, despite cloud sales jumping 39 per cent
item.description: Amazon reported third-quarter earnings of US$1.89 a share, below the roughly US$1.96 analysts expected, on revenue of US$201.94 billion, just under estimates. Its cloud arm, Amazon Web Services, grew 39.3 per cent to US$45.98 billion (CNBC, AP, Reuters).

item.title: Alphabet has its worst day ever, closing down 12.6 per cent and erasing about US$500 billion in value
item.description: Google’s parent fell 12.64 per cent on Thursday, its biggest one-day drop since going public. Investors reacted to negative free cash flow of US$9.1 billion, more than US$51 billion in quarterly AI spending and search revenue below expectations (CNBC, AP, NBC News).

item.title: Science corner: engineers keep a promising chip material working even when it is just a few atoms thick
item.description: Multiferroic materials have linked electric and magnetic properties, so data could be written with a tiny voltage and read back magnetically, using far less power than today’s chips. The catch is the “dead layer” effect: shave them thin enough for a chip and they stop working. A Brown University team led by Lucas Caretta reports in Nature Materials that it beat the problem in bismuth ferrite (Brown University, TechXplore, Six State Signal).

item.title: Mistral releases its trillion-parameter Large 4 model free to download, pitching it at cybersecurity work
item.description: Paris-based Mistral published the weights of Mistral Large 4, nicknamed “Le Chonk,” on Hugging Face on Thursday. It is a mixture-of-experts model with about one trillion parameters, of which about 52 billion are active for each word it produces (TechCrunch, The Verge, Mistral).

item.title: A salon glass door explodes on a new hire’s first shift, and her deadpan “Me when…” line wins over X
item.description: Security video from a salon in Katy, Texas, near Houston, shows a new employee gently sliding a glass door shut when it suddenly shatters into pieces around her. Nobody was hurt (KHOU, Inside Edition, USA Today).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Thursday, October 29, 2026 (morning edition)
item.description: Kutryk’s first spacewalk; Canada-EU summit opens without the “associate member” label; Alberta’s right-to-repair and lemon-law bill; North Korea missile barrage; Iran tanker mine claims; Eli Lilly lifts its forecast; Dutch AI-driven civil-service cuts; Liberty Biberty protest; Scare on the Square and new Edmonton concerts.

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Wednesday, October 28, 2026 (evening edition)
item.description: Evening edition: Alberta teachers one year after the back-to-work law, Quebec’s premier and the Canada-EU summit, Congo’s Ebola outbreak passing 10,000 cases, Spain’s crash toll and cause, the Fed’s split hold, Alphabet’s after-hours drop, the Bank of Canada’s hike, a snake-like gut robot, Gemini 4 Carbon, robot dog walkers, Samba the capybara, and Edmonton events.

item.title: A year after being ordered back to work, Alberta teachers say classes are still packed and the relationship with the province is “frosty”
item.description: One year after the province used the Back to School Act, with the notwithstanding clause, to end the teachers’ strike, Alberta Teachers’ Association president Jason Schilling says classrooms have not improved enough. He says some high school teachers report classes of 37 or more students, and that the government’s $200-million grant, meant to hire about 1,400 teachers, was aimed mostly at elementary and junior high schools (LiveWire Calgary, CTV News Edmonton, Edmonton Journal).

item.title: Quebec’s new premier is refused a speaking role at this week’s Canada-EU summit in Montreal, and turns down the dinner invitation
item.description: Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon asked to speak at the Canada-European Union summit, which runs Thursday and Friday in Montreal. Ottawa said no, and also declined Quebec’s request to host its own reception. Instead, the premier was invited to the leaders’ dinner and to greet EU leaders at the airport. He turned down both, accusing Ottawa on Facebook of offering Quebec little more than the chance to “serve the shrimp cocktails” (National Post / Montreal Gazette, Politico Europe, Le Journal de Québec).

item.title: Congo’s Ebola outbreak passes 10,000 cases, now the second-largest on record, as vaccine trials begin
item.description: The Democratic Republic of the Congo has recorded 10,141 cases of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus, with nearly 5,000 deaths, as of Monday, according to health ministry data shared by the World Health Organization. It is the country’s 17th and largest Ebola outbreak, and second only to the 2014–2016 West Africa epidemic. It has spread to eight provinces (UN News, AP, ABC News Australia).

item.title: Toll climbs to 68 as Spain says a control-centre order sent one train into another that was stopped on the track
item.description: Officials in Castilla-La Mancha say 68 people died in Wednesday’s crash near Urda, in Toledo province, with four bodies still trapped in the wreckage. Of the 544 people on the two trains, 107 went to hospital and 15 are in serious or critical condition. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez visited the site and declared three days of national mourning, Oct. 29 to 31 (The Guardian, AP, El Español).

item.title: The Fed holds U.S. rates at 3.75 to 4 per cent, but two officials vote to raise them
item.description: The U.S. Federal Reserve left its benchmark rate unchanged on Wednesday in a 10–2 vote. Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack dissented because they wanted a quarter-point increase to fight inflation (Federal Reserve, CNBC, Reuters).

item.title: Alphabet shares drop about 9 per cent after hours as heavy AI spending pushes its cash flow negative
item.description: Google’s parent company reported third-quarter revenue of US$127.58 billion, up about 25 per cent but slightly below forecasts. Search revenue of US$63.35 billion also missed. Spending on data centres and chips reached about US$51 billion, leaving free cash flow at minus US$9.07 billion, deeper than last quarter (CNBC, Reuters via Investing.com, AP).

item.title: Variable-rate borrowers will pay more after Macklem’s quarter-point move to 2.5 per cent, and more increases are possible
item.description: The Bank of Canada raised its key rate on Wednesday to 2.5 per cent, its first increase since July 2023. The bank rate is now 2.75 per cent and the deposit rate 2.45 per cent. Inflation is running near 3 per cent and the bank expects it to reach about 3.5 per cent by year-end; without gasoline it was 2.2 per cent (Bank of Canada, BNN Bloomberg, Financial Post).

item.title: Science corner: a snake-like soft robot can crawl through the small intestine to find and treat problems
item.description: Researchers at MIT and UT Southwestern have built a soft robotic scope that inches through the small intestine the way a snake or inchworm moves. Air-driven sections stretch and bend, while small balloons covered in tiny kirigami-cut needles grip the gut wall without damaging it. In tests in pigs it travelled about 2 metres (Science Robotics, MIT News, UT Southwestern).

item.title: Gemini 4 Carbon tops a major AI leaderboard, but at first only vetted cyber defenders can use it
item.description: Google has unveiled Gemini 4 Carbon, its new top AI model. For now it is only available to approved security teams through a new Fairwind Program, because the company says its hacking and bug-finding skills are strong enough to be misused. It ranks first on the independent Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, ahead of the newest models from Anthropic and OpenAI (Google, The Verge, Ars Technica).

item.title: Wanted: dog walkers, US$20 an hour. The catch: the dogs are robots, and you carry them home if they overheat
item.description: A San Francisco start-up called Dimensional posted an ad in a Bay Area jobs group on Facebook looking for people to walk its robot dogs on city sidewalks for four to six hours at a time. Applicants had to be able to carry about 33 pounds, because a robot that overheated had to be carried back to the office, which is in the Dogpatch neighbourhood (UPI, The New York Times via Quartz, Digital Trends).

item.title: Seven months after escaping, Samba the capybara turns up alive and well on a wildlife camera in England
item.description: Samba escaped from her enclosure at Marwell Zoo in Hampshire on March 17 and has dodged thermal drones, sniffer dogs and camera traps ever since. New photos from the zoo’s wildlife cameras show she is healthy and living on private land near the River Itchen (ITV News, The Independent, UPI).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Wednesday, October 28, 2026 (morning edition)
item.description: Morning edition: no leadership review for Smith and a pro-Canada pledge for party board hopefuls, the B.C. NDP’s interim-leader search, Spain’s deadly high-speed train collision, Israel’s count so far, today’s expected Bank of Canada hike, Celestica’s raised outlook, Nvidia’s Meta stake, laser-switched magnetism, Apple’s AI office apps, a Newfoundland whale rescue, and Edmonton events.

item.title: No leadership review before the next election, Smith’s party says, as would-be board members must pledge to respect the stay-in-Canada vote
