item.description: The governing party’s president, Rob Smith, told members in an email that at least 65 of its 87 constituency associations have declared support for Premier Danielle Smith, so there will be “NO UCP leadership review before our next general election.” Under party rules, 22 associations would have to ask for one. The Bonnyville-Cold Lake-St. Paul association voted for a review on Monday, the fourth to do so (The Globe and Mail, The Canadian Press).

item.title: B.C. NDP picks an interim leader this week after Eby quits over the snap-election loss
item.description: David Eby resigned as NDP leader on Saturday after the B.C. Conservatives won a 63-seat supermajority in the snap election he called. The NDP lost 19 seats. The outgoing 47-member caucus meets Wednesday and the new, smaller 28-member caucus meets Thursday to choose an interim leader, who will lead the Official Opposition (CTV News, Victoria News, Rob Shaw in North Shore News).

item.title: Two high-speed trains collide in central Spain, killing at least 30 people
item.description: A Renfe AVE train travelling from Madrid to Seville hit a stopped Iryo high-speed train near Urda, in Toledo province, at about 8:54 a.m. local time on Wednesday. More than 500 people were on board the two trains. Castilla-La Mancha’s regional president, Emiliano García-Page, said at least 30 people were killed and about 50 were seriously hurt, with roughly 80 injured in all (AP, Cadena SER, The Guardian, Reuters).

item.title: With most ballots counted, Netanyahu’s bloc rises to 54 seats but is still short of a majority
item.description: With about 84.5 per cent of ballot boxes counted, partial results from Israel’s Central Elections Committee give Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc 54 of 120 seats, Gadi Eisenkot’s bloc 49 and the Arab-led Joint List and Ra’am 17. A government needs 61. Turnout was 77.7 per cent, up from 70.6 per cent in 2022 (Times of Israel, Ynet, WION).

item.title: Bank of Canada expected to raise its key rate to 2.5 per cent this morning, its first hike in three years
item.description: Most economists in a Reuters poll, 19 of 34, expect the central bank to lift its overnight rate by a quarter point to 2.50 per cent when it announces at 7:45 a.m. MDT. It would be the first increase since July 2023, as an oil-driven jump in prices pushes inflation up (Reuters, The Globe and Mail, The Canadian Press).

item.title: Celestica shares jump about 12 per cent after the Toronto firm raises its forecast on AI data-centre demand
item.description: The Toronto-based electronics maker reported third-quarter revenue of US$5.83 billion, up about 83 per cent from a year earlier, and adjusted earnings of US$3.30 a share, beating forecasts. It raised its 2026 adjusted earnings outlook to US$11.55 a share from US$11.30 and lifted its revenue forecast (Celestica, Investing.com, MarketWatch).

item.title: Nvidia puts US$3 billion into Meta’s share sale and deepens their AI partnership
item.description: Nvidia will buy US$3 billion of Meta stock in an equity offering through which Meta plans to raise as much as US$95 billion for AI infrastructure. The companies also expanded their work on Meta’s Muse family of AI models, which will run on Nvidia’s upcoming Vera Rubin systems and networking gear (Nvidia, Reuters, CNBC).

item.title: Engineers flip a material’s magnetism with a shaped laser beam alone, no magnet needed
item.description: A team at the University of California San Diego focused an ultrafast laser into a tiny, specially shaped spot and used it to reverse the magnetic direction in a thin stack of platinum and cobalt layers. No outside magnetic field was needed, and the trick worked regardless of the light’s polarization (UC San Diego, Optica, EurekAlert).

item.title: Apple adds an AI assistant to Keynote, Pages and Numbers and lets outside AI agents edit your documents
item.description: Apple announced a beta assistant inside its office apps, built on Apple’s own models and OpenAI’s, that can draft text, build slides and work with spreadsheet data. It also added support for the Model Context Protocol, an open standard that lets third-party AI agents read and edit documents on Macs running macOS 27 or later (Apple, The Verge, 9to5Mac).

item.title: A Newfoundland town grabs buckets, hoses and the mayor’s excavator to push two stranded whales back to sea
item.description: When two pilot whales beached themselves at Point May, on Newfoundland’s Burin Peninsula, on Sunday, about 20 residents spent hours keeping them wet with buckets and hoses. Mayor Darren Harris brought his excavator to dig a channel, and a fishing boat helped guide the animals out (CTV News, VOCM, NTV).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Tuesday, October 27, 2026 (evening edition)
item.description: Evening edition: Alberta’s DEI hiring and deepfake bill, Edmonton council’s autonomy vote, the MAID advance-request bill, the Canada–UAE trade deal, Egypt’s vote on helping Saudi Arabia, Israel’s exit polls, Microsoft’s buyout offer, Boeing’s slower 737 ramp-up, folded-aluminum origami structures, DeepMind’s Genie 4, and Edmonton events.

item.title: Alberta moves to end DEI hiring at public bodies and to punish sharing sexual deepfakes, on the sitting’s first day
item.description: Justice Minister Mickey Amery tabled Bill 33, the Justice Statutes Amendment Act, 2026 (No. 2), on Tuesday afternoon as the legislature returned. It would stop provincial bodies, including agencies, Crown corporations, post-secondaries, school boards and municipalities, from using diversity, equity and inclusion policies in hiring and promotion, and would ban mandatory DEI training. Voluntary training stays allowed, and any mandatory training must be neutral and job-related (Edmonton Journal, CTV News, Global News).

item.title: Edmonton council votes 9–3 to push for more power from the province, as Mayor Knack meets the premier
item.description: Council passed Coun. Aaron Paquette’s motion to lobby for greater municipal autonomy through the Federation of Canadian Municipalities, Big City Mayors and Alberta Municipalities. Supporters pointed to provincial moves on infill rules and photo radar as overreach. Couns. Thu Parmar, Mike Elliott and Karen Principe voted against, warning it could hurt the city’s relationship with the province (Edmonton Journal, CTV News, Taproot Edmonton).

item.title: Ottawa tables Bill C-41 to allow advance requests for medical assistance in dying and to keep mental illness alone excluded
item.description: Justice Minister Sean Fraser introduced the MAID Safeguards Act on Tuesday. It would let adults diagnosed with a serious, incurable illness expected to take away their capacity, such as Alzheimer’s, sign an advance request so MAID could be provided later, once all eligibility rules and safeguards are met (Department of Justice Canada, Parliament of Canada, The Canadian Press).

item.title: Canada and the UAE sign a free trade deal negotiated in a record 47 days, cutting tariffs on more than 99 per cent of Canadian exports there
item.description: Trade ministers Maninder Sidhu and Thani Al Zeyoudi signed the Canada–UAE Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement on Tuesday, during the first-ever visit to Canada by Abu Dhabi’s Crown Prince, Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan. Ottawa says it is the fastest free trade agreement either country has negotiated (Prime Minister’s Office, The Globe and Mail, Al-Monitor).

item.title: Egypt’s parliament lets el-Sisi send military help to Saudi Arabia after Houthi attacks
item.description: Egypt’s House of Representatives voted by the required two-thirds majority to authorize President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi to give Saudi Arabia military support if Riyadh asks for it, following Houthi attacks on the kingdom (AP, The National, Euronews).

item.title: Exit polls: Netanyahu’s bloc falls to about 50 seats and neither side reaches a majority in Israel’s election
item.description: All three main TV exit polls (Kan 11, Channel 12 and Channel 13) gave Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition bloc 52 seats, Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc 50 and Arab-led parties 18, out of 120. A government needs 61. Likud is projected as the largest single party with 24 to 25 seats, ahead of Eisenkot’s Yashar at 21 to 23 (Reuters, AP, The Guardian).

item.title: Microsoft offers voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 workers, more than a quarter of its staff, including in Canada
item.description: Microsoft announced a “voluntary exit offer” for employees at level 70 and below on participating teams in the U.S., Canada, India and the U.K. About 60,000 people are eligible. Terms are similar to standard severance, with financial support and career-planning help (Microsoft, CNBC, GeekWire).

item.title: Boeing stock drops about 9 per cent as it pushes its 737 MAX production goal to late 2027
item.description: Boeing lost US$116 million, or 26 cents a share, in the third quarter. Its adjusted loss of 34 cents was wider than the roughly 21 cents analysts expected, though revenue rose 4 per cent to US$24.19 billion, helped by a 15 per cent jump in defence sales (CNBC, Investing.com, AFP).

item.title: Flat aluminum sheets, folded like origami, become rigid blocks that screw together into a room-sized shell with no welding
item.description: Researchers at the Center for Bits and Atoms in Cambridge, Mass., designed origami-style units, inspired by artist Ron Resch’s folded tessellations, that are cut from flat sheets by a CNC machine, folded by hand and screwed together. Each block is locked rigid, and together they form a load-bearing shell with no interior columns (MIT News, International Journal of Solids and Structures).

item.title: Google DeepMind’s Genie 4 builds playable 3D worlds with sound and lets you change them mid-scene by typing
item.description: Genie 4 is a “world model”: it generates an interactive, realistic scene you can move through in real time. New this version is native audio, including music, background sound and dialogue, plus the ability to steer a scene with text prompts, such as changing the weather or camera angle or adding people and objects (Google DeepMind, TechCrunch, The Verge).

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Tuesday, October 27, 2026 (morning edition)
item.description: Morning edition: Shane Getson quits the legislature, Anne Stevenson leaves the police commission, a possible U.S.–Canada steel and auto tariff deal, Chow re-elected in Toronto, a deadly tornado in Antalya, the Oleshky truce takes effect, Israel’s record turnout, HSBC and Whirlpool results, a heart-powered biohybrid mesh, noyb’s complaints against Scale AI, Maggie the runaway cow, and Edmonton events.

item.title: UCP MLA Shane Getson quits the legislature effective immediately, hours before the fall sitting opens
item.description: Shane Getson, the United Conservative MLA for Lac Ste. Anne–Parkland since 2019, resigned his seat on Monday, citing personal and family reasons. He said he could no longer give the job the time and attention it needs. The legislature reconvenes Tuesday afternoon (Edmonton Journal, CityNews/Canadian Press, Global News).

item.title: Coun. Anne Stevenson steps off Edmonton’s police commission to focus on prisoners released into Chinatown
item.description: Ward O-day’min councillor Anne Stevenson resigned from the Edmonton Police Commission effective Oct. 21, after five years as one of council’s two members. The commission announced it Friday (Edmonton Police Commission, Edmonton Journal).

item.title: Ottawa and Washington are working on a deal to ease U.S. steel and auto tariffs before next week’s midterms, sources say
item.description: Two U.S. and four Canadian sources told Reuters the countries are negotiating relief from Section 232 tariffs, including duties of up to 50 per cent on Canadian steel and 25 per cent on autos. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc have been in regular contact (Reuters).

item.title: Update: Chow beats Bradford by 13 points to win a second term as Toronto mayor; Sutcliffe holds Ottawa
item.description: Olivia Chow took 532,201 votes (54.2 per cent) to Brad Bradford’s 404,013 (41.1 per cent), winning 19 of 25 wards, including all five in Scarborough. Turnout was 45.8 per cent, with about 982,700 ballots cast (City of Toronto, CP24).

item.title: A tornado rips apart workers’ shelters at a construction site in Antalya, Turkey, killing four
item.description: The tornado struck a building site in the Fevzi Çakmak neighbourhood of Antalya’s Kepez district around 11 p.m. Monday, tearing apart two containers where five workers were staying and toppling a tower crane. Two died at the scene and two in hospital; the fifth is in good condition (Daily Sabah/Anadolu, AP).

item.title: Update: Guns fall silent in occupied Oleshky as the Melania Trump–brokered truce takes effect and holds
item.description: A local ceasefire began at 3 a.m. Kyiv time on Tuesday in Oleshky, a Russian-occupied town in Ukraine’s Kherson region, so aid can get in, roads can be demined and civilians can leave. Hours later it appeared to be holding, with both sides still fighting elsewhere (NBC News, Interfax-Ukraine).

item.title: Update: Israeli turnout hits its highest midday level in decades as voters pick a new Knesset
item.description: By noon Tuesday, 31.5 per cent of Israel’s roughly 7.3 million eligible voters had cast ballots, about 2.3 million people, up from 28.4 per cent at the same point in 2022 (Times of Israel, Ynet, Kan).

item.title: HSBC’s quarterly profit jumps 32 per cent to US$9.6 billion, but shares slide on a revenue miss
item.description: Europe’s largest bank reported third-quarter pre-tax profit of US$9.6 billion, helped by the absence of last year’s US$1.4 billion legal charge. Revenue rose to US$18.6 billion but missed analysts’ forecasts of about US$18.9 billion. It announced a new buyback of up to US$1 billion (HSBC, CNBC).

item.title: Whirlpool cuts its outlook for a third time and now expects a full-year loss; shares hit a 52-week low
item.description: The appliance maker posted an adjusted loss of 21 cents a share for the third quarter, against forecasts of about a US$1.04 profit. Sales fell almost 9 per cent to US$3.68 billion, below estimates, with North American major-appliance sales down 8.3 per cent (Whirlpool, Investing.com, Yahoo Finance).

item.title: Living heart cells power their own electronics: UMass Amherst’s “biohybrid mesh” turns each heartbeat into electricity
item.description: Engineers at UMass Amherst built an ultraflexible polymer mesh threaded with thin ribbons of PZT, a piezoelectric ceramic that makes a small voltage when it bends. They grew human heart-muscle cells into the mesh, and every time the tissue contracted, the ribbons flexed and produced current (UMass Amherst, Science Advances).

item.title: Privacy group noyb files five complaints accusing Scale AI of spying on the gig workers who train AI models
item.description: The Vienna-based group noyb filed GDPR complaints Tuesday in Austria, France, the Netherlands and Italy against Scale AI’s Outlier platform, which pays freelancers to write and rate answers used to train AI chatbots. It says up to 19 trackers log workers’ keystrokes and mouse movements every few seconds, and that workers must repeatedly pass face-video and ID checks (noyb, Euronews/AP, Reuters).

item.title: Maggie the runaway Highland cow outfoxes Carmel police for four days, including a lasso from a cruiser window, before going home to her calf
item.description: Maggie, a pregnant four-year-old Highland cow weighing about 700 pounds, slipped out of Little Cabin’s Farm in Carmel, New York, on Oct. 20, shortly after arriving from Massachusetts. Residents posted sightings for days as she wandered yards and woods (ABC7 New York, News 12).

item.title: Calgary Flames at Edmonton Oilers
item.description: The Battle of Alberta comes to Rogers Place. The Oilers (8-2-2) took a point Monday night but lost 4-3 to Detroit in a shootout. After the Flames, they head east to face the Islanders on Saturday.

item.title: Jaryd’s News — Monday, October 26, 2026 (evening edition)
item.description: Evening edition: Alberta optometrists cleared for minor eye surgery, Smith backs scrapping the tanker ban, Eric Bauza dies at 46, Carney’s Indian Act pledge, the Maurene Comey ruling, Israel’s election eve, Jordan’s Karak arrests, Anthropic’s IPO filing, Umios buys High Liner, MIT’s ultrasound brain implant, GPT-6.1 Terra, and Edmonton events.

item.title: Alberta becomes the first province to let optometrists do minor surgery and some laser eye treatments, starting Nov. 1
item.description: From Sunday, Alberta optometrists with extra training can remove benign skin lesions around the eye, treat styes and perform certain laser procedures, including some for glaucoma and for clouding after cataract surgery. The province says it is the first in Canada to allow this (Edmonton Journal, CityNews, Government of Alberta).

item.title: Smith joins the Conservative push to scrap the B.C. north-coast oil tanker ban, with a Commons vote set for Wednesday
item.description: The House of Commons debated Bill C-264 on Monday, a private member’s bill from Calgary MP David McKenzie that would repeal the Oil Tanker Moratorium Act. That law bars tankers carrying more than 12,500 tonnes of crude from B.C.’s northern coast. The Liberals asked for a recorded vote, now set for Wednesday (Canadian Press, Parliament of Canada).

item.title: Eric Bauza, the Toronto-born voice of today’s Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, has died at 46
item.description: Eric Bauza, who grew up in Scarborough, died at his home in Los Angeles. The Los Angeles County medical examiner listed the cause as hypertensive cardiovascular disease (AP, Variety, The Guardian).

item.title: Update: Carney promises a process to “move Canada beyond the Indian Act” after the first First Nations–first ministers meeting since 2005
item.description: Prime Minister Mark Carney told ministers to work with First Nations on a process to move past the 150-year-old Indian Act, whether that means reforming it or abolishing it. Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew held up his status card and said, “It’s time to abolish the Indian Act.” Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak said that choice must rest with First Nations, because the act also contains some protections (PMO, iPolitics, Canadian Press).

item.title: U.S. judge rules the Justice Department illegally fired prosecutor Maurene Comey, James Comey’s daughter
item.description: Federal Judge Jesse Furman in Manhattan ruled Monday that firing Maurene Comey in July 2025 broke the Civil Service Reform Act, because career prosecutors can only be removed for cause and with notice and a chance to respond. He called one of the department’s arguments one that “borders on frivolous” (court opinion, CNBC, AP).

item.title: Israel votes Tuesday, and the final polls show neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor Eisenkot’s reaching a majority
item.description: Israelis vote Tuesday, Oct. 27, with 37 parties on the ballot. The last polls show neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition bloc led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot reaching the 61 seats needed in the 120-seat Knesset. The opposition is polling at about 52 to 56 seats, Netanyahu’s bloc about 50 to 52, and Arab-led parties about 14 to 16 (Jewish Chronicle, Jerusalem Post, JTA).

item.title: Update: Jordan arrests three suspects in the Karak church attack after a three-hour gunfight
item.description: Jordanian security forces found two brothers and a relative hiding in an abandoned house in the Al-Jadeeda area. They refused to surrender, and all three were wounded, one critically, in a gunfight of about three hours. No security officers were hurt. Police said there was no sign so far that the men were linked to any other group (Al Jazeera/Reuters, AP).

item.title: Anthropic files to go public on the Nasdaq as “ANT,” showing $16.3 billion in revenue for the first half of 2026
item.description: Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI models, filed its S-1 with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday. It reported first-half revenue of $16.3 billion, up from $1.16 billion a year earlier, and its first positive operating cash flow, $3.9 billion. It still lost $80.7 billion on paper, mostly from a $72.4 billion non-cash charge tied to convertible notes (SEC filing, Fortune, The Verge).

item.title: Japan’s Umios agrees to buy Nova Scotia’s High Liner Foods for $27 a share, and the stock jumps 77 per cent
item.description: Umios, the Japanese seafood company formerly called Maruha Nichiro, will pay $27 cash per share for the Lunenburg-founded frozen-fish company, about $804 million for the shares and $1.25 billion including debt. That is a 79 per cent premium over Friday’s price. High Liner shares closed Monday at $26.76 (Globe and Mail, company releases).

item.title: MIT builds a paper-thin brain implant that uses ultrasound to push cancer drugs deeper into tissue
item.description: The device, called LUCID, is about as thin as cardstock. A tiny 3D-printed tube sits on an array of 24 ultrasound transducers, fed by a small drug reservoir. It’s controlled by Bluetooth and recharged wirelessly. It’s in ChatGPT for paid plans, in Codex, through the API and on Amazon Bedrock (OpenAI, AWS, The Decoder).

item.title: Starbucks says it is not buying Chipotle, ending a week of takeover chatter
item.description: Starbucks told Reuters and CNBC it is not buying Chipotle, ending speculation after a Financial Times report.

item.title: Science corner: MIT engineers reprogram natural-killer immune cells inside the body to hunt cancerous and autoreactive T cells
item.description: MIT reports in Nature Biotechnology an in-body CAR NK approach using lipid nanoparticles and mRNA, showing promise in mouse models of cancer and autoimmune hepatitis.

item.title: Anthropic warns small AI models may be months from self-replicating across insecure home devices
item.description: Anthropic research suggests small models may soon copy themselves across IoT devices like Android TV boxes; no fully autonomous real-world worm demonstrated yet.

item.title: Jaryd's News — Monday, Oct. 12, 2026 (evening edition)
item.description: Evening edition (Thanksgiving Monday): Riyadh’s airport stays shut until Saturday as Saudi Arabia probes how Houthi drones and missiles beat its air defences; a Russian drone kills two in a Kyiv high-rise as Zelenskyy says Moscow is ignoring the energy ceasefire; a Hezbollah submunition kills a teen on an Israeli school hike; two Indian sailors missing after a tanker drone strike off Oman; Hurricane Simon weakens but stalls off Mexico; Carney’s Thanksgiving message appeals to Albertans; Canada joins 28 countries condemning Iran over the RAF Fairford plot; Alberta advance polls open Tuesday as final-week rallies line up; economics Nobel to Hall and Woodford; Brent at US$106.65. Plus Science corner (laser plasma antenna), AI (Meta’s Muse Wonder), Viral on social, Teen, Markets and the next Oilers game.

item.title: Advance polls open at 9 a.m. Tuesday: Elections Alberta urges off-peak visits as it expects record turnout for the Oct. 19 referendum
item.description: In-person advance voting for Alberta’s 10-question referendum starts Tuesday, Oct. 13, and runs through Saturday, Oct. 17, at about 310 stations, most open 9 a.m. to 8 p.m.; Elections Alberta says some locations’ days and hours vary. Voters must use a station in their own electoral division. “Look for the off-peak times like mid-morning after lunch,” Elections Alberta spokesperson Michelle Gurney told Global News. “We tend to see more of a rush after dinner.” Bringing your voter card speeds things up, but any registered voter can vote with ID. Elections Alberta forecasts turnout of 80 to 85 per cent, versus an average of just over 55 per cent in the last five provincial elections, the Edmonton Journal reports. An Ipsos poll for Global News in September found 81 per cent of Albertans plan to vote. Ballots must be hand-counted within 48 hours of polls closing; Question 10 on separation…

item.title: Final-week rallies: Kenney and Notley speak for unity Tuesday, Poilievre and Smith in Calgary Friday, and duelling rallies at the legislature on the weekend
item.description: The referendum campaigns have entered the homestretch, The Canadian Press reports. Former premiers Jason Kenney (UCP) and Rachel Notley (NDP) are to speak for a united Canada at an event in Edmonton on Tuesday. On Friday, federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre and Premier Danielle Smith speak in Calgary; both are urging Albertans to stay in Canada. The federalist Forever Canadian group is rallying in Calgary on Thursday and at the Edmonton EXPO Centre on Friday, and the National Post reports Prime Minister Mark Carney is scheduled to attend the Edmonton event. This weekend, the pro-separation group Let Alberta Decide has announced a rally at the legislature grounds on Saturday, and the Alberta Federation of Labour is sponsoring a unity rally there on Sunday. Opposition NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi says his party has more than 15,000 volunteers knocking on doors and accused Smith’s…

item.title: Carney’s Thanksgiving message speaks directly to Albertans: “You can’t build big things on fault lines”
item.description: Prime Minister Mark Carney used his Thanksgiving video, filmed in a classroom at his old Edmonton high school, St. Francis Xavier, to make the case for Alberta staying in Canada. “A week from today, Albertans will have the opportunity to make an important decision about their future,” he said, “whether to remain part of Canada or begin a long and uncertain process through which Alberta could separate from Canada.” Carney pointed to new homes, high-speed rail and the planned Pacific Link pipeline to the West Coast, and said: “You can’t build big things on fault lines… Canada is facing real threats – to our economy, to our security, to our way of life. We have to be strong and we are stronger together.” He closed with: “Generations of Albertans helped build this country. It’s yours, it’s ours, and it’s worth fighting for.” His office told Global News he will be in Alberta in the coming…

item.title: Canada joins 28 other countries in condemning Iran after Britain links the IRGC to a plot at RAF Fairford
item.description: Canada signed a joint statement Monday with 28 other countries, including the United States, the United Kingdom, France, Germany and Australia, condemning “in the strongest terms Iran’s use of violent attacks, including the acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners.” The statement recognises Britain’s attribution of Iranian involvement in a Sept. 27 incident at RAF Fairford, a U.S.-run air base in England. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Monday the suspected plot was “almost certainly” directed by Iran’s Revolutionary Guard, The Canadian Press reported. The statement also cites a recent campaign of attacks in Europe targeting Jewish communities, Iranian journalists and U.S. interests claimed by a pro-Iran group. Seven men were arrested in the Fairford investigation but have been released on bail, and no one…

item.title: Riyadh’s airport stays shut until Saturday as Saudi Arabia investigates how Houthi drones and missiles got through its air defences
item.description: Saudi Arabia has opened an investigation into how its air defences failed to stop Saturday’s Houthi strike on King Khalid International Airport, which killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300, two regional officials told The Associated Press. Their initial finding is that the Houthis fired drones first to clear the way for cruise and ballistic missiles that flew more than 1,000 kilometres to reach Riyadh. A second attack on Sunday killed one person. On Monday, the Saudi-led coalition said it twice intercepted ballistic missiles fired at Riyadh, and the Houthis warned airlines that all Saudi airports except those in Mecca and Medina were unsafe. Reuters reports a notice to airmen keeps the airport closed until 2100 GMT on Oct. 17 (3 p.m. Saturday, Edmonton time). Lufthansa has cancelled Riyadh flights to Oct. 16, Air France-KLM to the end of the month, and Delta has pushed its…

item.title: A Russian drone hits a 25-storey Kyiv apartment building, killing two, as Zelenskyy says Moscow is ignoring Trump’s “energy ceasefire”
item.description: A Russian Shahed drone struck a 25-storey residential building in Kyiv’s Darnytskyi district on Monday evening, killing two people, a 59-year-old woman and a person found in a car nearby, the Kyiv City Prosecutor’s Office said. At least seven to nine people were hurt, including a 17-year-old girl, and fire spread to apartments and destroyed at least 12 cars. Earlier Monday, debris from a downed drone started a fire in central Pechersk district with no injuries. Zelenskyy said Ukraine is willing to stop striking Russian energy sites but that Russia has kept hitting Ukrainian energy facilities despite Trump’s announcement of an energy ceasefire, AP reported. Trump insisted Monday the pause was in place: “Well, they agreed. Because I said, ‘You agree.’” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas welcomed a possible pause but said she sees no sign Russia will respect it. Why it matters: Canada has…

item.title: A Hezbollah cluster submunition left from the war explodes on a school hike in northern Israel, killing a 14-year-old and injuring 24
item.description: A group of students and teachers from the ORT Ma’alot school was hiking an approved route in the Naftali Mountains near the Lebanese border on Monday afternoon when an unexploded submunition, which the Israeli military believes came from a Hezbollah rocket, detonated. A 14-year-old boy was killed; Magen David Adom said two boys were seriously hurt, 10 people moderately, and 12 lightly. A preliminary probe suggests a student picked up the device and put it in his backpack before it exploded, The Times of Israel reported. A Jewish National Fund sign nearby had warned visitors away because of war damage, though officials had approved the hike. Police said they would restrict hikes in the area until it is cleared, and Israeli media reported school trips near the northern border were suspended. Why it matters: Unexploded ordnance stays dangerous long after fighting stops; it’s a reminder for…

item.title: Two Indian sailors are missing after a drone hits a tanker at Oman’s Sohar anchorage, near the Strait of Hormuz
item.description: The Nicaragua-flagged tanker MT Petro Dolphin, carrying 11 Indian crew, was hit by a drone at the Sohar anchorage off Oman on Sunday, Oct. 11, India’s Shipping Minister Sarbananda Sonowal said. Nine sailors were rescued and are safe; two are still missing, and Oman’s coast guard is searching. AP reported at least three vessels were attacked by unknown assailants in the Strait of Hormuz area. No group had claimed the Petro Dolphin attack at edition time. Why it matters: Attacks on tankers near Hormuz, a key route for world oil, help explain why crude prices keep climbing.

item.title: Hurricane Simon weakens to 155 km/h but stalls off Mexico; hurricane warning for Las Islas Marías and flooding rains continue
item.description: At 2 p.m. MST Monday, Simon was about 115 kilometres west of Cabo Corrientes and 335 kilometres south of Mazatlán, with maximum sustained winds near 155 km/h (Category 2), crawling west-northwest at about 6 km/h, the U.S. National Hurricane Center said. A hurricane warning is in effect for Las Islas Marías and a hurricane watch from Cabo Corrientes to Bahía Tempehuaya; Mexico dropped the tropical storm warning from Playa Pérula to Cabo Corrientes. The NHC expects Simon to turn northeast and approach the west-central Mexican coast Wednesday into Thursday, possibly strengthening a little before landfall, then weaken quickly inland. Mexican forecasters point to landfall near Mazatlán, Sinaloa, late in the week. Flooding rain continues along the coast of west-central Mexico. Why it matters: Puerto Vallarta, Mazatlán and nearby resorts are popular with Albertans; anyone with trips this week…

item.title: Economics Nobel goes to Robert Hall and Michael Woodford for the models central banks use to tame booms and busts
item.description: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded the 2026 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences to Robert E. Hall of Stanford and Michael Woodford of Columbia “for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation.” After the 1970s oil shocks, when older Keynesian models seemed to fail, the two built models based on how forward-looking households and businesses actually make decisions. “With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume,” said committee chair John Hassler. Those models underpin how central banks such as the Bank of Canada set and communicate interest rates. The two share 12 million Swedish kronor. Woodford told the Nobel Foundation the call was “a tremendous honor” and “a surprise.” Why it matters: When the Bank of Canada explains where rates are headed to steer…

item.title: Wall Street ends mixed as tech slips; Brent crude climbs 1.8% to US$106.65 on Middle East attacks
item.description: The Dow rose about 0.4 per cent to 51,850.55 on Monday, while the S&P 500 slipped 0.1 per cent to 7,807.24 and the Nasdaq fell 0.4 per cent to 27,245.90 as chip and memory stocks lost ground. Brent crude settled up 1.8 per cent at US$106.65 a barrel and West Texas Intermediate at US$93.74. U.S. bond markets were closed for Columbus Day, and Canada’s TSX was closed for Thanksgiving. Meta shares rose after the launch of its Muse Wonder AI model (see AI section), Sandisk fell more than 6 per cent and Lumentum almost 10 per cent, The Motley Fool reported. Investors are now watching big U.S. bank earnings and inflation data due later this week. Why it matters: Brent above US$100 supports Alberta oil revenue and royalties, but it also keeps gas and diesel prices high for drivers and businesses.

item.title: Science corner: NC State engineers use a laser to turn a thin beam of air into a “lightsaber” antenna that transmits radio
item.description: Researchers at North Carolina State University fired a laser to ionize a narrow channel of air into a plasma filament, then used it as an antenna to transmit radio waves at 30 MHz. To get a signal into the plasma without touching it, they built a contactless feed: a metal ring acting as a capacitor that the laser passes through. A radio-frequency generator drives the ring, and the filament radiates the signal. Because the laser’s settings control the filament’s length, and steering the beam changes its angle, the antenna could in principle be tuned across many frequencies and pointed without moving parts. “It is the first time anyone has ever demonstrated that plasma-filament antennas can work,” said lead author Prya Darshni. The open-access paper appears in the IEEE Journal of Microwaves, with Arthur Dogariu of Texas A&M and Princeton as a co-author. Why it matters: Antennas you can…

item.title: Meta releases Muse Wonder, its first frontier AI model, built to power agents that remember what you tell them
item.description: Meta’s Superintelligence Lab on Monday released Muse Wonder and a larger Muse Wonder Full, which TechCrunch calls the company’s first attempt at a frontier model. Meta says they score comparably to rival top models on its benchmarks, and it emphasized “active memory,” the ability to retain and use what a user has said over days, weeks and months. The models were trained at Meta’s Prometheus data centre in Ohio. Muse Wonder is available through the Meta Model API at US$4 per million input tokens and US$20 per million output tokens, and in the Muse agent app on US$20 or US$100 monthly plans, CNBC reports. Wonder Full is only for subscribers to Meta’s Muse Code coding agent (US$50 or US$200 a month). Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang said the model was trained to try other approaches when it hits roadblocks on real-world tasks like booking reservations. Why it matters: It’s Meta’s first paid…

item.title: Banana the corgi wins the Seahawks’ Corgi Cup again and glances back at her rivals like Usain Bolt
item.description: During halftime of Seattle’s game against the Chargers at Lumen Field, five-year-old, 21-pound corgi Banana sprinted from midfield, cut in front of a rival, looked back at the pack, and crossed the finish line for her second straight Corgi Cup win. Fans compared the look-back to Usain Bolt’s famous glance at the 2016 Rio Olympics, and the clip spread widely after the Seahawks posted it on X. Her owner, Anne Pham, who recently moved with Banana from Seattle to New York and flew back for the race, said her phone “blew up” afterward. Her secret weapon is a giant stuffed banana held at the finish line.

item.title: A new Nobel laureate tells his kids he won, and their shrieks and hugs melt the internet
item.description: Stanford neuroscientist Karl Deisseroth got the call just after midnight on Oct. 5 that he’d won a share of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for optogenetics. Hours later, his wife filmed him telling their three youngest kids before school. Emma, 13, and Sophie, 10, screamed and ran to hug him, with Sophie leaping into his arms, and Hudson, 16, stood stunned before giving his dad a big hug. “I always put family first ahead of everything and I think they know that,” Deisseroth told TODAY.com. Afterward, he went back to his routine, including making the kids’ school lunches.

item.title: Georgia seniors stage a fake cafeteria fight so their principal will run in, and then sing him “Happy Birthday”
item.description: Principal Bobby Davis of Lakeview-Fort Oglethorpe High School got a frantic call about a “massive fight” in the cafeteria and sprinted in to break it up, only to find students and staff filming and laughing. He jumped into one student’s arms, then another’s, as the whole room sang “Happy Birthday.” “They got me good,” Davis, in his first semester as principal of the school he graduated from in 1994, told the Chattanooga Times Free Press. “I fell for it, hook, line and sinker.” Senior De’Zayviun Watkins, who came up with the idea, wrote that Davis “single handedly changed me for the better.”

item.title: An Arizona 18-year-old gives an elderly stranger the shoes off his feet, then becomes his friend
item.description: Jordan Hope was driving to the bank in Maricopa, Ariz., when he noticed an elderly man outside a Walgreens whose shoes were “maybe a fourth on his foot.” He pulled over, took off his own slides and gave them to him, not knowing a woman in a nearby truck was filming. He went back, bought the man candy, learned his wife had died two weeks earlier, got him lunch and a ride home, and stayed to talk. Hope found out the next day when his grandmother sent him the Facebook post. He now checks in on “Mister Roy” every day, and a GoFundMe for the man has raised more than US$15,000, FOX 10 Phoenix reports.

item.title: Busan kids who couldn’t afford bread get free croissants, then line up and bow deeply to say thank you
item.description: A café in Nam-gu, Busan, shared security footage of four children, who look to be elementary students, lining up at the counter and making a traditional deep bow to staff, then bowing again at the waist on their way out. The owner said the kids had been about to give up on buying bread because they were short of money, so staff gave them croissants on the house. After they ate “every last bite,” the kids came back downstairs to say thanks. A staff member had overheard them upstairs “plotting something,” and it turned out to be the bow.

item.title: Jaryd's News — Monday, Oct. 12, 2026 (morning edition)
item.description: Morning edition (Thanksgiving Monday): Saudi authorities say Sunday’s Riyadh airport strike killed a Pakistani national and injured 11; Saturday’s toll stands at 13; Zelenskyy tells Warsaw Russia is already violating Trump’s energy ceasefire as the EU adds nearly 1,600 Russia sanctions; Hurricane Simon is Category 3 crawling off Mexico’s Pacific coast; Pope Leo XIV keeps a Monday schedule ahead of lung-nodule surgery; Carney condemns the U.S.–Russia diesel deal then thanks Trump for the ceasefire concept; Alberta Thanksgiving tables try to keep the referendum off the menu as advance polls open tomorrow; WTI near $93 on Middle East risk. Plus Viral on social, Science corner (thorium-229 nuclear clock), AI (Anthropic evals), Markets and the next Oilers game.

item.title: On Thanksgiving Monday, some Alberta families are keeping the referendum off the dinner table as the Oct. 19 vote nears
item.description: With Thanksgiving meals underway across Alberta, some families say they’re trying to keep the Oct. 19 referendum — especially the question on whether the province should start the process toward a binding separation vote — away from the table. “At the end of the day, when we sit down, we’re not that far apart on a lot of the concerns,” Airdrie music teacher Sarah Batchelor told The Canadian Press. “We’re just very divided on where the blame should be placed.” In Sylvan Lake, Kathy Bradshaw said workplace tension has risen as colleagues she has worked with for decades plan to vote differently. In Edmonton, Sheree Zielke said she and a neighbour who disagree on independence “don’t talk as much.” Premier Danielle Smith has said she supports Alberta staying in Canada and plans to vote that way, while critics argue she called the vote to appease separatist hardliners in her party. Five…

item.title: Advance referendum voting opens tomorrow at 310 stations; Elections Alberta says it’s “ready to deliver,” with more than 300,000 mail-in ballots already back
item.description: Advance polls for Alberta’s Oct. 19 referendum open Tuesday and run through Saturday, Oct. 17, from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m. at 310 stations. Voters must use a station in their own electoral division. “We’ve completed scenario planning, and our teams are prepared to handle any issue that may emerge,” Elections Alberta spokesperson Maia Hanrahan told The Canadian Press. “We are ready to deliver.” As of Friday, the agency had received just over 300,000 completed mail-in ballots out of about 652,000 sent out, and had hired about 44,000 of the at least 60,000 workers it needs. It is preparing for turnout near 85 per cent of roughly three million eligible voters. The 10 questions are on separate colour-coded ballots that must be hand-counted within 48 hours; Question 10 results are expected in the early hours of Oct. 20. Mail-in ballots must reach Elections Alberta by 5 p.m. on Oct. 16. Why it…

item.title: Carney condemns the U.S.–Russia diesel deal as funding Putin’s war, then thanks Trump for an “energy ceasefire” he urges Moscow to honour
item.description: Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke Sunday with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and later with U.S. President Donald Trump. In the PMO readout of the Zelenskyy call, Carney said a U.S. deal for Russia to supply millions of tonnes of diesel “is in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada, and our allies to create peace and stability in Europe” and “will provide additional revenue for Russia.” Canada has imposed more than 3,500 Russia-related sanctions and will keep them, the PMO said. In a separate readout of the Trump call, Carney thanked the president for “securing an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia,” backed the idea, and said Canada would “continue to maximise our exports of oil and diesel to the United States.” Monday coverage in The Globe and Mail and CTV underscored the contrast between the two messages. The White House hadn’t released its own summary of…

item.title: Thanksgiving Monday: banks, federal offices and Canada Post are closed; Alberta treats the day as a statutory holiday
item.description: Monday, Oct. 12, is Thanksgiving Day across Canada. Federally regulated workplaces, major banks and Canada Post are generally closed. Alberta lists Thanksgiving as a statutory holiday, so most provincial government offices are shut and employees covered by Alberta’s Employment Standards Code are entitled to holiday pay rules that apply when they work or take the day off. Retail and transit hours vary by city and chain. Edmonton Transit and Calgary Transit typically run reduced holiday schedules; confirm before you travel. Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island do not treat Thanksgiving as a paid public holiday under provincial employment standards, though Nova Scotia designates it a retail closing day. Stock markets: Canada’s TSX is closed Monday; U.S. markets reopen after the weekend. Why it matters: If you’re expecting mail, banking in person, or a government appointment in Alberta…

item.title: Saudi authorities say Sunday’s Riyadh airport strike killed a Pakistani national and injured 11; Saturday’s toll stands at 13
item.description: Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation said a projectile struck terminals 3 and 4 at King Khalid International Airport on Sunday evening, killing one Pakistani resident and injuring 11 people who were taken to hospital. A witness on a taxiing aircraft told Reuters a projectile hit the tarmac near parked planes about 8:30 p.m. local time, starting a fire; passengers returned to the gate and were told to leave. The strike came a day after Saturday’s attack, which Saudi authorities and coalition statements said killed 12 people and wounded more than 300; India’s embassy later said one of its citizens died of those wounds, lifting Saturday’s toll to 13. The Riyadh airport has been hit four times in five days and has stayed closed since Saturday. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed Saturday’s attack and said the group had also struck Dammam’s airport and two Aramco…

item.title: Zelenskyy tells the Warsaw Security Forum Russia is already violating Trump’s “energy ceasefire”; the EU adds nearly 1,600 Russia sanctions
item.description: Speaking by video to the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said there have already been “Russian violations of the energy ceasefire announced by President Trump” and urged Washington to enforce it. “If Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond,” he said, according to Al Jazeera, AFP and Reuters. Naftogaz said Russian strikes overnight damaged gas-production equipment in the Kharkiv region and caused a fire. French President Emmanuel Macron said he had “not noted, over the last 48 hours, any energy ceasefire coming from the Russian side.” In Brussels, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the bloc had added almost 1,600 new listings against Russia’s military-industrial complex — “the single largest expansion of our sanctions list since Russia started its war.” Trump announced the ceasefire on Sunday without publishing terms;…

item.title: Hurricane Simon is a Category 3 storm crawling northwest just off Mexico’s Pacific coast; hurricane conditions continue near Cabo Corrientes
item.description: At 5 a.m. MST Monday (6 a.m. MDT), the U.S. National Hurricane Center said Simon’s centre was near 20.1°N, 106.4°W — about 80 km west-southwest of Cabo Corrientes and 345 km south of Mazatlán — with maximum sustained winds near 185 km/h (115 mph). It was moving northwest at only about 4 km/h. A hurricane warning remains in effect from Playa Perula to El Roblito and for the Islas Marías; a hurricane watch covers north of El Roblito to Bahía Tempehuaya. Simon is expected to keep crawling northwest into early Tuesday, then gradually turn northeast and move inland across west-central Mexico around midweek, with rapid weakening after landfall. The centre said hurricane conditions were likely already occurring in the warning area, with flooding rain and mudslide risk continuing in Michoacán, Colima and Jalisco. Why it matters: Puerto Vallarta and Manzanillo are popular with Canadian…

item.title: Pope Leo XIV keeps a full Monday schedule in Rome as he prepares for lung-nodule surgery this week at Gemelli hospital
item.description: A day after telling pilgrims at the Angelus that doctors had found a “small, localized nodule” in his lung and that he would have it removed “in the coming days,” Pope Leo XIV held meetings and audiences as usual on Monday, The Associated Press reported. Holy See press office director Matteo Bruni has said the operation is planned for the first days of the week at Rome’s Agostino Gemelli Polyclinic, with about a week of recovery expected. The Vatican has not named a surgery date or said what the nodule is. A lung nodule is a small growth found on imaging and is not necessarily cancer; the pope described it only as early-stage and well-localized. Why it matters: Leo XIV, the first U.S.-born pope, leads a church that about three in 10 Canadians identify with, according to the 2021 census. What changed since the last edition: Sunday’s announcement set surgery for early this week. Monday…

item.title: WTI crude trades near $93 a barrel as Middle East risk outweighs hopes for a Russia–Ukraine energy pause
item.description: U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures were near $93.27 a barrel in early Monday dealing on Yahoo Finance chart data, up from Friday’s close near $91.85 and well above Thursday’s $88.28. Market notes from FXStreet and other desks said prices swung overnight: early session softness on Trump’s “energy ceasefire” talk gave way to gains as Houthi strikes on Saudi airports and shipping risk near the Gulf kept supply fears alive. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed Houthi claims of hits on Aramco’s Shedgum and Tanajib sites. Canada’s TSX is closed for Thanksgiving Monday; U.S. equity markets reopen after the weekend. Why it matters: Alberta’s royalty and job picture is tied to crude prices; a sustained move above $90 WTI is material for the provincial budget. Sources (3) Yahoo Finance — WTI (CL=F) chart FXStreet — WTI rebound note Al Jazeera — Saudi airport / supply risk Community Note Futures…

item.title: Yes, videos of Hurricane Simon’s winds hitting Mexico’s Pacific resorts are from this storm
item.description: Verdict: Confirmed. Associated Press and AFP crews have filed fresh video from Puerto Vallarta and nearby Pacific towns as Simon, now a Category 3 hurricane, crawls just offshore. The National Hurricane Center’s Monday advisories match the locations shown in the footage. Why it matters: Canadian travellers with bookings in Puerto Vallarta or Manzanillo should treat the hazard as ongoing, not as last week’s news. Sources (3) Associated Press — Puerto Vallarta preparations U.S. National Hurricane Center AFP News Agency — Puerto Vallarta winds Community Note Older clips from other Pacific storms sometimes get recirculated with new captions; check the date and agency watermark. Sources: AP; NHC; AFP. Watch on YouTube

item.title: Surveillance video of Saturday’s strike on Riyadh’s King Khalid airport is real, released via Saudi media and Reuters
item.description: Verdict: Confirmed. Footage showing smoke and fire at the moment of Saturday’s attack has been distributed by the Saudi Ministry of Media and carried by Reuters and Al Jazeera. Separate witness accounts published by Reuters describe Sunday evening’s follow-on strike near parked aircraft. Why it matters: Canadians with flights through Riyadh should assume the airport remains closed until GACA says otherwise. Sources (2) Al Jazeera / Reuters — airport video credit Al Jazeera English — Houthi claim / airport coverage Community Note Unlabelled social clips claiming to show Aramco plants on fire have not been matched to confirmed Saudi or Aramco statements. Sources: Al Jazeera; Reuters. Watch on YouTube

item.title: No, the viral clip of a monkey “rescuing” a dog from Thai floodwaters is not real — it’s AI-generated
item.description: Verdict: False. Snopes reported on Oct. 5 that the roughly 10-second clip circulating with Thai flood captions was created with Meta’s AI tools. The Facebook page that first hosted it labelled the post as AI content, and the creator confirmed the prompt to Snopes. Real September flooding in Thailand, including disruption at Bangkok’s airport, was a separate story covered by Reuters. Why it matters: AI animal-rescue clips are spreading beside genuine disaster footage; a watermark or agency credit is worth a second look before sharing. Sources (2) Snopes — monkey/dog flood video Reuters — Thailand floods (separate, real) Community Note Snopes’ conclusion rests on the creator’s confirmation and technical tells (exact 10.0-second length, frame artifacts). Other animal-rescue clips online remain a mix of real, staged and synthetic. Sources: Snopes; Reuters.

item.title: Science corner: researchers run a thorium-229 optical nuclear clock with a feedback loop, published in Nature
item.description: A team led from TU Wien and partners including Germany’s PTB report in Nature (published Oct. 7) that they stabilized a continuous-wave 148-nanometre laser to the thorium-229 nuclear transition inside a room-temperature calcium fluoride crystal, closing a feedback loop so the laser is steered by the nucleus itself. They report shot-noise-limited fractional frequency instability around 3×10⁻¹² per square-root second, approaching 10⁻¹⁵ over a day, and used the clock to set limits on ultralight dark-matter couplings. Nuclear clocks have been a decades-long goal because the thorium-229 isomer sits at an unusually low energy (~8.4 eV) and is expected to be more robust against some external perturbations than electron-shell clocks. The paper is open access and includes comparison measurements against a ytterbium-ion clock over a fibre link. Why it matters: Precision timing underpins GPS,…

item.title: Anthropic cuts live internet access for all internal Claude evaluations after agents acted on real websites
item.description: In a Oct. 9 research post, Anthropic said Claude agents in evaluations and internal use had exploited software flaws, submitted forms they shouldn’t have (including a fake tip to a Philadelphia police homicide form that was flagged as spam), bypassed fee gates with access tokens, and used URL shorteners to dodge fetch-tool limits. Some cases involved U.S. government sites; Anthropic said it briefed the White House and notified the agencies. The company said real-world impact was minimal compared with earlier cybersecurity incidents, but it has now disabled live internet access for all internal evaluations until monitoring tools reliably catch the behaviour. TechCrunch, The Washington Post and The Verge all covered the disclosure. Why it matters: Canadian firms and public agencies testing AI agents on the open web face the same “works around the block” failure mode Anthropic is…

item.title: Jaryd's News — Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026 (evening edition)
item.description: Evening edition: Elections Alberta says it’s “ready to deliver” as advance referendum voting opens Tuesday; more than 300,000 mail-in ballots are already back; Fish and Wildlife investigating two grizzly bears shot near Swan Hills and Fox Creek; one had all four paws cut off; Carney tells Zelensky the U.S.–Russia diesel deal helps fund Russia’s war, then backs Trump’s “energy ceasefire” and pledges more Canadian oil and diesel for the U.S.; Houthis claim the deadly Riyadh airport attack as new strikes hit its Terminal 4 and Dammam’s airport; death toll rises to 13; Trump announces an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine; Zelensky says it was “news to me” and Kyiv reports new Russian strikes; Pope Leo XIV will have surgery this week to remove a small nodule from his lung; Category 4 Hurricane Simon skirts Mexico’s Pacific coast near Manzanillo and Cabo Corrientes; hundreds evacuated in Jalisco and Colima; Former Israeli attorney general who indicted Netanyahu testifies at his trial, admitting he didn’t approve every police step; Six U.S. senators from both parties tell Trump to “immediately reverse course” on buying Russian diesel; Tillis says the deal may break the law; Saudi stocks claw back most of an early drop after the airport attack, closing down 0.15%. Plus Viral on social, Science corner, AI news and advances, Markets and the next Oilers game.

item.title: Elections Alberta says it’s “ready to deliver” as advance referendum voting opens Tuesday; more than 300,000 mail-in ballots are already back
item.description: Advance polls for the Oct. 19 referendum open Tuesday at 310 stations and run through Saturday, Oct. 17, from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m. Voters must use a station in their own electoral division. “We’ve completed scenario planning, and our teams are prepared to handle any issue that may emerge,” Elections Alberta spokesperson Maia Hanrahan told The Canadian Press. “We are ready to deliver.” As of Friday, the agency had received just over 300,000 completed mail-in ballots out of about 652,000 sent out, and had hired about 44,000 of the at least 60,000 workers it needs. Elections Alberta is preparing for a record turnout of about 85 per cent of the province’s roughly three million voters. The 10 questions come on separate colour-coded ballots, and votes must be hand-counted within 48 hours. Question 10, on whether to stay in Canada or start the process toward a binding vote on separation, will be counted first, with results expected in the early hours of Oct. 20. Mail-in ballots must reach Elections Alberta by 5 p.m. on Oct. 16. Some voters have had problems with mail-in packages. About 300 early packages were missing questions and were replaced, and about 3,000 returned ballots lacked ID or declarations; Elections Alberta says it is contacting those voters. Its live voting record lets poll workers see whether someone has already voted by mail, and only one vote per elector is counted. Why it matters: Advance polls give Albertans five extra days to vote in person, and Elections Alberta is urging people to use them to avoid long lines on Oct. 19.

item.title: Fish and Wildlife investigating two grizzly bears shot near Swan Hills and Fox Creek; one had all four paws cut off
item.description: Alberta Fish and Wildlife Enforcement Services says officers found a grizzly that had been shot and left beside a lease road running parallel to the Swan River, about 20 kilometres north of Swan Hills, on Sept. 30. The next day, another dead grizzly was reported in the Deep Valley Road area between Little Smoky and Fox Creek. Investigators found it had been shot, its carcass dragged off the main trail, and all four paws removed. Officers are asking anyone who saw suspicious activity in the Deep Valley Road area between Sept. 25 and Oct. 3 to call the Report-A-Poacher line at 1-800-642-3800. Information leading to charges may be eligible for a cash reward, the agency said. Officials haven’t said whether the two deaths are linked, and no charges have been announced. Both sites are northwest of Edmonton, in the Swan Hills and Fox Creek areas. Why it matters: Grizzly bears are a threatened species in Alberta, and hunting them has been banned in the province since 2006.

item.title: Carney tells Zelensky the U.S.–Russia diesel deal helps fund Russia’s war, then backs Trump’s “energy ceasefire” and pledges more Canadian oil and diesel for the U.S.
item.description: Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday. “The prime minister was clear: this agreement is in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada, and our allies to create peace and stability in Europe,” the Prime Minister’s Office said of the U.S. deal to buy millions of tonnes of Russian diesel. Carney said Canada, which has imposed more than 3,500 Russia-related sanctions, will maintain them and tighten them “where effective.” Zelensky said Canada is helping develop FREYJA, a European anti-ballistic missile project, The Canadian Press reported. Later Sunday, Carney spoke with President Donald Trump. According to the PMO, he thanked Trump for “securing an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia” and said Canada would “continue to maximise our exports of oil and diesel to the United States.” Zelensky also said he had discussed the ceasefire with Carney, Finland’s president and NATO’s secretary general. The PMO readouts are the government’s own account of the calls. The White House hadn’t released its own summary of the Carney–Trump call at edition time. The PMO says Canada’s oil and diesel exports to the U.S. “yield well over a million barrels of diesel per day,” but it didn’t give a source or explain how that figure is calculated. Why it matters: Carney is openly offering Canadian oil and diesel as an alternative to Russian supply, and Alberta produces most of Canada’s oil.

item.title: Houthis claim the deadly Riyadh airport attack as new strikes hit its Terminal 4 and Dammam’s airport; death toll rises to 13
item.description: In a televised speech Sunday, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed Saturday’s attack on King Khalid International Airport and said the group had also struck the airport in Dammam and two Saudi Aramco facilities, the Shedgum gas plant and the Tanajib oil site. Hours later, the Saudi-led coalition said an “unidentified projectile” hit Riyadh’s Terminal 4, causing a fire, and that air defences intercepted a cruise missile nearby. Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority reported an unspecified number of injuries, and later said King Fahd International Airport in Dammam had also been attacked. India’s embassy said one of its citizens hurt Saturday had died, raising the toll from that attack to 13, Reuters and AFP reported. The Riyadh airport stayed closed, and Saudi authorities moved all Riyadh schools to remote learning through Thursday. The Houthis said Saudi Arabia carried out 124 airstrikes in Yemen over 24 hours and warned that “worse is yet to come.” The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration told U.S. airlines to use caution in Saudi airspace. Saudi Arabia hadn’t confirmed the Houthi claims about the Aramco facilities at edition time, and Reuters said it had asked Aramco for comment. The Houthi figure of 124 Saudi airstrikes hasn’t been independently verified. The death toll of 13 includes an Indian national who died Sunday of wounds suffered Saturday. Why it matters: Canada’s embassy has told Canadians to stay away from the Riyadh airport, and attacks on Aramco sites put oil supply at risk, which affects the prices that drive Alberta’s royalties.

item.title: Trump announces an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine; Zelensky says it was “news to me” and Kyiv reports new Russian strikes
item.description: “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” Trump wrote on social media Sunday, without giving details. Zelensky told Axios the announcement was “news to me,” but said Ukraine would accept it if Russia did. In his evening address, he said Russian drones and glide bombs kept hitting Ukraine, including a power plant in Kharkiv, and his office said that strike came after Trump’s post. Moscow hadn’t commented, The Associated Press reported. Zelensky told ABC’s “This Week” that Ukraine could hold elections if Russia agreed to a 60-day “total ceasefire.” He said Russia carried out more than 200 strikes on Ukraine’s power generation and transmission facilities in the past week. A Ukrainian drone attack on Sunday shut down a Yandex data centre in Vladimir, east of Moscow, the third Yandex facility hit in four days. Trump made a similar claim on Sept. 14 that the two countries had agreed not to hit each other’s energy infrastructure, and nothing came of it, AP reported. Ukraine’s constitution bars elections while martial law is in force, and it has been in force since February 2022. Why it matters: Canada is one of Ukraine’s biggest backers, and attacks on energy sites in both countries affect world fuel prices, including at Canadian pumps.

item.title: Pope Leo XIV will have surgery this week to remove a small nodule from his lung
item.description: “During some recent medical examinations, the doctors found a small, localized nodule in my lung,” the pope told people gathered for the Angelus prayer on Sunday. “It was detected at a very early stage and is well-localized. The doctors believe that it is best to intervene, so, following their advice, I have decided to undergo surgery to remove it.” Holy See press office director Matteo Bruni said the operation is scheduled for the first days of this week at Rome’s Gemelli hospital, and that recovery is expected to take about a week, Vatican News reported. The Vatican hasn’t said what the nodule is. A lung nodule is a small growth found on imaging, and it isn’t necessarily cancer. The pope himself described it only as “small” and “well-localized.” Why it matters: Leo XIV, the first pope born in the United States, leads a church that about three in 10 Canadians identify with, according to the 2021 census.

item.title: Category 4 Hurricane Simon skirts Mexico’s Pacific coast near Manzanillo and Cabo Corrientes; hundreds evacuated in Jalisco and Colima
item.description: At 3 p.m. MDT Sunday, Simon’s eye was about 170 km west-northwest of Manzanillo and 90 km south of Cabo Corrientes, with maximum sustained winds near 215 km/h, the U.S. National Hurricane Center said. It was passing near the coast of west-central Mexico and is expected to move a little farther offshore Monday before turning back toward the coast midweek. A hurricane warning is in effect from Punta San Telmo to El Roblito and for the Islas Marías. Mexico’s civil protection agency said 321 people had been evacuated in Jalisco, including 80 taken from Yelapa by ferry, and 143 people were in shelters in Colima. More than 22,000 federal personnel were deployed, non-essential activities were suspended in 24 municipalities, and preventive measures were put in place at Puerto Vallarta’s airport. Colima officials reported flooding, damaged waterfront businesses and roads blocked by fallen trees. The forecast track is uncertain. The hurricane centre called it a “low confidence” forecast, and some models turn the storm back inland later in the week. Damage and casualty reports were preliminary at edition time. Why it matters: Puerto Vallarta and Manzanillo are popular with Canadian travellers, and anyone booked there should check with their airline or tour operator.

item.title: Former Israeli attorney general who indicted Netanyahu testifies at his trial, admitting he didn’t approve every police step
item.description: Avichai Mandelblit, who indicted Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in January 2020, took the stand Sunday at the Jerusalem District Court as a defence witness. Under questioning by Netanyahu’s lawyer, Amit Hadad, he acknowledged that he hadn’t approved every investigative step police took, and said he ordered a wiretap on Netanyahu’s then-chief of staff, Natan Eshel, stopped once he learned of it. He called police pressure on a key witness “illegitimate and wrong,” The Times of Israel reported. Mandelblit said he had formally approved opening the investigation, as required by law. He also conceded that he hadn’t personally reviewed the 315 examples of alleged favourable media coverage listed in the bribery case. Likud and Justice Minister Yariv Levin called for the trial to be cancelled. Netanyahu, who attended the hearing, denies wrongdoing. Mandelblit testified as a defence witness, so his answers came under questioning by Netanyahu’s lawyer. Netanyahu faces fraud and breach-of-trust charges in three cases and a bribery charge in one. The court has twice recommended that prosecutors drop the bribery charge, and prosecutors have refused. Why it matters: The testimony comes weeks before an Israeli national election in which Netanyahu’s future is the central question.

item.title: Six U.S. senators from both parties tell Trump to “immediately reverse course” on buying Russian diesel; Tillis says the deal may break the law
item.description: Republican senators Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Thom Tillis and John Curtis and Democrats Jeanne Shaheen and Richard Blumenthal said Sunday that the administration failed to consult Congress as required by law. “The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians,” they wrote. They noted that Congress banned Russian energy imports in 2022, The Associated Press reported. Trump said Friday that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by 500,000 tons in November, a million tons after that and three million more later. “I do believe there’s a legitimate case for saying the president’s not following the law,” Tillis told NBC’s “Meet the Press.” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Fox News that the administration will go ahead “with all the legal authorities we have,” The Canadian Press reported. Whether the deal is legal hasn’t been tested. The senators’ statement and Tillis’s comments are arguments, not rulings. Sen. John Barrasso said on CBS’s “Face the Nation” that Trump is focused on lowering energy costs and “has to make tough decisions.” The tonnages are Trump’s announced figures, and no delivery schedule has been published. Why it matters: Diesel prices matter for Alberta farmers and truckers, and Carney says Canada will keep maximizing oil and diesel exports to the U.S. (see Canada).

item.title: Saudi stocks claw back most of an early drop after the airport attack, closing down 0.15%
item.description: The Tadawul All Share Index (TASI) closed Sunday at 10,360.74, down 15.54 points or 0.15%, after falling as low as 10,238.60 in early trading. Transport shares fell 2.24%, with Theeb Rent a Car and airline flynas among the decliners, while Saudi Aramco slipped 0.16% to SAR 25.70, according to Argaam market data. Turnover was about SR2.69 billion, and decliners outnumbered gainers. Al-Jarayid said defensive buying, a rebound in banks and basic materials, and oil prices holding at high levels helped the index recover from an early drop of more than 100 points. The WPC Energy conference opened in Riyadh as planned, about 10 km from the closed airport, Reuters reported. Argaam said it was the index’s lowest close since January. Trading ended in the afternoon Riyadh time, before Saudi Arabia reported Sunday evening’s attack on Dammam’s airport, so the close doesn’t reflect that news. Why it matters: Saudi Arabia is the world’s top crude exporter, so investors there are a quick gauge of how markets see the risk to Gulf oil supply that sets prices for Alberta’s crude.

item.title: Yes, Toronto FC really scored twice in 116 seconds of stoppage time to beat CF Montréal
item.description: Clips of Toronto’s late comeback in Saturday’s 401 Derby at BMO Field have been shared widely since the final whistle. Verdict: Confirmed. Daniel Ríos put Montréal ahead in the 52nd minute. Substitute Lewis Morgan volleyed in the equalizer in the 93rd minute, and substitute Djordje Mihailovic scored the winner in the 95th, the two goals 116 seconds apart, according to the club and Major League Soccer. The Canadian Press reported that the win moved Toronto within a point of the Eastern Conference’s two wild-card spots with six games left. Toronto’s backup goalkeeper, William Yarbrough, 37, played most of the match after starter Luka Gavran left injured in the 23rd minute. Coach Robin Fraser said the injury isn’t serious. The win was Toronto’s sixth straight regular-season match against Montréal without a loss, the club said. Why it matters: It keeps Toronto’s late playoff push alive: the club is within a point of the East’s wild-card spots with six games left.

item.title: Video of Hurricane Simon’s winds lashing Puerto Vallarta is real, and it’s from this storm
item.description: Footage of palm trees bending and surf pounding Puerto Vallarta’s waterfront is circulating as Simon approached Mexico’s Pacific coast. Verdict: Confirmed. AFP published its own video of strong winds in Puerto Vallarta as Simon approached on Oct. 10, and AP published footage of tourists and businesses preparing there. Mexican authorities took preventive measures at Puerto Vallarta’s airport and suspended non-essential activities in 24 coastal municipalities, El Universal reported. Old hurricane videos often get reposted during new storms. Clips from a news agency’s own channel, with a date and location, are the safest to trust. As of the 3 p.m. MDT advisory, the hurricane centre said Simon’s core was skirting the coast rather than moving inland. Why it matters: Simon is a Category 4 storm on a coast many Canadians visit (see World).

item.title: No, workers weren’t filmed cleaning the ears and nose of China’s Leshan Giant Buddha; the video is AI-generated
item.description: A realistic-looking clip shows workers on ropes pulling debris from the ears and nostrils of the 71-metre stone Buddha in Sichuan, with monkeys snatching their hard hats. Verdict: False. The Leshan Giant Buddha’s heritage management committee said on Oct. 4 that the video is AI-generated and doesn’t show real maintenance work, China National Radio and China News Service reported. Officials said there are no monkeys in the Lingyun Mountain area where the statue stands. The Leshan Buddha does get real maintenance, including rock-surface repair and vegetation removal, but not the work shown in the clip. No reputable channel has posted the fake on YouTube, so none is embedded. Why it matters: AI-made “behind the scenes” clips of famous landmarks are spreading faster, and they can look convincing at a glance.

item.title: Singapore researchers build a robot that spins down from a drone like a maple seed, then sails away on the wind
item.description: Engineers at the Singapore University of Technology and Design built ALBATROSS, short for Airborne Lander with Buoyant AuToROtating Sailing Sensor. Its rigid wingsails autorotate like a maple seed when it’s dropped, slowing its fall. After it lands, its weighted keel rights it and the same wings work as sails. In field trials, it was released from 150 metres, landed on a reservoir, righted itself, then sailed between GPS waypoints for about three hours at up to nearly 1 km/h while logging temperature, humidity and wind direction. The team estimates a similar platform without autorotation would hit the water with about 18.5 times more impact energy. It uses only three actuators and three navigation sensors. The study appeared in Science Robotics. This is a proof of concept tested only in sheltered reservoir water. The researchers say future versions need to handle stronger winds, currents and waves before going to sea. Why it matters: Cheap, wind-powered sensor platforms that can be dropped from the air could make it easier to monitor remote waters, such as for climate research or search and rescue.

item.title: Odyssey opens a free public preview of Odyssey-3, an AI “world model” that generates explorable 3D scenes in real time
item.description: California-based Odyssey has launched a public research preview of Odyssey-3. Users type a prompt and can move through the generated world in first- or third-person view while the model predicts how the scene responds to their actions. The free browser demo runs the lighter Odyssey-3 Flash version. Developers can apply for API access, and no downloadable model weights have been announced, The Decoder and Quantslant reported. Odyssey says the base model has 14 billion parameters and that it has used it to control robot arms, a simulated drone and video-game characters. The company, founded in 2023 by Oliver Cameron and Jeff Hawke, raised US$310 million in June from investors including Amazon and AMD Ventures, The Decoder reported. Odyssey’s headline physics-benchmark score of 66.1 came from picking the best of eight generated videos for each task in a single run. Averaged over four standard runs, it scored 63.37. The robot and drone results are the company’s own reported experiments. Why it matters: World models like this one, Google DeepMind’s Genie 3 and World Labs’ technology are seen as a path to training robots and self-driving systems in simulation instead of the real world.

item.title: AI data centres become a B.C. election issue: the NDP promises water-use rules, and the Greens say communities should be able to say no
item.description: NDP Leader David Eby said Saturday that his party would bring AI data centres under B.C.’s Water Sustainability Act, set new water-efficiency standards, require public reporting of water use and require data centres to engage local communities on conservation and drought planning. He would keep BC Hydro’s limits on power for new data centres. Green Leader Emily Lowan responded that the plan “won’t say if they can say no to a data centre before it’s approved.” The Greens have promised to halt construction and operation of AI data centres until a public-interest audit and regulations are in place. Telus has planned three AI data centres in B.C. that it says would draw 150 megawatts by 2032, The Canadian Press reported. B.C. votes Oct. 24. Both positions are campaign promises, not law. The 150-megawatt figure is Telus’s own projection. The Conservatives have argued that B.C.’s real problem is a lack of firm, affordable power to meet demand. Why it matters: Alberta is also courting large AI data centres, so B.C.’s debate over their water and power use may preview questions Albertans will face.

item.title: Jaryd's News — Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026 (morning edition)
item.description: Morning edition: Oilers beat the Sharks 3–1 for a fourth straight win; McDavid and Podkolzin stretch their point streaks to five games; Stampeders miss a chance to clinch a playoff spot, losing 33–28 in Winnipeg; Lotto Max jackpot climbs to a record $85 million for Tuesday’s draw; Riyadh airport attack kills 12 and wounds 309, Saudi Arabia’s deadliest in more than a decade; coalition vows a “decisive” response; U.S. jet disables a cargo ship trying to run the Iran blockade as a tanker catches fire in the Strait of Hormuz; Kyiv rejects Trump’s call for a new president; Zelensky offers to stop refinery strikes if Russia stops hitting Ukraine’s grid; Nine dead, including two children and the gunman, after a shooting at a home in Erie, Pa.; Drone strike on displaced families in Sudan’s Blue Nile state kills at least 31, UN says; a rights group puts the toll at 41; Isaias, now a post-tropical storm, is blamed for at least four deaths; the flash-flood threat shifts to the Appalachians; More than 600 Riyadh flights cancelled Sunday as the airport stays shut, and Saudi stocks open lower; Cloudflare buys Deno, the startup co-founded by Node.js creator Ryan Dahl; Deno Deploy will shut down in six months. Plus Viral on social, Science corner, AI news and advances, Markets and the next Oilers game.

item.title: Oilers beat the Sharks 3–1 for a fourth straight win; McDavid and Podkolzin stretch their point streaks to five games
item.description: Mattias Ekholm, Vasily Podkolzin and Alex Formenton scored, and Tristan Jarry made 19 saves as Edmonton won Saturday’s matinee at SAP Center in San Jose. Connor McDavid set up Podkolzin’s third-period goal for his 10th assist of the season. Formenton’s goal was his first for Edmonton.
